local_topics.title: Reinforcement-based weight adjustment with DCIR
local_topics.description: Zhang et al. (2022) introduce a reinforcement mechanism to adapt dynamic classifier weights ω_d after each labeled instance, with a focus on class imbalance. The adjustment is triggered once the true label y_t is known and only if the sample belongs to a minority class according to the damped class imbalance ratio (DCIR). For such samples, each dynamic classifier’s weight is multiplicatively increased if it predicts correctly and decreased if it predicts incorrectly, as formalized in Algorithm 4. This strategy reinforces classifiers that perform well on minority classes, thereby improving performance under imbalance.

local_topics.title: Damped Class Imbalance Ratio (DCIR)
local_topics.description: The DCIR metric quantifies class imbalance in a data stream by considering the number of observations collected so far for each class. For each class κ, DCIR_κ summarizes its relative frequency in a damped manner, and a class is treated as minority when DCIR[y_t] < 1/K. This condition is used to decide when to apply special weight updates in Algorithm 4, focusing learning effort on underrepresented classes. DCIR thus operates as a streaming-aware imbalance indicator guiding active adaptation of the ensemble.

canonical_topic.name: Stream-based Active Learning under Class Imbalance
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses how stream-based active learning ensembles can adapt to class imbalance using reinforcement-style weight updates. After each queried and labeled instance in the stream, dynamic classifier weights are adjusted with a focus on minority classes, reinforcing classifiers that correctly predict rare examples and penalizing those that fail. The damped class imbalance ratio (DCIR) is used as a streaming-aware metric to detect minority classes based on their observed frequencies so far. Only when DCIR indicates that the current label belongs to an underrepresented class are special multiplicative weight updates applied, concentrating learning capacity on difficult, scarce classes. This mechanism provides a principled way to couple active label acquisition in streams with imbalance-aware model adaptation.

local_topics.title: Empirical class probability from committee votes
local_topics.description: The class membership probabilities are estimated empirically from committee predictions using the pBAG function. For each pixel and class ω, pBAG is computed as the relative frequency with which committee members assign that class, implemented via the Kronecker delta operator δ to count votes. The numerator counts how many times a pixel is classified as ω across k models, normalized by the total number of predictions across all Ni predicted classes. This provides an empirical probability distribution over classes for each unlabeled sample.

local_topics.title: Normalized entropy query-by-bagging heuristic
local_topics.description: The normalized entropy query-by-bagging (nEQB) heuristic selects unlabeled pixels by maximizing a normalized entropy measure of committee predictions. First, HBAG(xi) is computed as the Shannon entropy of the empirical class probability distribution pBAG for pixel xi. This entropy is then normalized by log(Ni), where Ni is the number of distinct classes predicted for that pixel, to bound the uncertainty score and mitigate hotspots in regions where many classes overlap. The selection rule is ˆx_nEQB = arg max_{xi∈U} HBAG(xi) / log(Ni), making the method naturally suited to multiclass settings.

canonical_topic.name: Committee-Based Bagging with Normalized Entropy Acquisition
canonical_topic.description: This topic describes a committee-based active learning strategy where class probabilities are estimated empirically from the votes of an ensemble (bagging) of classifiers. For each unlabeled sample, an empirical distribution over classes is built by counting how often committee members assign each class, using the Kronecker delta to accumulate votes. On top of this, a query-by-bagging acquisition function uses the Shannon entropy of this empirical distribution as an uncertainty measure. The entropy is then normalized by the logarithm of the number of distinct predicted classes to bound the score and reduce the dominance of regions with many overlapping classes. The resulting normalized entropy criterion selects unlabeled samples with maximal normalized uncertainty, making the approach particularly suitable for multiclass settings such as remote sensing image classification and directly applicable as an acquisition function in deep active learning frameworks.

canonical_topic.name: Auxiliary Uncertainty Networks in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers model-aspect enhancements in deep active learning that attach auxiliary probabilistic or loss-prediction heads to improve both predictive performance and acquisition quality. Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) are used to replace standard classification and localization heads, yielding full predictive distributions (means and variances) over class labels and bounding boxes, which serve as richer uncertainty measures for query selection. These MDN-based heads provide competitive or superior active learning performance compared to MC dropout and ensembles, while reducing inference cost and model size. Related approaches employ loss prediction networks that are jointly trained with the backbone model to estimate sample-wise prediction loss, using this estimated error as an acquisition signal rather than relying solely on softmax-based uncertainty. Overall, these auxiliary networks enable more expressive, task-aware uncertainty estimates that directly drive the active learning selection process.

canonical_topic.name: Imbalance-Aware Adaptation in Stream-Based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns mechanisms for handling class imbalance in active learning for data streams by adaptively reweighting ensemble classifiers. A damped class imbalance ratio (DCIR) is used as a streaming-aware indicator of how underrepresented each class is, based on its observed frequency over time. When a newly labeled instance is identified as belonging to a minority class via DCIR, a reinforcement-based update adjusts the dynamic classifier weights: classifiers are multiplicatively rewarded if they correctly predict the minority instance and penalized otherwise. These updates occur online after each queried label, allowing the active learner’s ensemble to quickly adapt its focus toward poorly represented classes in the evolving stream. The approach tightly couples label acquisition in a streaming setting with imbalance-aware model adaptation, improving performance on minority classes under limited annotation budgets.

First, HBAG(xi) is computed as the Shannon entropy of the empirical class probability distribution pBAG for pixel xi. This entropy is then normalized by log(Ni), where Ni is the number of distinct classes predicted for that pixel, to bound the uncertainty score and mitigate hotspots in regions where many classes overlap. The selection rule is ˆx_nEQB = arg max_{xi∈U} HBAG(xi) / log(Ni), making the method naturally suited to multiclass settings.

canonical_topic.name: Committee-Based Uncertainty and Normalized Entropy Selection
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers committee-based acquisition strategies where empirical class probabilities are derived from model vote distributions and then used for uncertainty-driven querying. For each unlabeled pixel, an ensemble (committee) of models produces class predictions, and an empirical class probability pBAG is computed as the relative voting frequency per class, yielding a discrete probability distribution over classes. A normalized entropy query-by-bagging (nEQB) heuristic then measures uncertainty by the Shannon entropy of this empirical distribution, normalized by the logarithm of the number of distinct predicted classes to avoid bias toward regions with many overlapping classes. The most informative samples are selected by maximizing this normalized entropy, making the approach particularly suitable for multiclass settings and ensemble-based deep active learning pipelines.

canonical_topic.name: Auxiliary Uncertainty Networks for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of auxiliary neural modules to enhance uncertainty estimation and acquisition quality in deep active learning. Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) are integrated into detection architectures by replacing standard classification and localization heads with MDN heads that output full predictive distributions, including variances for both class labels and bounding boxes; these variances are then used as selection criteria in active learning loops. Such MDN-based approaches can match the empirical performance of MC dropout and ensembles while being more efficient in inference time and model size. More generally, model-aspect DAL methods attach auxiliary networks, such as loss prediction networks, that are trained jointly with the backbone to predict future classification errors or losses, and these predictions directly guide sample acquisition. These designs explicitly tailor the model to produce acquisition-relevant signals, going beyond raw softmax scores to richer, DAL-specific uncertainty measures.

local_topics.title: G-optimality for predictive performance
local_topics.description: G-optimality is presented as an optimality criterion focused on predictive quality rather than solely parameter estimation. It seeks to minimize the maximum prediction variance v(x) over a region of interest R, solving min_D max_{x∈R} v(x). This provides protection against worst-case prediction uncertainty within the specified input domain.

local_topics.title: G-, I-, and V-optimality via prediction variance
local_topics.description: G-optimality focuses on minimizing the maximum prediction variance over a region R, using the scaled prediction variance v(x) that depends on the information matrix (X⊤X)⁻¹ and the model-expanded point x(m). Because it protects against the highest possible variance, G-optimality can be heavily influenced by anomalous observations. I- and V-optimality address this by integrating or averaging prediction variance over R, targeting overall rather than worst-case prediction accuracy.

canonical_topic.name: Optimal Experimental Design Criteria in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of classical optimal experimental design criteria, such as G-, I-, and V-optimality, as acquisition strategies in active learning. G-optimality selects points that minimize the maximum prediction variance over a region of interest, thereby controlling worst-case predictive uncertainty in the input space. In contrast, I- and V-optimality integrate or average the prediction variance over the region, aiming to improve overall predictive accuracy rather than focusing solely on extreme cases. Within deep and stream-based active learning, these criteria guide the selection of new samples to label so as to improve the predictive model under limited annotation budgets, with different trade-offs between robustness to worst-case uncertainty and global performance. The choice among these criteria affects sensitivity to anomalous observations and the spatial distribution of queried instances.

local_topics.title: A-optimality for parameter variance minimization
local_topics.description: A-optimality is defined as minimizing the sum of the variances of the regression coefficients, which correspond to the diagonal elements of (XᵀX)⁻¹. In terms of the moment matrix M(D), an A-optimal design D* minimizes tr[M(D)]⁻¹. This focuses on improving average precision of parameter estimates across all coefficients.

local_topics.title: D-optimality and ellipsoid volume reduction
local_topics.description: D-optimality considers both variances and covariances of the regression coefficients by maximizing the determinant of the moment matrix M(D). Equivalently, it minimizes the total volume of the confidence ellipsoid for β, leading to designs that are highly informative in a joint, multivariate sense. A D-optimal design D* satisfies max_D |M(D)| = |M(D*)|.

local_topics.title: E-optimality via eigenvalue control
local_topics.description: E-optimality aims to shrink the confidence ellipsoid by minimizing the maximum eigenvalue of the covariance matrix of β̂. By controlling this worst-case eigenvalue, E-optimal designs reduce the largest principal axis of the ellipsoid, improving the least well-estimated linear combination of parameters. This yields a more balanced precision across directions in parameter space.

local_topics.title: A-, D-, and E-optimality criteria
local_topics.description: A-, D-, and E-optimality are optimal design criteria expressed in terms of a confidence ellipsoid around model parameters. A-optimality seeks to shrink the hyper-rectangle enclosing the ellipsoid (minimizing average parameter variance), D-optimality minimizes the ellipsoid volume (maximizing determinant of information), and E-optimality reduces the length of the longest axis (minimizing worst-case parameter variance). These criteria guide where to place design points to optimally reduce parameter uncertainty.

canonical_topic.name: A-, D-, and E-optimal Design Criteria for Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers classical optimal experimental design criteria (A-, D-, and E-optimality) used to guide query selection by minimizing parameter uncertainty. A-optimality minimizes the sum of variances of the regression coefficients, or equivalently the trace of the inverse information (moment) matrix, focusing on improving the average precision of parameter estimates. D-optimality maximizes the determinant of the information matrix, which corresponds to minimizing the volume of the confidence ellipsoid around the parameters and encourages globally informative designs in a joint, multivariate sense. E-optimality minimizes the largest eigenvalue of the parameter covariance, shrinking the longest axis of the confidence ellipsoid and improving the worst-estimated linear combination of parameters. In an active learning context (including data streams), these criteria determine where to place or request new design points so as to most efficiently reduce model uncertainty under limited labeling budgets.

This architecture allows the selector to exploit contextual information when deciding which instances to query.

local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems are a class of fuzzy systems that can adapt and change over time in response to new data or environmental changes. They dynamically modify their internal structure, particularly rules and membership functions, to maintain performance in non-stationary settings. This adaptability makes them suitable for streaming and continually changing data scenarios.

local_topics.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for streaming data
local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems (EFS) are presented as soft-computing models tailored to time-varying data streams, capable of dealing with novelty and ongoing knowledge expansion. They are self-developing, self-learning fuzzy rule-based or neuro-fuzzy systems that adapt both their parameters and structure on the fly as new data arrive. By dynamically growing and updating fuzzy rule bases, EFS aim to mimic human-like reasoning over data streams through a formal learning process. This provides an alternative paradigm for handling evolving concepts compared to traditional parametric models.

local_topics.title: Evolving Fuzzy Systems architecture
local_topics.description: Evolving Fuzzy Systems (EFS) use fuzzy rules of the form mapping input variables to outputs via parametric consequents, with each rule associated to prototypes (focal points) and parameters. Their architecture includes a structure-evolving scheme and a parameter-updating scheme that together maintain and adapt the rule base. With every new labeled example, these learning modules update both structure and parameters to track the evolution of the data stream in an online manner.

local_topics.title: Rule generation, merging, and pruning in EFS
local_topics.description: The structure-evolving scheme in an EFS decides when to add new fuzzy rules, based on criteria indicating that the current rule base is insufficient to model new data. It also merges rules whose similarity exceeds a threshold and prunes redundant rules, thereby simplifying the model while preserving performance. This process controls model complexity in streaming settings where concepts and data distributions change over time.

local_topics.title: Overlap and novelty in fuzzy rule antecedents

Novelty content in the antecedent space quantifies how much new information incoming data bring, guiding when rule evolution or knowledge expansion is needed. Together, these measures steer the adaptive refinement of the fuzzy rule base in data streams.

local_topics.title: Sliding-window forgetting strategy
local_topics.description: A sliding-window-based strategy discards labeled instances that will not belong to the future training window when their labels arrive. The current window Wn at time tx_n and the future training window Dn at time ty_n are compared, and all labeled instances (ai = 1) that lie in Wn but not in Dn form the forgetting set On. This prevents the learner from training on soon-to-be outdated observations, better aligning the model with the temporally relevant portion of the data stream.

local_topics.title: Sliding-window kNN active learning with dual distance criteria
local_topics.description: Kurlej and Woźniak (2011) introduce a sliding-window active learning approach built on a k-nearest neighbors classifier whose reference set is a moving window. The window is updated either in a FIFO manner or by retaining examples selected through active learning, enabling adaptation to concept drift and time-varying data streams. The sampling strategy uses two distance-based criteria: a margin-like rule that queries instances close to neighbors from different classes, and a greedy-diversity rule that targets instances with large minimum distance to the current reference set. Both criteria are enforced via thresholds on pairwise distances.

canonical_topic.name: Sliding-Window Strategies in Stream-Based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on sliding-window mechanisms for stream-based active learning, where only a temporally limited subset of recent data is retained for model updates. A forgetting strategy discards labeled instances that will fall outside a future training window once their labels arrive, preventing the learner from training on soon-to-be outdated observations and keeping the model aligned with the most relevant segment of a non-stationary data stream. A kNN-based approach maintains a moving reference set updated either in FIFO fashion or by preferentially retaining actively selected examples, thereby adapting to concept drift. Its query strategy combines a margin-like distance criterion, which targets instances near conflicting class neighborhoods, with a diversity criterion, which selects samples far from the current reference set via distance thresholds. These ideas are directly applicable when designing deep active learning systems for evolving data streams, where both temporal relevance and diversity must be managed under limited labeling budgets.

local_topics.title: Bayesian committee framework for unknown-class discovery
local_topics.description: Loy et al. (2012) propose a Bayesian online active learning framework that uses committee consensus to balance exploration and exploitation. Exploration aims to discover new, previously unknown classes, while exploitation refines decision boundaries for known classes. The model employs a Pitman–Yor process (PYP) prior together with a Dirichlet process mixture model (DPMM), a non-parametric clustering and classification approach that flexibly models the data-generating process and supports the emergence of new classes.

local_topics.title: Dirichlet process mixture active querying
local_topics.description: A Dirichlet process mixture model (DPMM) is used to cluster streaming data, where each cluster defines a class probability distribution and the number of clusters is governed by a Dirichlet process allowing a potentially infinite, but effectively finite, number of clusters. At each time step, two hypotheses are sampled from the model and their posterior class predictions for the current point are compared. The label is queried when the two hypotheses disagree (disagreement-based querying) or when both predict a new class index K+1, enabling novel-class detection. This integrates nonparametric Bayesian clustering with selective labeling in a data stream setting.

canonical_topic.name: Bayesian Stream-Based Active Learning for Novel Class Discovery
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers Bayesian online active learning methods for data streams that can both refine known classes and discover previously unknown classes. The models use nonparametric Bayesian clustering, such as Dirichlet process mixture models and Pitman–Yor process priors, to allow a flexible and potentially unbounded number of clusters/classes. Query selection is typically committee-based and disagreement-driven: labels are requested when sampled hypotheses disagree on the current instance, or when they jointly indicate assignment to a novel class index. This balances exploration (unknown-class discovery) with exploitation (improving decision boundaries among known classes) under a selective labeling budget in streaming settings. The result is an integrated framework for active querying and incremental class discovery without fixing the class set in advance.

canonical_topic.name: Batch Selection and Redundancy in VHR Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns active learning in very high resolution (VHR) remote sensing imagery where labels are obtained via on-screen photointerpretation. Due to strong spatial correlation, selecting many neighboring pixels with similar appearance leads to highly redundant training sets that slow learning and contribute little new information. To counter this, active learning is typically run with many iterations and relatively small query batches, which makes it feasible to use more complex selection heuristics. Diversity-promoting strategies, especially those enforcing spectral diversity among queried samples, are emphasized to reduce redundancy and better explore the feature space. The computational cost of these diversity-based acquisition functions increases rapidly with batch size, further reinforcing the small-batch regime in VHR active learning workflows.

local_topics.title: Breaking Ties uncertainty sampling strategy
local_topics.description: The Breaking Ties (BT) strategy is an uncertainty-based active learning heuristic that exploits conditional label probabilities p(y*i = ω|xi) for each unlabeled candidate xi. It uses the predicted label y*i = arg maxω f(xi, ω) and the associated class probabilities, analogous in spirit to the EQB method mentioned earlier. Such probabilities can be produced by probabilistic neural networks, maximum likelihood classifiers, or other models that output calibrated class likelihoods. BT focuses on candidates where the classifier is most ambiguous between top classes, effectively targeting decision-boundary regions.

local_topics.title: Breaking Ties uncertainty sampling heuristic
local_topics.description: The Breaking Ties (BT) heuristic selects unlabeled samples for which a classifier is most uncertain, quantified as the smallest difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities. In both binary and multi-class settings, a small gap between these top probabilities indicates that the classifier is nearly indifferent between competing labels. The heuristic thus prioritizes samples that lie near decision boundaries, where model confidence is lowest.

canonical_topic.name: Breaking Ties Uncertainty Sampling in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: The Breaking Ties (BT) strategy is an uncertainty-based query method for pool-based active learning that selects samples where the classifier is most ambiguous between the top predicted classes. It typically measures uncertainty as the smallest difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities p(y|x), so samples with nearly tied top probabilities are prioritized. These points tend to lie close to the decision boundary and are thus expected to be highly informative when labeled. BT can be implemented with any probabilistic classifier, including probabilistic neural networks and maximum likelihood models, as long as they output calibrated class likelihoods. By relying on a single probabilistic model rather than an ensemble, BT offers computational efficiency while still exploiting posterior information for query decisions in deep or non-deep active learning setups.

local_topics.title: Dominant labeling and class-balanced sampling
local_topics.description: Dominant labeling assigns to each superpixel the majority class label of its pixels, then propagates this label to every pixel in the region, avoiding detailed boundary delineation. Cai et al. (2021) combine this with a class-balanced sampling strategy to preferentially select superpixels that contain minority classes, improving class balance in queried data. Their results show that dominant labeling with superpixels significantly outperforms precise patch-level labeling under the same number of annotation clicks, highlighting gains in annotation efficiency.

local_topics.title: Adaptive merging and splitting of superpixels
local_topics.description: Building on dominant labeling, Kim et al. (2023) propose adaptively merging spatially adjacent and similar superpixels, while splitting those that are complex. This dynamic adjustment produces region units that better match underlying structures, potentially improving both label consistency and uncertainty estimation. The adaptive scheme achieves better performance than the fixed superpixel approach of Cai et al. (2021).

canonical_topic.name: Superpixel-Based Annotation and Labeling in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on superpixel-based annotation strategies that reduce labeling cost in deep active learning for medical images. Dominant labeling assigns the majority class label within each superpixel and propagates it to all pixels in the region, trading exact boundary delineation for substantially improved annotation efficiency. Combined with class-balanced sampling, superpixels containing minority classes are preferentially queried, improving class balance in the labeled set under a fixed annotation budget. Building on this idea, adaptive merging of similar neighboring superpixels and splitting of complex ones yields region units that better align with anatomical structures, enhancing both label consistency and uncertainty estimation. These superpixel-centric methods outperform precise patch-level labeling under equal click budgets and improve the effectiveness of region-level query strategies in DAL.

local_topics.title: Upper Confidence Bound in bandits
local_topics.description: The Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm is used in multi-armed bandit problems to trade off exploration and exploitation by combining the predicted mean reward and its uncertainty (standard deviation), scaled by a tunable parameter. By assigning higher scores to arms with either high estimated reward or high uncertainty, UCB guides the sequential selection of arms to maximize long-term reward. It operationalizes exploration–exploitation balance via confidence intervals on expected rewards.

canonical_topic.name: Bandit-Based Label Budget Allocation in Active Learning

Querying a label is modeled as pulling an arm, with each model (or arm) having an unknown difficulty that must be estimated online. Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) principles are used to balance exploration and exploitation, combining estimated performance and uncertainty to decide which model to query next. Extensions such as trace-based UCB and norm-thresholding provide refined uncertainty measures for guiding budget allocation, aiming to learn all models uniformly well under shared annotation constraints. This bandit-based perspective makes the budgeting and selection mechanism explicit, aligning acquisition decisions with formal exploration–exploitation guarantees.

local_topics.title: Linear margin-based online prediction
local_topics.description: The learner uses a linear predictor parameterized by a weight vector w ∈ R^d to classify each incoming instance in a data stream. At time t, after observing xt, the predicted label is the sign of the inner product wᵀ_{t−1} xt, and this inner product defines the margin p_t. The margin quantifies the confidence of the current model on xt and later serves as a key quantity in the querying rule.

local_topics.title: Second-order online active learning
local_topics.description: Second-order online active learning augments traditional margin-based (first-order) strategies by explicitly modeling the classifier’s parameter uncertainty. The weight vector w ∈ R^d is assumed to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution w ~ N(μ, Σ), where μ encodes the current estimate and the variances and covariances in Σ encode confidence about each feature weight and their dependencies. This allows the method to consider both the margin value and the associated uncertainty when deciding whether to query a label and update the model.

canonical_topic.description: This topic analyzes how backbone pretraining and resulting feature quality affect deep active learning performance, especially under dataset bias and spurious correlations. Using ResNet18 with and without ImageNet-1K pretraining, the studies show that pretrained models provide richer, more semantic feature representations that shift attention from backgrounds to objects, thereby improving DAL query selection. Budgeted accuracy curves across methods and datasets quantify how pretraining influences label efficiency, robustness to group imbalance, and the comparative behavior of uncertainty- and diversity-based DAL strategies.

canonical_topic.name: Model Mismatch Between Query and Successor Models in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns the problem of query–successor model mismatch, where the model used to select instances for labeling differs from the final deployment model. Such mismatches commonly arise when a lightweight model is used during active querying for efficiency, while a heavier or updated model (often a deep model) is later trained on the collected labeled pool. Differences in inductive biases between these models can undermine or even negate the expected performance gains from active learning, since the queried samples may not be optimal for the successor model. Empirical studies show that this issue can substantially affect the long-term utility of AL-collected datasets, motivating methods that explicitly account for or mitigate query–successor mismatch when designing active learning strategies.

local_topics.title: Adaptive Maximum Disagreement query rule
local_topics.description: The Adaptive Maximum Disagreement (AMD) heuristic selects unlabeled samples whose predictions across views are most uncertain according to a multiview entropy criterion. Formally, given a partition of the d-dimensional input space into V views, AMD selects the candidate ˆxAMD in the unlabeled pool U that maximizes HMV(xi). This aligns active learning with areas where committee members (views) disagree the most, focusing labeling effort on the most informative pixels. AMD thus operationalizes disagreement in a principled, entropy-based way.

local_topics.title: Candidate subset selection to reduce computation

Specifically, candidate pixels are those for which the committee (the set of view-based classifiers) has predicted the largest number of distinct classes, indicating high disagreement. AMD is then applied within this reduced subset, maintaining informativeness while lowering processing effort. This strategy balances query quality and scalability for large remote sensing datasets.

local_topics.title: Application to spinal cord compression grading
local_topics.description: The proposed deep active learning and semi-supervised framework is applied to grading metastatic epidural spinal cord compression in MRI images. This involves assigning severity grades to lesions, a critical task for clinical decision-making. local_topics.title: Active learning for spinal cord compression diagnosis
local_topics.description: This topic concerns active learning for classifying metastatic epidural spinal cord compression from spine MRI. An in-house MRI dataset with 7,295 images is split in a 7:1:2 ratio, and only a fraction of the data (e.g., 10% plus an additional 5%) is labeled for training within a deep classification framework. The focus is on reducing annotation cost while maintaining diagnostic performance in a high-stakes spine imaging setting.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Spinal Cord Compression Grading
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning, combined with semi-supervised learning, to grade metastatic epidural spinal cord compression on spine MRI. A deep classification framework is trained with only a small fraction of labeled images (e.g., 10% plus an additional actively selected 5%), aiming to reduce annotation costs while preserving high diagnostic performance. The active learning component selectively queries the most informative MRI samples for expert labeling, which is critical in this high-stakes, labor-intensive medical imaging setting. Experimental results show that this strategy effectively improves performance for automated severity grading of spinal cord compression, demonstrating the practical value of DAL in clinical decision support.

local_topics.title: Patch-based fundus eye image dataset
local_topics.description: Another entry concerns fundus (retinal) eye images, citing work by Otálora et al. (2017) presented at MICCAI-W. It references the e-ophtha dataset and describes a patch-based setup with 20,148 patches, split into 17,520/656/1,972 for training, validation, and testing, plus a figure of 160 (likely indicating images or positive samples). This reflects a common medical imaging strategy where large numbers of small patches are extracted from fundus images for tasks such as lesion or structure detection and segmentation.

local_topics.title: Federated Fundus Retina Vessel Segmentation
local_topics.description: This topic involves segmenting retinal vessels from fundus eye images using the Fed-Fundus dataset, which contains 1,060 images split into 849 and 211 samples. The task is to delineate vessel structures in retinal images, a key step for diagnosing various ophthalmic and systemic diseases. The federated dataset context is relevant for privacy-preserving and distributed deep active learning workflows.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Fundus Image Datasets for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers retinal fundus image datasets and setups commonly used in deep active learning for medical image analysis. Patch-based configurations, such as those built on the e-ophtha dataset with tens of thousands of patches split into training, validation, and test subsets, enable lesion or structure detection with fine-grained supervision and flexible sampling of informative regions. Vessel segmentation tasks on fundus images, exemplified by the Fed-Fundus dataset, provide benchmarks for delineating retinal vasculature, which is crucial for diagnosing ophthalmic and systemic diseases. The federated nature of some fundus datasets supports privacy-preserving and distributed deep active learning workflows, where acquisition and labeling decisions must respect data locality and confidentiality constraints.

local_topics.title: Multi-view uncertainty and disagreement for superpixels
local_topics.description: Superpixel selection can be driven by both uncertainty and disagreement across different viewpoints or models. Siddiqui et al. (2020) use these criteria to choose the most informative superpixels for annotation, prioritizing regions where multiple views diverge or exhibit high predictive uncertainty. This leverages ensemble-like or multi-view signals to guide region-level labeling.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Edge-based entropy and divergence in OCT
local_topics.description: For OCT segmentation, superpixel informativeness is modeled using edge-based entropy and divergence metrics. Kadir et al. (2023) focus on highly uncertain superpixels, especially around edges where class transitions occur, to better capture boundary information. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of these edge-focused uncertainty measures for selecting superpixels to annotate.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Regional consistency and combined uncertainty metrics
local_topics.description: Li et al. (2023) use superpixels to compute a regional consistency measure, defined as the difference between the model prediction and the dominant class within each superpixel. This regional consistency is combined with other metrics such as entropy and diversity to identify the most uncertain foreground and background superpixels. By focusing queries on these regions, their approach aims to reduce annotation cost while targeting areas where model predictions are least aligned with local dominant labels.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Superpixel-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that operate at the superpixel (region) level to guide annotation in medical image segmentation. Instead of querying individual pixels, methods aggregate model evidence within superpixels and prioritize regions with high uncertainty or disagreement across multiple views or models, as in ensemble or multi-view settings. Edge-focused criteria, such as entropy and divergence around boundaries in OCT images, are used to capture uncertain class transitions and refine segmentation along object borders. Other approaches introduce regional consistency, comparing each superpixel’s dominant class to the model’s prediction and combining this with entropy and diversity metrics to find the most informative foreground and background regions. By selecting superpixels with high uncertainty, disagreement, or low regional consistency, these methods reduce annotation cost while focusing labeling effort on the most informative parts of the image.

local_topics.title: Quality assessment modules predicting IoU
local_topics.description: Quality assessment modules are trained to predict task-specific evaluation scores, such as the average IoU for each image slice, and use these predictions as performance surrogates. Zhou et al. (2021b, 2022) compute a predicted average IoU per slice and interactively select slices with the lowest predicted scores from each volume for annotation. This directs labeling effort toward regions where current segmentation performance is expected to be poorest.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Uncertainty-based key slice selection
local_topics.description: Key image slices are selected using uncertainty measures rather than annotating all slices. Zhou et al. (2021b) introduced a quality assessment module that predicts the average Intersection over Union (IoU) score for each slice and selects those with the highest predicted IoU for annotation. This approach prioritizes slices expected to yield better segmentation quality. It reduces labeling effort by focusing on informative slices while leveraging predicted performance metrics.

local_topics.title: IoU-Based Quality Prediction for 3D Segmentation
local_topics.description: In 3D medical image interactive segmentation, a quality predictor network is used to estimate the reliability of current segmentations. This predictor outputs a predicted Intersection-over-Union (IoU) score for each slice relative to an ideal segmentation. Slices with lower predicted IoU are automatically suggested for expert annotation, where users can provide corrections via scribbles, bounding boxes, or extreme clicks. This mechanism focuses expert effort on low-quality slices, integrating prediction quality assessment with interactive refinement.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Performance-Prediction-Based Slice Selection in DAL
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that use learned quality predictors to guide slice selection in 3D medical image segmentation. A dedicated quality assessment module is trained to predict task-specific performance metrics, typically the per-slice Intersection-over-Union (IoU), and these predicted scores act as surrogates for true evaluation. The predicted IoU values are then used as acquisition signals to prioritize slices for annotation, either by targeting low-scoring slices where the current segmentation is likely poor or by selecting key slices expected to strongly improve the model. In interactive segmentation setups, experts are prompted to correct slices with low predicted IoU using scribbles, bounding boxes, or clicks, tightly coupling performance estimation with human-in-the-loop refinement. This yields a DAL framework where query selection is driven by explicit predictions of segmentation quality under a limited annotation budget.

local_topics.title: Training paradigms and fine-tuning regimes
local_topics.description: The text contrasts earlier deep learning paradigms, such as training from scratch, with pre-train–finetune strategies using supervised or self-supervised pre-trained models. It then introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and prompt tuning, where only a small fraction of model parameters (e.g., 5%) are updated for downstream tasks. This evolution in training regimes forms the technical backdrop for how AL strategies might need to adapt.

local_topics.title: Active learning under PEFT and prompt tuning
local_topics.description: With fewer trainable parameters in PEFT and prompt-tuning settings, the section proposes that AL can further reduce the number of annotated samples needed. It stresses the need to reassess existing AL methods in this new regime and to discover AL strategies specifically suited to PEFT and prompt tuning. This reframes AL not just as sample selection but as co-designed with low-parameter adaptation mechanisms.

local_topics.title: Prompt-based AL for liver tumor segmentation
local_topics.description: Bai et al. (2023) are cited as integrating prompt tuning with AL for liver tumor segmentation. A segmentation model pre-trained on public datasets is adapted to in-house data using a novel prompt updater and a mixed AL strategy combining uncertainty and diversity. The method achieves performance comparable to fully supervised finetuning while using only about 5% of samples and 6% of tunable parameters, exemplifying the efficiency gains possible with AL plus PEFT.

canonical_topic.name: Active Learning with Foundation Models and PEFT
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on how deep active learning must adapt to foundation models and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) regimes. Instead of training large models from scratch, modern workflows rely on supervised or self-supervised pre-trained models that are adapted using PEFT or prompt tuning, where only a small subset of parameters is updated. In this setting, active learning is reframed as co-designed with low-parameter adaptation mechanisms, aiming to jointly minimize the number of labeled samples and the number of tunable parameters. The literature highlights the need to reassess classical AL strategies and to develop acquisition methods specifically suited to PEFT and prompt tuning. A concrete example is prompt-based AL for liver tumor segmentation, where a pre-trained segmentation model is adapted to in-house data using a prompt updater and a mixed uncertainty–diversity selection strategy, achieving near fully supervised performance with about 5% of samples and 6% of parameters tuned.

local_topics.title: CNN-based DeepAL for Text Classification
local_topics.description: [251] proposes an active learning strategy for CNN-based sentence and text classification that selects instances expected to induce the largest updates in word embeddings. The method targets samples whose embeddings are likely to change with the greatest magnitude, rapidly learning discriminative, task-specific representations. This approach outperforms traditional AL baselines on both sentence and document-level text classification tasks.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: RNN-Based Acquisition in Text DeepAL
local_topics.description: [7] introduces a DeepAL framework for text classification that uses an RNN as the acquisition function to drive sample selection. By learning which text instances are most informative, the method reduces the number of labeled examples needed while maintaining accuracy. It also decreases training time compared to standard deep learning with full supervision.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Text Classification
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on deep active learning methods tailored to text classification, where both the predictive model and the acquisition strategy are built on deep neural architectures. One line of work applies CNN-based sentence and document classifiers and selects unlabeled instances expected to induce the largest updates in word embeddings, explicitly targeting samples that most reshape task-specific representations. Another approach uses an RNN as a learned acquisition function that directly predicts which text instances are most informative to query. These strategies reduce the number of labeled examples and training time compared to fully supervised deep learning, while outperforming traditional, hand-crafted active learning baselines on sentence- and document-level tasks.

local_topics.title: Online active learning with expert forecasters
local_topics.description: A committee-based framework is proposed where an online learner follows predictions from a pool of N experts and aims to minimize the number of label queries while maintaining strong predictive performance. The learner adapts forecaster algorithms such as the exponentially weighted average forecaster (EWAF) and the greedy forecaster, forming its prediction as a weighted average of expert predictions and updating expert weights based on incurred loss. Performance is analyzed via cumulative regret, defined as the difference between the learner’s cumulative loss and that of each expert over time. In EWAF, expert weights are set proportional to the exponential of their cumulative regret, emphasizing experts with better historical performance.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Active EWAF and GF with limited labels
local_topics.description: Hao et al. extend the Exponentially Weighted Average Forecaster (EWAF) and the Generalized Forecaster (GF) to an online active learning setting where the true label yt is not always observed. They introduce a binary variable Zt ∈ {0,1} to decide whether to request a label at round t, and define the cumulative loss Li,T of each expert only over the queried instances. The active forecaster’s prediction pt is obtained by projecting an underlying prediction pt into [0,1], and is designed to approximate what would be obtained in a fully supervised setup. This framework formalizes how expert-advice forecasters operate under label budget constraints.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Confidence-based querying in AEWAF and AGF
local_topics.description: The sampling strategy for active expert-advice forecasters is based on confidence conditions that bound the difference between the fully supervised prediction pt and the active prediction pt. In AEWAF, a label is considered unnecessary if the maximum pairwise disagreement between any two experts’ outputs is below a tolerance δ, which guarantees |pt − pt| ≤ δ; a robust variant is proposed to handle noisy or bad experts violating this assumption. In AGF, the confidence condition is instead defined via the maximum deviation of each expert’s prediction from pt, again ensuring |pt − pt| ≤ δ when this deviation is small. These criteria operationalize when the forecaster is confident enough to skip querying a label while keeping the active prediction close to the fully supervised one.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Online Active Learning with Expert Advice
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers online active learning algorithms built on expert-advice forecasters for data streams. A learner aggregates predictions from a pool of experts (e.g., EWAF and GF), updates expert weights based on incurred loss, and analyzes performance via cumulative regret relative to the best expert. The forecasters are extended to an active setting by introducing a query variable that decides whether to request the current label, defining each expert’s cumulative loss only over queried instances to respect a label budget. Active variants (AEWAF and AGF) maintain predictions close to their fully supervised counterparts by using confidence-based querying rules that bound the difference between the active and fully supervised predictions. These confidence conditions are implemented via thresholds on pairwise expert disagreement or deviation from the aggregated prediction, with robust variants designed to handle noisy or unreliable experts.

local_topics.title: Per-round regret as evaluation metric
local_topics.description: Per-round regret measures the difference in loss between a forecaster (or learning algorithm) and the best expert at each iteration of the active learning process. It originates from online learning and bandit theory and focuses on cumulative or step-wise suboptimality rather than classification accuracy alone. Using per-round regret emphasizes how quickly an active learner approaches the performance of the best possible strategy. This metric is particularly suited to decision-making scenarios framed as expert advice or bandit problems.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Regret and error metrics vs trial budget
local_topics.description: An alternative evaluation approach for bandit algorithms focuses on regret or prediction error as functions of the number of trials. Here, performance is measured by how quickly an algorithm reduces regret or error given a specified trial budget, reflecting its learning speed and efficiency over time. Studies such as those by Riquelme et al. (2017a), Sudarsanam and Ravindran (2018), and Fontaine et al. (2021) exemplify this trial-based evaluation methodology.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Regret-Based Evaluation in Stream Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of regret and related error measures as evaluation metrics for active learning and bandit-style algorithms on data streams. Instead of focusing solely on final classification accuracy, per-round and cumulative regret quantify how far the learner’s loss is from that of the best expert or strategy at each iteration. Evaluating regret (or prediction error) as a function of the number of trials or labeling budget emphasizes learning speed and efficiency over time, which is crucial in streaming and bandit formulations of active learning. Such metrics align naturally with online decision-making settings, highlighting how rapidly an active learner approaches optimal performance under budgeted interaction.

local_topics.title: CT-based polyp and embolism candidate detection
local_topics.description: This topic describes a classification task labeled as polyp detection that operates on CT data of the lung using an in-house dataset of pulmonary embolism (PE) candidate samples. The dataset comprises 6,255 PE candidate instances, split into 3,840/2,415, suggesting automated identification of suspicious regions in chest CT scans. It illustrates how deep active learning can be applied to detect lesion-like or thrombus-related candidates in volumetric imaging.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Pulmonary embolism detection from CT
local_topics.description: A pulmonary embolism (PE) detection task is specified using CT images of the lung, focusing on "PE candidate" data. The dataset contains 6,255 samples (3,840/2,415), and the task is handled as a classification problem. This showcases deep active learning in identifying PE candidates within lung CT scans to support diagnostic workflows.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Pulmonary Embolism Detection in CT
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to detect pulmonary embolism (PE) candidates in chest CT scans. The task is formulated as a classification problem on PE candidate regions extracted from volumetric CT data, using an in-house dataset of 6,255 candidate samples split into 3,840 and 2,415 instances. Deep active learning is employed to selectively query labels for the most informative or uncertain candidate regions, thereby reducing the annotation burden associated with large 3D CT volumes. This approach aims to improve automated identification of lesion- or thrombus-like structures in support of clinical PE diagnosis workflows.

local_topics.title: Active learning setup on hyperspectral data
local_topics.description: For the hyperspectral Pavia dataset, 20,000 labeled pixels were allocated between the initial training set X and the unlabeled candidate pool U for active learning. Ten independent experiments were conducted, each starting with 25 labeled pixels (5 per class), with the rest placed in U, to evaluate robustness across runs. When using Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), the initial labeled set was increased to 150 pixels (30 per class) to satisfy model requirements that the number of training samples exceed the feature dimensionality.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Hyperspectral dataset preprocessing and sampling
local_topics.description: A hyperspectral image is treated as a challenging classification problem due to strong mixing of class signatures, requiring removal of 20 water absorption channels and exclusion of classes with fewer than 100 labeled pixels. This results in a 12-class problem with 10,171 labeled pixels. Of these, 7,000 pixels are allocated to the labeled (X) and unlabeled (U) sets for active learning, with experiments initialized from 5 labeled pixels per class and the remaining 3,171 pixels reserved for testing generalization.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Sampling strategy for VHR active learning
local_topics.description: For the VHR QuickBird dataset, 20,000 pixels are selected to form the labeled (X) and unlabeled (U) pools used in active learning experiments. Each run starts with a small, balanced seed set of 5 labeled pixels per class (45 pixels total), reflecting a realistic low-label regime. The dataset exhibits strong overlaps, particularly between asphalt and soil classes, as confirmed by both spectral profiles and manifold visualizations, underscoring the difficulty of the classification task.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

canonical_topic.name: Active Learning Experimental Setup for Remote Sensing Imagery
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers how hyperspectral and very high resolution (VHR) remote sensing datasets are configured for pool-based active learning experiments under low-label regimes. The labeled dataset is split into an initial, very small seed set (typically 5 labeled pixels per class) and a large unlabeled candidate pool U, with an additional held-out test set used to assess generalization. Preprocessing steps include removing noisy spectral channels and excluding classes with too few labeled pixels, resulting in a multi-class classification task with carefully controlled labeled and unlabeled pools. The setup explicitly allocates tens of thousands of pixels between X and U to simulate realistic annotation budgets and data scarcity, while also dealing with strong class overlaps and high intra-class variability. Model-specific constraints, such as the need for Linear Discriminant Analysis to have more training samples than feature dimensions, can require increasing the initial labeled set size, illustrating how classifier properties interact with active learning design.

local_topics.title: Multiclass level uncertainty criterion
local_topics.description: Multiclass level uncertainty (MCLU) extends margin sampling from binary to multiclass SVM classification by considering the distance to the margin for the two most probable classes. The criterion f(x_i)^MC is defined as the difference between the maximum per-class decision value and the maximum decision value among all remaining classes. Samples with small f(x_i)^MC are considered unreliable and are selected for labeling, formalized by x̂_MCLU = argmin_{x_i∈U} f(x_i)^MC. This provides an uncertainty measure that directly leverages all SVM decision values across classes.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: MCLU versus margin sampling in mixed regions
local_topics.description: MCLU is contrasted with standard margin sampling (MS) in areas of the feature space where three classes overlap. Because MCLU is computed from all per-class decision values, it yields maximal uncertainty in highly mixed regions, whereas MS yields uncertainty values slightly lower than along two-class decision boundaries. This leads to better identification of ambiguous samples in complex multiclass regions, particularly in the illustrated top-right area of the feature space. The comparison emphasizes MCLU's advantage when more than two classes interact locally.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

canonical_topic.name: Multiclass Uncertainty Criteria for Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the Multiclass Level Uncertainty (MCLU) criterion, which generalizes margin-based uncertainty sampling from binary to multiclass classification settings. MCLU leverages all per-class decision values of a classifier (e.g., SVM) to define uncertainty as the difference between the highest decision value and the highest value among the remaining classes, selecting points with the smallest gap for labeling. Compared to standard margin sampling, MCLU better captures ambiguous regions where more than two classes overlap by producing maximal uncertainty in highly mixed multiclass areas rather than only along pairwise decision boundaries. As an acquisition function, it refines uncertainty-based selection for pool-based active learning in complex multiclass scenarios and can be adapted to deep models that output per-class scores or logits.

local_topics.title: Pairwise stable–dynamic classifier strategy
local_topics.description: The pairwise strategy uses two models: a stable classifier Cs trained on all labeled data seen so far (L1, …, Lt−1) and a dynamic classifier Cd trained only on the most recent batch Lt−1. Predictions for an incoming instance xt are obtained via a weighted combination fE(xt) = ωs fCs(xt) + ωd fCd(xt). When the dynamic classifier outperforms the stable one, Cs is replaced by Cd, enabling rapid adaptation to concept drift by emphasizing recent data and discarding older, potentially obsolete information. However, this hard replacement leads to forgetting older patterns and is ineffective for gradual drifts that require longer-term memory.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Ensemble reactive models for mixed drifts
local_topics.description: To better handle both gradual and abrupt drifts, Shan et al. extend the pairwise approach by replacing the single reactive classifier with an ensemble of dynamic classifiers. In this variant, the stable classifier continues to learn from all labeled instances, while multiple dynamic classifiers are trained on multilevel recent windows of the stream. This ensemble of reactive models provides a richer representation of recent concepts over different temporal scales, enabling simultaneous responsiveness to sudden changes and robustness to slow, gradual shifts.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Stable–dynamic ensemble for concept drift
local_topics.description: The method uses an ensemble composed of one stable classifier and multiple dynamic classifiers to handle concept drift in data streams. The final prediction fE(x_t) is a weighted combination of the stable classifier output and the outputs of D dynamic classifiers. The stable classifier has a fixed weight (ω_s = 0.5) and is responsible for learning the overall trend, while the dynamic classifiers specialize in recent behavior and drift. This structure enables both long-term stability and short-term adaptability to changing concepts.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Stable–Dynamic Ensembles for Stream Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers stable–dynamic ensemble designs used in active learning for data streams with concept drift. A pairwise strategy maintains a stable classifier trained on all labeled data seen so far and a dynamic classifier trained only on the most recent labeled batch, combining their predictions via a weighted output and replacing the stable model when the dynamic one consistently performs better; this favors rapid adaptation to abrupt drift but risks forgetting older patterns and struggles with gradual drifts. To better cope with mixed drift types, the reactive component is extended from a single dynamic model to an ensemble of dynamic classifiers, each trained on recent windows at different temporal scales, while the stable classifier continues to learn from all labeled instances. A more general stable–dynamic ensemble fixes the stable classifier’s weight (e.g., ω_s = 0.5) and uses multiple dynamic classifiers specialized on recent behavior, achieving a balance between long-term trend modeling and short-term responsiveness. These designs serve as base learners within stream-based active learning systems, allowing queried labels from evolving streams to update both persistent and reactive components in a drift-aware manner.

local_topics.title: Red blood cell detection in microscopy
local_topics.description: This topic concerns detecting red blood cells in microscopy images of blood. The table indicates an in-house image dataset of 208 samples (188 for training, 20 for testing), used for an object detection task. The cited work (Shi et al., 2019, MICCAI) exemplifies how deep learning-based detection models are evaluated on relatively small, specialized medical datasets. Such tasks often require methods that can cope with limited labeled data while accurately localizing individual cells.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Peripheral blood cell type classification
local_topics.description: This topic describes a microscopy-based image classification task using the BloodMNIST dataset. It focuses on classifying peripheral blood cell images into different cell types, with 17,092 images divided into 11,959/1,712/3,421 for training, validation, and testing. The task is representative of fine-grained cellular classification problems commonly used to benchmark deep active learning strategies in hematological imaging.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Blood Cell Imaging
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning applications in microscopy-based blood cell analysis, including both detection and fine-grained classification tasks. Red blood cell detection in small, in-house microscopy datasets illustrates scenarios with very limited labeled samples, where DAL is used to prioritize informative regions or instances for annotation to improve object localization performance. Peripheral blood cell type classification with datasets like BloodMNIST provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating DAL strategies on fine-grained, multi-class cellular recognition under constrained labeling budgets. Across these tasks, DAL methods are assessed on their ability to achieve high diagnostic accuracy while minimizing the number of labeled microscopy images required, reflecting real-world constraints in hematological imaging.

local_topics.title: Multiview entropy uncertainty measure
local_topics.description: The multiview entropy HMV(xi) quantifies uncertainty over class labels by aggregating predictions from classifiers built on each view. It is defined as the Shannon entropy of a multiview class probability distribution pMV(y*i = ω | x_i^v), summing over all classes ω. High entropy indicates strong disagreement or uncertainty among the views’ predictions, making the corresponding sample a prime candidate for querying. This measure directly drives sample selection in the AMD heuristic.

local_topics.title: View-class weighting matrix for prediction fusion
local_topics.description: The probability pMV(y*i = ω | x_i^v) used in multiview entropy is computed via a weighting matrix W^ε−1 that encodes each view’s ability to discriminate each class. An indicator δ(y*i,v, ω) counts when a classifier built on view v predicts class ω, and these counts are weighted and normalized over views and classes using W^ε−1. At each iteration ε, W is updated based on the true labels of newly sampled pixels, then its columns are normalized to sum to one. This adaptive weighting increases the influence of views that prove more reliable for specific classes over the course of active learning.

canonical_topic.name: Multiview Entropy and Adaptive View Weighting in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers multiview entropy as an uncertainty-based acquisition function in active learning, where predictions from classifiers trained on different views are fused into a multiview class probability distribution. The Shannon entropy of this fused distribution, HMV(xi), quantifies disagreement across views, and high-entropy samples are prioritized for querying. A key component is a view–class weighting matrix that encodes how discriminative each view is for each class, used to compute the fused probabilities. This matrix is iteratively updated using the true labels of newly queried samples and then normalized, so that more reliable view–class combinations gain higher influence over time. The result is a dynamic acquisition strategy that jointly exploits multiview uncertainty and adaptive reliability estimation to guide sample selection.

local_topics.title: Determinantal point process-based sampling
local_topics.description: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are probabilistic models that favor subsets of mutually dissimilar items, thereby directly enforcing diversity among selected samples. In active learning, separate DPPs can be constructed for uncertainty-based scores and for exploration near decision boundaries, with their sampled outputs sent for annotation. The section notes that while DPPs can match clustering in performance, they are significantly more computationally expensive; k-Means++ is highlighted as a cheaper alternative with similar effectiveness in experiments, including for medical image reconstruction.

local_topics.title: Determinantal point processes for diversity

Active-DPP is a representative example, and BADGE uses DPPs as a post-processing diversity mechanism on top of its gradient embeddings. The determinant serves as a global diversity measure, penalizing redundant samples.

canonical_topic.name: Determinantal Point Processes for Diverse Query Selection
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) in deep active learning to explicitly promote diversity in queried batches. DPPs define a probability distribution over subsets via a pairwise similarity (kernel) matrix, favoring sets whose elements are mutually dissimilar by maximizing the determinant of this matrix. In DAL, DPPs can be applied directly to uncertainty scores or feature/gradient embeddings (as in Active-DPP and as a post-processing step in BADGE) to remove redundancy in the selected samples. This yields globally diverse, non-overlapping query batches that better cover the data space and decision boundaries than purely uncertainty-driven selection. However, the computational cost of constructing and sampling from DPPs is substantial, and practical studies report that cheaper clustering-based approaches such as k-Means++ can achieve similar effectiveness in some applications, including medical image analysis, while being more scalable.

local_topics.title: Chunk-partitioned ensemble for stream learning
local_topics.description: A window-based active learning method constructs an ensemble E by partitioning the data stream S into chunks and training each of k base models on different chunks. This chunking strategy structures the stream into manageable segments that can be separately modeled, supporting ensemble-based adaptation to temporal changes. The ensemble framework forms the basis for active learning decisions over evolving data.

local_topics.title: Chunk-based ensemble active learning
local_topics.description: The data stream is divided into chunks St, each used to train a current classifier Ct, while an ensemble retains the k−1 most recent past classifiers Ct−k+1, …, Ct−1 trained on labeled subsets Lt−k+1, …, Lt−1. At each time t, the ensemble is used to predict labels for the unlabeled instances Ut in the current chunk. Classifier predictions are combined via weights ωt−k+1, …, ωt−1, and a weight updating rule adapts the ensemble to evolving data streams. This framework allows reuse of past models even when raw historical data are no longer available.

canonical_topic.name: Chunk-Based Ensembles for Stream Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers window- or chunk-based ensemble frameworks for active learning on data streams. The incoming stream is partitioned into successive chunks, and separate base models are trained on each chunk, forming an ensemble that reflects different temporal segments of the data. At any time step, the ensemble—composed of the current and several recent chunk models—predicts labels for the unlabeled instances in the current chunk and guides which instances should be queried for labeling. Weighting and weight-update rules adapt the influence of past models to concept drift, enabling reuse of historical knowledge even when raw past data are unavailable. This structure provides a DAL-relevant mechanism to make informed, budget-aware annotation decisions under evolving data distributions in streaming settings.

local_topics.title: MAO: Most Ambiguous and Orthogonal heuristic
local_topics.description: The MAO (Most Ambiguous and Orthogonal) heuristic introduces an explicit diversity notion by constraining margin sampling with an angular distance in feature space. It starts from a subset of samples selected by pure margin sampling (UMS) and iteratively chooses new samples that are both ambiguous (high uncertainty) and as orthogonal as possible to the already selected ones. Orthogonality is quantified via the angle between feature vectors, which acts as a diversity metric to spread labeled points across the feature space. This leads to iterative batch selection where each new pixel maximizes angular diversity relative to the current batch.

local_topics.title: User-defined diversity measures: MAO, cSV, ABD
local_topics.description: The general diversity-based framework allows plugging in different diversity criteria to compare pixels in the candidate set U* with those already in the batch S. Examples mentioned include MAO (angle-based orthogonality in feature space), cSV, and ABD, which are alternative measures of dissimilarity or coverage between pixels. By computing these metrics during selection, the algorithm can favor samples that expand the coverage of the feature space or decision boundary. This modularity enables tailoring the diversity notion to specific remote sensing data characteristics.

local_topics.title: MAO kernel-based diversity selection
local_topics.description: The MAO (maximum angle-based outlier) criterion selects new samples from the unlabeled margin set by minimizing their maximum kernel similarity to already selected samples. This enforces diversity in the batch S by preferring candidates that are least similar (in kernel feature space) to current selections. The process is formalized as an optimization over the unlabeled set U_MS using the kernel function K(·,·).

canonical_topic.name: Angle-Based Diversity for Batch Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers MAO (Most Ambiguous and Orthogonal / maximum angle-based outlier) and related angle-based diversity criteria for batch-mode active learning in remote sensing classification. Starting from a margin-based uncertainty set, MAO iteratively selects samples that are both highly ambiguous and as orthogonal as possible to already chosen points in feature or kernel space, thus explicitly enforcing diversity within each batch. Orthogonality or dissimilarity is quantified via angular distance or kernel similarity between feature vectors, preferring candidates that are least similar to the current batch. The framework is modular and allows user-defined diversity measures such as MAO, cSV, and ABD, enabling tailoring of the diversity notion to specific data characteristics while remaining grounded in an active learning selection loop.

local_topics.title: Challenges of high-dimensional density estimation
local_topics.description: Density-based AL relies on accurate density estimation, which becomes difficult in high-dimensional feature spaces. Common density estimators like kernel density estimation and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) struggle with scalability and accuracy as dimensionality increases. This limitation constrains the effectiveness of density-based representativeness measures in modern high-dimensional medical image representations.

canonical_topic.name: Density-based Representativeness in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on density-based active learning strategies that aim to select representative samples by modeling the data distribution, particularly in deep representations of medical images. It highlights that traditional density estimators such as kernel density estimation and Gaussian Mixture Models become unreliable and inefficient in high-dimensional feature spaces common in deep models. These limitations reduce the effectiveness of representativeness-based acquisition functions in modern deep active learning pipelines. To address this, the topic proposes the use of advanced generative density estimators, especially normalizing flows, which are better suited to high-dimensional distributions. Integrating such high-capacity density models into density-based active learning could yield more accurate representativeness measures and improve sample selection for complex medical image datasets.

local_topics.title: General diversity-based batch selection algorithm
local_topics.description: Algorithm 2 formalizes a generic procedure for diversity-based selection in a single active learning iteration. Starting from a reduced candidate set U* (already filtered by a base heuristic like margin sampling), the algorithm first picks the best candidate under the base criterion, then repeatedly adds samples that maximize a user-defined diversity measure with respect to the current batch S. After q pixels are selected, the batch is labeled, added to the training set, and removed from the candidate pool. This process operationalizes batch-mode active learning where exploitation (uncertainty) and exploration (diversity) are explicitly balanced.

Using self-supervised features, it performs k-Means clustering and then selects samples from high-density regions of each cluster, effectively choosing prototypical points. This typicality-driven strategy aims to maximize the representativeness of the initial labeled set, improving label efficiency in the cold-start phase. It contrasts with purely uncertainty-based selection by prioritizing data density and coverage.

canonical_topic.name: TypiClust: Density-Based Typicality for Cold-Start Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: TypiClust is a deep active learning strategy that prioritizes querying "typical" samples based on data density in a learned feature space, particularly targeting the cold-start phase with very limited annotation budgets. To ensure coverage and reduce redundancy, TypiClust performs clustering (e.g., k-Means) and selects high-density, prototypical points from each cluster, yielding a diverse yet representative initial labeled set. This approach contrasts with purely uncertainty-based selection by emphasizing representativeness and coverage of the data manifold rather than model predictive uncertainty. As a result, TypiClust aims to improve label efficiency early in the active learning process, where uncertainty estimates are often unreliable.
