These methods are evaluated on benchmarks such as OPUS, UNPC, IWSLT, and WMT across various language pairs, with improvements typically measured by BLEU under constrained human translation budgets. Overall, the focus is on optimizing which sentences to translate so as to achieve better MT performance than non-active, random, or heuristic selection given the same labeling cost.

Expected loss/error reduction methods estimate how much the test error or predictive variance would decrease if an instance were labeled and used for training, often requiring a model of label or parameter uncertainty to evaluate hypothetical updates. Closely related are expected model change strategies, which prioritize points whose (unknown) labels are predicted to induce the largest change in model parameters or predictions, for example via estimated gradient updates. In deep active learning and streaming settings, these ideas are instantiated with approximations that make repeated retraining or gradient estimation tractable, while still directly targeting performance improvement. Together, these approaches form a principled family of acquisition functions that explicitly link each query to anticipated gains in generalization.

canonical_topic.name: Human-in-the-Loop Interaction in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic views active learning explicitly as a human-in-the-loop framework where models iteratively solicit targeted supervision from human annotators. It emphasizes how query strategies and acquisition decisions must be coupled with effective human–computer interaction mechanisms, including interfaces, feedback modalities, and interaction protocols that support annotators. In streaming or online active learning for data streams, the interaction design becomes time-critical, as humans must respond to real-time queries for the most informative instances. The discussion also highlights that different labeling scenarios and annotator configurations (e.g., multiple experts, varying expertise, or task constraints) can shape how queries are presented and how labels are acquired over time, directly influencing the efficiency and effectiveness of deep active learning under budget constraints.

local_topics.title: Drift detector categories in streams
local_topics.description: The section distinguishes three macro-categories of drift detectors for data streams: error-based, data distribution-based, and multiple hypothesis testing methods. Error-based detectors monitor online changes in the classifier’s error rate (e.g., DDM, ADWIN), while the other two focus on detecting changes in data distributions or use statistical testing. The text emphasizes that error-based methods usually require full label availability, whereas the latter two can be implemented in an unsupervised way. This classification frames which detectors are suitable under label-scarce active learning conditions.

local_topics.title: Error-based drift detection with sparse labels
local_topics.description: To address the need for labels in detecting concept drift, Krawczyk et al. propose applying an error-based drift detector to the few labeled instances obtained during online active learning. They employ ADWIN to monitor changes in performance on this sparse labeled subset and decide when to update or replace the current model. This yields a general framework that fuses active query selection with incremental model adaptation under drift. The approach leverages limited supervision efficiently instead of assuming labels for all instances.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: ADWIN-driven ensemble adaptation under drift
local_topics.description: An ensemble of N classifiers is maintained for online active learning in non-stationary data streams. The ADWIN drift detector monitors performance and, upon detecting concept drift, the classifier with the highest error is replaced by a newly trained model, enabling continual adaptation. This ensemble replacement mechanism allows the active learner to track evolving concepts while operating under streaming constraints.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Concept Drift Detection in Stream-based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic examines how concept drift detectors are integrated into stream-based active learning under label scarcity. It contrasts error-based drift detectors, such as DDM and ADWIN, which traditionally require continuous labeled feedback, with distribution-based and multiple-hypothesis testing approaches that can operate in an unsupervised manner—highlighting their suitability when query budgets are tight. The cluster focuses on reusing the sparse labels acquired by an online active learner to drive error-based drift detection, enabling performance monitoring without assuming full supervision. Within this framework, ADWIN-triggered adaptation is applied to ensembles, where the worst-performing classifier is replaced upon drift detection, allowing the active learner to continually track evolving concepts in non-stationary data streams. Overall, the topic emphasizes the fusion of query selection and incremental model adaptation to handle drift efficiently with limited annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Time-variable uncertainty thresholds for budgeting
local_topics.description: The section presents a time-variable thresholding scheme to adapt the labeling budget around detected drifts. Given a base uncertainty threshold and an adjustment parameter r, the threshold is progressively reduced when ADWIN signals a warning or a confirmed drift, making the classifier request more labels in those periods. This ensures the labeling rate during drift is strictly higher than in static conditions, so the model can quickly gather representative samples of the new concept. The mechanism explicitly connects drift signals to dynamic budget allocation in online active learning.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Piecewise constant labeling rate control
local_topics.description: A related strategy by Castellani et al. introduces a piecewise constant budget function for non-stationary data streams with verification latency. The labeling rate is raised from its nominal value α to a higher rate α_high when a drift is detected, then lowered to α_low, and finally restored to α. The durations of these phases are chosen so that the long-term average labeling rate equals the original α. This method offers a simple, interpretable control policy linking drift events to temporary budget boosts and reductions.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Adaptive labeling rate around drift events
local_topics.description: The labeling rate α is dynamically adjusted to focus annotation effort around suspected drift periods. When a drift warning or detection occurs, α is increased (to αhigh) to collect more labels and better characterize the new concept; it is later reduced (to αlow) and eventually restored to its nominal value as stability returns. This behavior is formalized as a piece-wise constant budget function that modulates the sampling rate over time relative to drift detection and recovery intervals.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Drift-Aware Budget Control in Stream-Based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses how stream-based active learning systems dynamically allocate labeling budget in the presence of concept drift. Drift detectors such as ADWIN trigger temporary increases in querying activity by either lowering uncertainty thresholds or raising the labeling rate, so that more informative samples are labeled when the underlying data distribution changes. Budget control is often modeled as a piecewise constant function over time, with phases of high, low, and nominal labeling rates tied to drift warnings, confirmed drifts, and post-drift stabilization. These strategies are designed so that the long-term average budget respects a predefined annotation rate, while still concentrating label requests during critical adaptation periods. The explicit coupling between drift signals and budget scheduling is a core design element for effective online deep active learning on non-stationary data streams.

local_topics.title: Intra- and extra-cluster sampling for batch streams
local_topics.description: Ienco et al. (2013) adapt a pre-clustering-based active learning method from pool-based to stream-based batch scenarios where only part of each block can be labeled. Their sampling strategy uses an extra-cluster metric to rank clusters and an intra-cluster metric to rank instances, relying on cluster homogeneity (number of predicted classes) to detect uncertain clusters and on representativeness (distance to centroid) and posterior-class probabilities to measure instance certainty. The learner alternates label queries across ranked clusters and their top-ranked instances.

local_topics.title: Micro-cluster based adaptive stream classification
local_topics.description: Yin et al. (2023) propose a data stream classification method that maintains and updates micro-clusters built from initial training data. Labels for new instances are acquired using a mixed querying strategy that combines random sampling with a class-weighted margin score, and the micro-cluster model is dynamically updated. This enables adaptation to concept drift while controlling labeling effort.

canonical_topic.name: WI-DL Hybrid Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic centers on WI-DL (Weighted Incremental Dictionary Learning) as a deep active learning framework that combines unsupervised feature learning with supervised fine-tuning under limited annotation budgets. Within a Deep Belief Network setting, WI-DL first performs unsupervised pretraining on both labeled and unlabeled data to learn representations, then applies supervised fine-tuning only on labeled samples to improve task performance efficiently in AL cycles. local_topics.title: KL-max heuristic using KL divergence
local_topics.description: The KL-max heuristic selects candidates whose inclusion in the training set maximizes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between posterior distributions before and after labeling. For each candidate, one estimates how much the posterior p(y|x) over the data would change if the candidate were added with its most likely label, and then chooses the sample producing the largest KL divergence. This strategy has been applied in remote sensing with probabilistic classifiers, including Maximum Likelihood classifiers, to prioritize pixels expected to induce the greatest model update. It formalizes informativeness in terms of distributional change rather than local uncertainty alone.

local_topics.title: KL-divergence active learning criterion
local_topics.description: A Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence-based criterion selects the next pixel to label by comparing posterior class distributions with and without including a candidate sample. For each candidate xi, a new posterior p+(ω|x) is computed using an augmented training set X+ that includes xi labeled with its most probable class y*i. The KL divergence between p+(ω|x) and the original posterior p(ω|x) is accumulated over all other unlabeled pixels, and the pixel that maximizes this expected divergence (equations (17) and (18)) is chosen. This approach explicitly targets samples that most change the model’s predictive distribution over the unlabeled pool.

local_topics.title: Posterior KL-max with multiple models
local_topics.description: Posterior KL-max is an active sampling heuristic that uses posterior class probabilities p(y|x) from multiple models and selects samples by maximizing a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence-related criterion. The notation '(q − 1) models' suggests an ensemble of probabilistic classifiers, each providing p(y|x), whose disagreement or divergence is exploited to measure informativeness. This approach targets samples where model posteriors differ most, aiming to reduce model uncertainty efficiently.

local_topics.title: KL-divergence-based Gaussian model update
local_topics.description: When a label yt for instance xt is queried, the Gaussian distribution over the classifier weights is updated by minimizing an objective based on the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. This constrains the posterior distribution to remain close to the previous one while incorporating the new labeled information, effectively performing a conservative update of μ and Σ. The KL-based formulation formalizes the trade-off between adapting to new data and preserving previous model knowledge in the streaming setting.

canonical_topic.name: KL-Divergence-Based Acquisition in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers active learning criteria that use Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to quantify the expected change in a model’s predictive distribution when querying a label. KL-max heuristics select instances whose inclusion in the labeled set maximizes the KL divergence between posterior class distributions before and after labeling, often aggregating this effect over the remaining unlabeled pool. Variants extend this idea to ensembles of probabilistic models, where disagreement in posterior class probabilities across models is captured via KL-related measures. In streaming settings with Bayesian or probabilistic models, KL-divergence is also used to regularize updates of the weight posterior, balancing adaptation to newly labeled data against staying close to the previous posterior. These KL-based criteria provide model- and task-agnostic acquisition functions that can be instantiated with deep probabilistic models in pool- and stream-based Deep Active Learning.

canonical_topic.name: Repeated Runs and Statistical Reporting in Deep Active Learning

These procedures enable more rigorous and fair comparison of deep active learning strategies across datasets and budget settings.

local_topics.title: Linear contextual bandits and active regression
local_topics.description: Linear bandits, a form of contextual bandit, assume that the expected reward of each arm is a linear function of its feature vector and an unknown parameter vector, with observed rewards modeled as r(x) = xᵀθ* + ε. The learner interactively chooses arms x to best estimate θ* under noise, closely mirroring active linear regression where informative data points are selected to learn an underlying linear system. This establishes a tight conceptual link between pure exploration in linear bandits and active learning for regression.

local_topics.title: Contextual-bandit ensemble for query selection
local_topics.description: Wassermann et al. (2019) model the sampling routine in online active learning as a contextual bandit problem where rewards measure the usefulness of query decisions. The learner receives positive reward ρ+ when requesting a label prevents a misclassification and negative reward ρ− when a query was unnecessary, thus penalizing ex-post useless label requests. An ensemble of models (experts) each decides whether to query based on prediction certainty exceeding a threshold, and experts are weighted by how past suggestions were rewarded and their agreement with others. The objective is to maximize cumulative reward over a time horizon T while adaptively allocating decision power across experts.

canonical_topic.name: Contextual Bandit Formulations for Stream-based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic frames stream-based active learning as a contextual bandit problem, where the decision to request a label is modeled as an action whose reward reflects its utility. Linear contextual bandits are tightly connected to active linear regression, since the learner sequentially selects feature vectors (arms) to estimate an unknown parameter vector under noise, mirroring informative sample selection for regression. In more applied settings, query selection is cast as maximizing cumulative reward, with positive rewards for label requests that prevent misclassifications and negative rewards for unnecessary queries. Ensembles of experts decide whether to query based on prediction certainty thresholds, and are adaptively weighted according to their past reward and agreement, yielding a learned querying policy. These formulations provide a principled, policy-learning view of acquisition strategies that can be combined with deep models in deep active learning for data streams.

local_topics.title: Informative hierarchical margin cluster sampling (hMCS-i)
local_topics.description: hMCS-i extends margin-based cluster sampling by hierarchically partitioning candidate data while explicitly handling bounded support vectors to reduce redundancy. At each iteration, a dataset composed of MCLU-optimized candidates (U_MCLU) and bounded support vectors from the previous iteration is recursively split in a binary fashion, always subdividing the largest current cluster. The process continues until q clusters that contain no bounded support vector are obtained, and then selection is restricted to candidates within those clusters, again minimizing the margin-based objective. This design controls overlap between iterations and maximizes informativeness by avoiding repeatedly sampling points near existing bounded support vectors.

canonical_topic.name: Evaluation Protocols for Stream-based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers how active learning methods for data streams are evaluated, with an emphasis on choosing protocols that match stream properties such as stationarity and concept drift. In stationary settings, a fixed holdout test set is commonly used to repeatedly assess performance as more labeled examples are acquired, enabling clear tracking of improvements due to the active sampling strategy. For non-stationary or drifting streams, prequential (online) evaluation is preferred, often combined with forgetting mechanisms such as sliding windows or fading factors so that performance estimates reflect current rather than historical behavior. The choice between holdout and prequential evaluation is thus closely tied to whether the active learning algorithm is designed to handle drift. In parallel, some works focus purely on theoretical analysis—studying sample or label complexity and regret bounds—without relying on empirical protocols, contributing formal guarantees that complement empirical evaluation of stream-based active learning.

canonical_topic.name: Transductive Experimental Design in Bandit-Based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers transductive experimental design in multi-armed bandit formulations of active learning, where queries are chosen from a set X to optimize predictions or decisions over a separate, fixed target set Z. Rather than aiming for global generalization, the learner exploits unlabeled points in Z to guide which arms in X to pull so as to improve performance specifically on Z. In the transductive best-arm identification setting, methods seek to infer the best arm or preference structure over Z using strategically selected pulls from X. Recent work also extends this to online and streaming scenarios, explicitly balancing time complexity (how many unlabeled instances are scanned) against label complexity (how many labels are queried) to determine when to stop and confidently declare the best arm. This framework directly connects bandit algorithms, label-efficiency, and task-focused generalization in active learning for data streams.

local_topics.title: Active distillation and teacher-student bias
local_topics.description: Active distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger pre-trained teacher model while actively selecting informative samples. Confirmation bias here arises when the student overfits to the teacher’s predictions, reproducing incorrect outputs instead of correcting them. To mitigate this, sample selection focuses on instances where the teacher is likely to err, encouraging the student to learn from discrepancies rather than blindly copying.

local_topics.title: Best-versus-second-best margin uncertainty
local_topics.description: Uncertainty of an unlabeled instance x_t is quantified as the difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities, margin(x_t) = p(y = c_b | x_t) − p(y = c_sb | x_t). This "best-versus-second-best" margin is highlighted as an effective uncertainty measure when many classes are present. The approach combines this with a Manhattan-distance-based similarity between unlabeled observations, but requires computing similarity and uncertainty for all unlabeled samples in a batch, making it unsuitable for single-pass streaming active learning.

canonical_topic.name: Margin-Based Uncertainty in Streaming Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on margin-based uncertainty measures as acquisition functions in deep and traditional active learning for data streams. One approach defines uncertainty as the distance of an instance to the classifier’s decision boundary or hyperplane (e.g., absolute perceptron margin), which makes points near the boundary more likely to be queried in streaming settings. Another widely used measure is the best-versus-second-best margin, which computes the difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities and is particularly effective in multi-class problems. These uncertainty scores are sometimes combined with similarity measures (e.g., Manhattan distance) to encourage diversity among selected instances, though such combinations may require computing uncertainty and similarity for all unlabeled samples, limiting their applicability in strict single-pass streaming scenarios. Overall, the topic highlights how different operationalizations of “distance to the decision boundary” govern label selection behavior under budget constraints in stream-based active learning.

local_topics.title: Bernoulli b-sampling query strategy
local_topics.description: The b-sampling method casts the query decision as a Bernoulli random variable whose parameter controls the probability of requesting a label. Proposed in early online active learning work by Cesa-Bianchi et al., this approach adjusts the Bernoulli parameter dynamically based on properties of the current instance. It provides a probabilistic alternative to hard thresholding, allowing stochastic control of labeling effort.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Margin-dependent query probability function
local_topics.description: The probability of querying the label at time t is defined as P_t = b / (b + |p_t|), where p_t is the current margin and b is a tuning parameter. This Bernoulli parameter decreases as the absolute margin increases, meaning that points near the decision boundary (low |p_t|) are more likely to be queried. The mechanism formalizes uncertainty sampling in a probabilistic way, linking model confidence directly to labeling probability.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Logistic Margin Sampling Probability
local_topics.description: This topic focuses on the logistic margin sampling rule where the label-query decision is modeled as a Bernoulli variable Z_t with parameter P_t = e^{−γ|p_t|}. The probability of querying decreases exponentially with the absolute margin, again interpreting uncertainty as distance from the decision hyperplane. Compared to the traditional b-sampling P_t = b / (b + |p_t|), the logistic form yields a different sampling distribution over margins, affecting how sharply the querying probability decays as confidence increases.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Randomized querying via Bernoulli and exponential mechanism
local_topics.description: To privatize the querying process, labeling decisions are modeled either as a Bernoulli random variable with parameter p (or 1−p) depending on whether c(t) is below or above a threshold τ, with p < 1/2, or via the exponential mechanism. In the latter, a Bernoulli with parameter q(t) assigns a constant labeling probability to points within a sampling region of radius α and an exponentially decaying probability to points outside, with q(t) defined using ε and Δ = (1 − α/M)^M under the assumption ||x_t|| ≤ M. These constructions inject controlled randomness while still favoring informative, near-boundary instances in the data stream.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Probabilistic Margin-Based Querying for Data Streams
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers stream-based active learning strategies that model the label-query decision as a Bernoulli random variable whose parameter encodes instance informativeness. Classical b-sampling and related rules define the query probability as a function of the current margin, so that points near the decision boundary receive higher labeling probability, turning uncertainty sampling into a smooth, probabilistic acquisition function. Variants include rational forms such as P_t = b / (b + |p_t|) and logistic/exponential forms like P_t = e^{−γ|p_t|}, which control how sharply the querying rate decays as model confidence increases, thereby tuning the trade-off between exploration and label budget. Further extensions introduce randomized querying mechanisms (including exponential mechanisms) that adjust Bernoulli parameters based on distance to a sampling region and privacy parameters, injecting controlled randomness while still favoring near-boundary instances in a data stream. These probabilistic query schemes are directly applicable in deep active learning pipelines by plugging them into streaming or online deep models to manage annotation effort over time.

local_topics.title: Label delay and verification latency
local_topics.description: This topic addresses the impact of label delay (verification latency) in online active learning, defined as the time between a query and the oracle’s provision of the label. If latency is not considered, the learner may issue redundant label requests for similar instances while earlier queries are still unresolved. Latency is categorized into null, intermediate, and extreme latency, with null latency corresponding to the common but idealized case of immediate label availability. Sampling strategies must explicitly account for these latency regimes to manage queries and model updates effectively in streaming scenarios.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Label latency in online active learning
local_topics.description: The text distinguishes different regimes of label latency in data streams, ranging from extreme latency (labels never arrive) to intermediate latency, where labels are delayed by a finite but non-zero time L. Extreme latency pushes the problem toward unsupervised learning, as no oracle feedback is ever obtained. Intermediate latency settings must explicitly handle delayed supervision, affecting how and when models can be updated using oracle-provided labels.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Handling verification latency via spatial information
local_topics.description: To cope with verification latency, the authors leverage the spatial locations of queried but not yet labeled points to guide future sampling. By recognizing regions where many nearby instances already have high utility (low confidence), the method avoids oversampling in those areas while labels are pending. This spatial awareness helps distribute queries more effectively across the input space under delayed feedback. It adapts active learning decisions to the structure of unlabeled regions and ongoing queries.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Verification latency in streaming active learning
local_topics.description: Verification latency refers to the delay between querying a label for a selected instance and receiving it from the oracle (tyi > txi). During this delay, the learner continues to process new instances without being able to update its utility function or decision threshold, which can lead to redundant label requests for similar instances and policy updates based on outdated information. This latency critically affects methods whose querying decisions depend on recently labeled neighbors or timely classifier updates in drifting data streams.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Label quality and imperfect oracles
local_topics.description: The effectiveness of online active learning heavily depends on the quality of labels obtained from human annotators or other oracles. Real-world annotators may introduce errors, biases, or inconsistent interpretations of labeling instructions, and oracle imperfections must be considered, including cases like knowledge distillation where the oracle itself is a model. Additionally, label delays or latency complicate learning from streams, as highlighted earlier in the survey.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Postponed annotation and verification latency
local_topics.description: This topic covers active learning settings where there is a temporal gap between querying an instance and receiving its label, modeled as verification latency. Methods that explicitly consider delayed labels must handle scenarios where the learner continues to operate and query new data while earlier queries remain unlabeled. This affects query strategies, buffer management, and how models are updated when labels eventually arrive.

local_topics.title: Real-world sources of delayed labels
local_topics.description: This topic highlights practical situations where label revelation is inherently delayed, such as physical quality inspections or medical treatments that must complete before an outcome is known. In these domains, the ground-truth label corresponds to the result of a process that unfolds over time, creating structured delays between data collection and annotation. Active learning strategies must therefore accommodate non-instantaneous feedback loops.

canonical_topic.name: Verification Latency in Streaming Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers verification latency (label delay) in streaming and online active learning, where there is a temporal gap between querying an instance and receiving its label from the oracle. Latency regimes range from null (immediate labels), through intermediate (finite delay), to extreme (labels never arrive, approaching unsupervised learning), each imposing different constraints on how query strategies and model updates can be designed. During the delay, the learner continues to process and query new instances, risking redundant requests in regions where multiple unlabeled, high-utility samples accumulate and forcing policy updates to rely on outdated information under concept drift. Methods therefore need mechanisms such as spatial awareness of pending queries, buffer management, and explicit handling of delayed supervision to distribute queries effectively across the input space and time. The discussion also emphasizes realistic sources of delayed labels (e.g., medical outcomes, physical inspections) and the compounding effects of imperfect oracles, making verification latency a central practical concern for stream-based active learning systems.

canonical_topic.name: Annotation Burden in Medical Image Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This cluster highlights the substantial time and expert labor required for fine-grained annotation of medical images, especially for tasks such as detailed segmentation and pathology slide analysis. Because annotations must be precise and clinically reliable, they demand intensive involvement of highly trained medical professionals, whose time is scarce. This high annotation cost is a primary motivation for deep active learning in medical imaging, where methods are designed to minimize the number of labeled samples needed while maintaining performance. In the DAL context, these constraints directly shape query strategies, budget allocation, and evaluation criteria, as algorithms aim to alleviate the annotation bottleneck in real-world clinical workflows.

local_topics.title: Stopping Criteria for Active Learning
local_topics.description: Determining when to stop querying is treated as a key component of the AL process, balancing further performance gains against additional annotation cost. Stopping criteria can be based on model confidence, validation performance, stability of predictions, or budget limits. The survey devotes a subsection to summarizing and comparing these stopping methods in NLP applications.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Need for and heuristics of AL stopping
local_topics.description: In practical applications, it is important to know when to stop active learning so that annotation is halted once model performance approaches its upper bound, before the labeling budget is exhausted. This requires stopping criteria that monitor appropriate metrics during AL. Simple heuristic criteria include stopping when all unlabeled instances lie farther from an SVM’s support vectors than labeled ones, or when no new n-grams are present in the unlabeled pool for machine translation.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Metrics for active learning stopping decisions
local_topics.description: Designing stopping criteria involves choosing appropriate metrics, which may include performance on a development set, cross-validation estimates, or query-strategy-derived measures. Standard dev sets can be too small and cross-validation may be biased due to AL’s non-uniform sampling. Alternative metrics include uncertainty or confidence scores, disagreement among models, estimated performance, expected error, confidence variation, actual performance on queried instances, and stability of predictions between consecutive AL iterations.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Threshold and trend-based stopping conditions
local_topics.description: Stopping conditions typically compare metric values against thresholds, but directly thresholding a single iteration’s metric (e.g., uncertainty or error below a fixed level) is sensitive to the specific model and task. To improve robustness, some approaches cascade multiple criteria, while others track metric trends over several AL iterations. Trend-based strategies stop when confidence consistently drops, the rate of performance change flattens, or prediction outputs stabilize across iterations.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Relation to performance prediction and early stopping
local_topics.description: Stopping active learning is related to broader tasks such as predicting final model performance and performing early stopping during training. This connection is particularly important in early AL stages, which correspond to low-resource learning scenarios where data are scarce. Determining when to halt learning in these stages may require specialized early-stopping considerations aligned with AL’s incremental annotation process.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Predefined DeepAL stopping criteria
local_topics.description: Many DeepAL systems rely on simple, predefined stopping rules such as maximum iteration count, minimum change in accuracy, minimum number of labeled samples, or expected accuracy thresholds. These criteria determine when to stop querying labels from the oracle. However, the survey notes that such simple heuristics can lead to suboptimal performance through either premature stopping or unnecessary labeling.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Stopping Strategies for Deep Active Learning
local_topics.description: This topic covers criteria and algorithms for deciding when to stop querying additional labels in DeepAL. It includes performance-based heuristics, convergence indicators, and uncertainty or stability measures that signal diminishing returns from further annotation. Effective stopping strategies balance annotation cost with target performance and prevent over-acquisition of redundant labeled data.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Stopping Criteria in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers methods for deciding when to stop querying additional labels in (deep) active learning so as to balance annotation cost against achievable performance. Stopping criteria leverage a variety of metrics, including development-set performance, cross-validation estimates adapted to non-uniform AL sampling, uncertainty or confidence scores, model disagreement, estimated error, prediction stability, and simple budget limits. Beyond single-threshold rules, more robust approaches cascade multiple conditions or track trends over several AL iterations, e.g., flattening performance gains or stabilized prediction outputs. In Deep Active Learning, many systems still rely on predefined heuristics such as maximum iteration count, minimum labeled sample size, or target accuracy thresholds, which risk premature stopping or unnecessary over-labeling. The literature also connects AL stopping decisions to broader questions of performance prediction and early stopping in low-resource, incremental training scenarios.

local_topics.title: Norm-thresholding for online active regression
local_topics.description: Riquelme’s norm-thresholding algorithm applies A-optimality ideas to online active linear regression in data streams. Only observations whose (scaled) norms exceed a threshold τ are selected for labeling, where τ is set so that P(∥x∥ ≥ τ) = α, with α representing the desired fraction of labeled points in the stream. This yields a near A-optimal design by preferentially including more informative, high-norm covariate vectors.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Norm-thresholding for online active regression
local_topics.description: The section presents a norm-thresholding criterion for selecting which streaming data points to label in online active linear regression. A point xt is queried if its leverage score x_t^T (X^T X)^{-1} x_t exceeds a threshold τ, approximating a target sampling rate α. This design-optimality-based rule aims to prioritize points that most reduce prediction variance by using the current labeled design matrix X. The criterion is formalized in Equation (43) and operationalized within Algorithm 5.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Norm-Thresholding for Stream-Based Active Regression
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers norm-thresholding criteria for online active learning in linear regression over data streams. The core idea is to select only those streaming instances whose norm or leverage score exceeds a threshold, thereby prioritizing samples that most reduce prediction variance. The threshold is calibrated to match a target labeling rate α, so that only a desired fraction of incoming points are queried, enabling explicit control of the annotation budget in a streaming setting. By connecting selection to A-optimal design, the method yields near design-optimal labeled sets using either scaled norms or leverage scores computed from the current labeled design matrix. These strategies exemplify theory-driven acquisition rules for stream-based active regression that can inform analogous designs in deep active learning contexts.

local_topics.title: K-Means on self-supervised features
local_topics.description: Pourahmadi et al. perform K-Means clustering on off-the-shelf self-supervised feature embeddings extracted from medical images. Cluster centers in this feature space are then selected as informative samples for annotation. This approach combines representation learning without labels with a simple clustering-based selection strategy in active learning.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: K-Means++ with silhouette-based model selection
local_topics.description: Jin et al. use K-Means++ for clustering self-supervised medical image features and employ the silhouette coefficient to automatically determine the optimal number of clusters. This combination improves cluster quality and robustness of the active learning selection process. Their method is applied to lung segmentation in chest X-rays and lesion segmentation in dermoscopic images, achieving strong performance with reduced annotation.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Clustering-Based Deep Active Learning with Self-Supervised Features
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers clustering-based deep active learning methods that operate on self-supervised feature embeddings, primarily in medical image analysis. Off-the-shelf self-supervised models are used to extract rich representations from unlabeled medical images, on which K-Means or K-Means++ clustering is performed. Cluster centers in this feature space are selected as representative and informative samples for annotation, effectively approximating diversity-based selection without requiring label information. Silhouette-based model selection is employed to automatically determine the optimal number of clusters, improving cluster quality and the robustness of the acquisition process. These methods have been shown to reduce annotation effort while maintaining strong performance in tasks such as lung and lesion segmentation.

local_topics.title: Multiple remote sensing scenarios for evaluation
local_topics.description: The study evaluates active learning heuristics on three challenging remote sensing classification scenarios, illustrating them in Figure 2 and detailing their data distributions in Figure 3. This multi-scenario design ensures that algorithm performance is assessed across diverse spatial and spectral conditions. It emphasizes the need for robust active learning methods that generalize beyond a single dataset.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Evaluation on multispectral and hyperspectral datasets
local_topics.description: The surveyed heuristics are applied to three challenging remote sensing datasets covering multispectral and hyperspectral image classification tasks. Performance comparisons analyze classification behavior, advantages, and drawbacks across these different spectral resolutions. This experimental setup assesses how active learning strategies scale and adapt to high-dimensional spectral data.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

canonical_topic.name: Active Learning Evaluation in Remote Sensing Scenarios
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the evaluation of active learning heuristics across multiple remote sensing classification scenarios, emphasizing robustness and generalization beyond a single dataset. Studies assess performance on diverse spatial and spectral conditions, including both multispectral and hyperspectral imagery. The experimental setups compare how different active learning strategies behave, highlighting their advantages and drawbacks when faced with varying spectral resolutions and high-dimensional feature spaces. These multi-scenario benchmarks are particularly relevant for designing and testing deep active learning methods for remote sensing, where scalability and adaptability to complex spectral data are critical.

local_topics.title: Selective Sampling Perceptron with b-sampling
local_topics.description: This topic describes an online active learning algorithm that processes a data stream using a linear perceptron model under a labeling budget. At each time step, the model computes the margin p_t = wᵗx_t, predicts the label via the sign of the margin, and draws a Bernoulli random variable Z_t with parameter P_t = b / (b + |p_t|) to decide whether to query the true label. Label requests are thus more likely when the margin is small (high uncertainty), causing the sampling probability to approach 1 as |p_t| → 0, and the algorithm tracks and constrains labeling cost c ≤ B over a time horizon T. This embodies a probabilistic uncertainty-based sampling strategy tailored for data streams.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Online Active Learning for Real-time Spam Filtering
local_topics.description: This topic describes an application-focused comparison of online active learning models—perceptron and SVM—in the context of real-time spam filtering. The study evaluates three instance selection criteria: fixed margin thresholding (Dasgupta et al., 2005), Bernoulli-based b-sampling (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004), and a newly proposed logistic margin sampling strategy. The perceptron is updated with Dasgupta-style reflection updates, while the SVM is retrained on all labeled data whenever new labels are acquired, enabling a comparative analysis of model-update regimes and querying policies for streaming spam data.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Passive-Aggressive Variant of Selective Sampling
local_topics.description: This topic refers to an extension of the selective sampling perceptron where a passive-aggressive learning rule is used in an online active learning setting. At each time step, a Bernoulli random variable Z_t is again drawn to decide whether to query the label of the current instance x_t, but the parameterization of Z_t and the subsequent model update follow a passive-aggressive scheme rather than a standard perceptron update. This integrates margin-based selective querying with more aggressive corrective updates when misclassifications occur.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Passive-aggressive updates for online learning
local_topics.description: Instead of the traditional perceptron rule that updates only on misclassified examples, passive-aggressive learning updates the weight vector wt ∈ R^d whenever the current loss ℓt(wt−1; (xt, yt)) is nonzero. The new parameter vector is given by wt = wt−1 + τt yt xt, where the step size τt is computed according to different policies involving the loss, the norm of xt, and a penalty cost parameter κ. This aggressive update strategy ensures that even correctly classified but low-confidence examples can influence the model, reducing the risk of wasting informative data points.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Online active learning with expert advice
local_topics.description: This algorithm processes a data stream sequentially, using the predictions of N experts fi,t(xt) to form a combined prediction pt for each incoming instance xt under a labeling budget B and time horizon T. A Bernoulli random variable Zt with parameter Pt = b / (b + |pt̃|) governs whether the instance is considered for labeling, and Equations 24 or 25 (referenced but not shown) determine the final sampling decision. If the condition is not met, the true label yt is queried and the labeling cost counter c is incremented. This setup formalizes online querying decisions driven by expert advice and a probabilistic sampling mechanism.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Selective Sampling in Online Active Learning for Data Streams
canonical_topic.description: This cluster focuses on stream-based online active learning methods that use probabilistic, margin-based selective sampling under an explicit labeling budget. Core algorithms compute a prediction margin and then draw a Bernoulli random variable with parameter b / (b + |margin|) to decide whether to query the label, making low-margin (uncertain) instances much more likely to be labeled while keeping the total labeling cost within a budget over a time horizon. Variants differ mainly in the underlying online learner, including perceptron and passive-aggressive update rules, where the latter adjusts the step size based on the incurred loss to more aggressively correct low-confidence or misclassified examples. Another variant aggregates predictions from multiple experts and applies the same Bernoulli-based querying mechanism to the combined margin, formalizing expert-advice–driven querying. These strategies are evaluated in application settings such as real-time spam filtering, comparing different margin-based querying rules (fixed threshold, Bernoulli b-sampling, logistic margin) and model-update regimes for streaming data.

local_topics.title: Incremental training across AL cycles
local_topics.description: Incremental training, where a deep model is updated rather than retrained from scratch in each active learning cycle, is highlighted as an important research direction. Training from scratch every cycle is computationally prohibitive, but naïve incremental updates can lead to parameter drift and degraded performance. Despite limited existing work, the potential resource savings make improved incremental training schemes highly attractive.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Incremental training in active data streams
local_topics.description: Incremental training updates model parameters using small batches of new labeled data without restarting training from scratch. This allows the model to incorporate new information while preserving previously acquired knowledge, often via fine-tuning or techniques such as elastic weight consolidation to prevent catastrophic forgetting. It is particularly suited to streaming and online active learning scenarios where data arrive continuously and queries are limited.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Complete retraining for evolving data streams
local_topics.description: Complete re-training creates a new model from scratch using all labeled data accumulated so far, discarding the previous model’s parameters. This strategy is typically chosen when a substantial amount of new data arrives, concept drift makes the previous model obsolete, or architectural changes are required. While potentially more accurate in such situations, it can lose previously encoded structure and is computationally more expensive, directly impacting online active learning efficiency.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Incremental vs Full Retraining in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Deep active learning often proceeds in multiple cycles or within continuous data streams, forcing a design choice between incremental training and complete retraining. Incremental training updates a model with newly labeled data while retaining prior parameters, greatly reducing computational cost but risking parameter drift and catastrophic forgetting if not carefully controlled. In streaming and online active learning, such incremental schemes—possibly augmented with regularization methods like elastic weight consolidation—are especially attractive because data and queries arrive continuously. By contrast, complete retraining from scratch on all accumulated labeled data can yield better adaptation under substantial distribution or concept drift, or when architectural changes are needed, but is far more expensive and can reduce overall efficiency of online active learning. Balancing these strategies is therefore a key practical question for scalable and adaptive deep active learning systems.

local_topics.title: Model-agnostic active learning for regression
local_topics.description: The authors propose developing model-agnostic active learning methods that can be applied across diverse regression models. Such approaches would not depend on specific model internals (e.g., gradients or posterior forms) and thus could be reused with different nonlinear or linear regressors. This flexibility is viewed as valuable for broad applicability in streaming regression tasks.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Single-model versus ensemble strategies
local_topics.description: The table contrasts online active learning methods that use a single model with those employing ensembles across different data stream assumptions and processing modes. Ensemble-based approaches are especially noted under stationary and drifting classification tasks, where multiple models can provide diverse uncertainty estimates or robustness to drift. Single-model strategies, in contrast, are more prevalent for regression, evolving streams, and object detection, reflecting differing complexity and resource trade-offs.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Model-agnostic single-pass active learning
local_topics.description: The authors highlight future research opportunities in developing model-agnostic and single-pass online active learning strategies. Model-agnostic methods can interface with diverse underlying learners without relying on model-specific assumptions, improving generality and ease of adoption. Single-pass algorithms must process each streaming instance at most once, aligning with practical constraints on memory and computation in real-world systems. This topic focuses on algorithmic design goals that enhance scalability and applicability of active learning for data streams.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Model-Agnostic Online Active Learning for Data Streams
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on model-agnostic active learning strategies designed for streaming scenarios, including both classification and regression tasks. The emphasis is on methods that do not rely on specific model internals, enabling reuse across diverse linear and nonlinear learners in online and single-pass settings. In data streams, such approaches must work under strict memory and computation constraints, often processing each instance at most once while deciding whether to query its label. The cluster also contrasts single-model and ensemble-based strategies: ensembles are highlighted for stationary and drifting classification streams where diverse uncertainty estimates and robustness to drift are beneficial, whereas single-model approaches are more common in regression, evolving streams, and object detection due to complexity and resource trade-offs.

local_topics.title: Influence of active learning batch size
local_topics.description: The study evaluates the impact of AL batch size b on DAL performance, comparing sizes such as 500, 1000, and 2000. Results show that batch size has relatively little effect on performance for methods like Entropy, which achieve similar AUBC across different batch sizes. This weak sensitivity is important in practice because larger batches can be used to reduce the number of AL training cycles without significantly affecting model quality.
local_topics.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Batch size scaling and large-scale AL
local_topics.description: The section analyzes how batch size affects active learning performance, contrasting strategies optimized for small batches with work advocating very large query sizes (e.g., 10k–500k samples). One approach scales AL to large datasets by integrating hundreds of models and reusing intermediate checkpoints to search training data in a distributed manner at low computational cost. Empirical results indicate that training on the full dataset is not necessarily optimal and that carefully selected subsets via AL can yield superior performance.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Batch Size and Scalability in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic examines how the query batch size in deep active learning influences performance and scalability. Empirical studies show that for common uncertainty-based methods such as Entropy, performance metrics like AUBC are often weakly sensitive to batch size, allowing practitioners to use larger batches to reduce the number of AL cycles without substantial quality loss. At the same time, other work explores scaling AL to very large datasets with large query sizes (e.g., 10k–500k samples), leveraging distributed training, multiple model instances, and checkpoint reuse to search the pool efficiently. These results highlight that carefully selected subsets via AL can outperform training on the full dataset, and that batch size is a key practical lever for balancing annotation efficiency, computational cost, and model performance in DAL.

The method’s accuracy improves over successive annotation steps, indicating how BADGE selects informative samples under a constrained labeling budget. The reported means and variances provide insight into both effectiveness and stability across runs.

local_topics.title: BADGE performance across labeling budgets
local_topics.description: The section presents area under the curve (AUC) scores for the BADGE active learning strategy at several annotation budget levels, each reported with mean and standard deviation (e.g., 0.5601 ± 0.0373 to 0.6172 ± 0.0890). This quantifies how BADGE’s classification performance improves as more labeled data are acquired. The use of AUC suggests evaluation over the full operating range of the classifier rather than at a single threshold.

local_topics.title: Active learning for cardiac MRI segmentation
local_topics.description: This topic covers the evaluation of multiple active learning strategies for cardiac MRI segmentation on the ACDC dataset. Methods such as BADGE, Core-Set-L2, Core-Set-Cosine, Random, Confidence, Entropy, and Margin are compared against a fully supervised baseline. local_topics.title: Fine-grained partial-structure querying
local_topics.description: Partial-structure active learning decomposes structured outputs into fine-grained annotation units and queries only some of them, such as individual tokens, word boundaries, syntactic-unit pairs, or mention pairs. Query strategies at this level resemble classification AL but typically require inference to compute marginal probabilities for sub-structures. When full structured labels are ultimately needed, semi-supervised methods like self-training are used to automatically fill in unannotated parts with pseudo-labels.

local_topics.title: Learning models from partial annotations
local_topics.description: Under partial-structure AL, output modeling must accommodate incomplete labels. Local discriminative models that treat each sub-structure independently can use partial labels directly, while global structured models require specialized algorithms to learn from incomplete annotations. Global models exploit constraints and label interactions so that annotated parts reduce the uncertainty of unannotated parts, enabling better query selection, efficient batch-mode selection via cheap re-inference, and interactive correction where annotator edits propagate through the structure.

local_topics.title: Partial feedback for large-label classification
local_topics.description: Classification tasks with many possible labels can be reframed as structured prediction with partially observed outputs to simplify annotation. Instead of requiring a full label choice, annotators provide partial feedback such as answering yes/no queries about specific labels or eliminating clearly incorrect classes. This reduces per-instance annotation difficulty while still providing informative supervision for active learning.

canonical_topic.name: Partial-Structure Queries and Partial Feedback in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers active learning settings where only parts of a structured output or label space are annotated, reducing annotation burden while preserving informative supervision. In partial-structure active learning, complex outputs (e.g., token sequences, syntactic units, mention pairs) are decomposed into fine-grained units, and query strategies select which sub-structures to label, often requiring inference to obtain marginal probabilities over these components. Learning from such incomplete annotations demands models that can exploit structure: local discriminative models treat sub-structures independently, whereas global structured models use constraints and label interactions so that annotated parts decrease uncertainty in unannotated regions, enabling better query selection, efficient batch selection, and interactive correction. Semi-supervised techniques such as self-training or pseudo-labeling are used to fill in unannotated portions when full labels are ultimately needed. Relatedly, large-label classification can be reframed as structured prediction with partial feedback, where annotators answer yes/no questions about candidate labels or eliminate clearly incorrect classes, simplifying annotation while still guiding the active learner.

local_topics.title: Submodular information measures and SMI-based selection
local_topics.description: An active learning framework based on submodular information measures addresses challenges like rare classes, redundancy, and out-of-distribution samples by carefully designing submodular objectives. In object detection, a reference set of minority-class examples is used and unlabeled samples are selected according to their submodular mutual information (SMI) with this reference, thereby prioritizing labels that resemble the classes of interest. SMI between two sets A and B is defined from an underlying submodular function g as ISMI = g(A) + g(B) − g(A ∪ B), quantifying their shared information. This approach generalizes representativeness-based selection to set-level similarity and supports targeted querying for specific classes.

local_topics.title: Submodular mutual information for minorities

canonical_topic.name: Submodular Information Measures for Targeted Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that employ submodular information measures, particularly submodular mutual information (SMI), as acquisition functions to guide sample selection. By defining SMI between a labeled reference set and unlabeled candidates via an underlying submodular function, these methods quantify set-level shared information, enabling simultaneous modeling of informativeness, diversity, and redundancy control. In object detection and classification, a reference set is often constructed from minority-class or target-class examples, and unlabeled samples are selected based on high SMI with this set to prioritize annotations that resemble underrepresented or clinically important classes. The submodular structure allows for efficient, near-optimal subset selection, generalizing representativeness-based querying to targeted, class-aware selection. Empirical results on medical imaging datasets such as X-rays, pathology, and dermoscopy demonstrate that SMI-based selection can substantially improve performance on minority classes under limited labeling budgets.

canonical_topic.name: One-shot Annotation in Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
canonical_topic.description: One-shot annotation is a deep active learning setting where all samples to be labeled are selected in a single acquisition round, removing the need for repeated interactions with medical experts. It is motivated by practical constraints in medical image analysis, where physicians and radiologists are not continuously available and iterative annotation cycles can stall AL workflows. This setting focuses on maximizing the utility of a fixed, one-time labeling budget, requiring acquisition strategies that can identify a globally informative batch without feedback from later model updates. While it is related to cold-start active learning, one-shot annotation usually assumes a larger upfront annotation budget but strictly prohibits subsequent querying, which changes how sampling criteria and budget allocation are designed. As a result, one-shot strategies must carefully balance uncertainty, diversity, and coverage in a single selection to effectively bootstrap deep models for segmentation and other medical imaging tasks.

local_topics.title: BADGE: diverse gradient embeddings for batch AL
local_topics.description: BADGE (Batch Active learning by Diverse Gradient Embeddings) is highlighted as a pioneering deep learning–era method that selects samples using gradient-based embeddings. It computes gradients only for the final-layer parameters, using the model’s most confident class predictions as pseudo-labels, and then applies k-Means++ clustering on these gradient embeddings to choose a diverse, informative batch. The method achieves competitive performance across various datasets, architectures, and hyperparameter settings.

canonical_topic.name: BADGE Gradient-Embedding Hybrid Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers BADGE (Batch Active learning by Diverse Gradient Embeddings), a deep active learning strategy that uses per-sample loss gradients as joint representations of uncertainty and diversity. BADGE constructs gradient embeddings—typically for the final-layer parameters—using pseudo-labels from the model’s most confident predictions, and then applies k-Means++ clustering in this gradient space to select a batch that is both high-magnitude (informative) and well-dispersed (diverse). The gradient magnitudes serve as an uncertainty proxy grounded in how much a labeled update would change the model, while the clustering step explicitly mitigates redundancy, enabling a single acquisition rule to balance uncertainty and diversity without extra hyperparameters. Empirically, BADGE achieves strong and often state-of-the-art label efficiency across datasets and tasks (including classification and segmentation), especially in low-budget regimes, though its performance can degrade under distribution shifts or in very high-budget settings. Comparative studies show consistent AUBC gains over pure diversity methods such as k-Means, and performance competitive with or superior to leading uncertainty-based strategies, highlighting the effectiveness of gradient-informed hybrid selection in deep active learning.

local_topics.title: Margin sampling and support-vector targeting
local_topics.description: This topic focuses on the margin sampling (MS) heuristic, which seeks unlabeled pixels most likely to become support vectors if added to the training set. It leverages the sparse nature of SVMs, targeting points within the current margin as they are likely to receive non-zero αi weights. The text also notes MS as the most studied active learning algorithm in remote sensing, mentions early applications, and discusses subsequent variants that reduce the risk of selecting non-support-vector points.

local_topics.title: Margin sampling heuristic for SVMs
local_topics.description: Margin sampling (MS) exploits the geometric properties of SVMs, particularly that unbounded support vectors lie exactly on the margin with decision function value equal to one. The heuristic selects unlabeled samples whose minimum absolute distance to any class hyperplane is smallest, i.e., they are closest to some decision boundary. Formally, it chooses the unlabeled point minimizing the inner minimum over classes of |f(x_i, ω)|, where f(x_i, ω) is the SVM decision function (distance) for class ω. This operationalizes the idea of querying the most uncertain instances near the margin.

local_topics.title: Multiclass one-against-all distance modeling
local_topics.description: In a multiclass SVM setting, the method adopts a one-against-all decomposition, learning one hyperplane per class. For each candidate sample, its distance to each class-specific hyperplane is represented, as illustrated in Figs. 1(d–f). The margin sampling heuristic then operates over this set of per-class distances to determine which unlabeled sample lies closest to some decision boundary. This connects the geometric SVM view with multiclass active query selection.

local_topics.title: Over-confidence in deep neural uncertainty
local_topics.description: The section highlights that straightforward probability-based uncertainty metrics using a single forward pass are problematic for deep neural networks due to their tendency toward over-confidence. Over-confidence means assigning very high probabilities (e.g., 0.99) to incorrect predictions and extreme probabilities to inherently uncertain cases, which distorts the true uncertainty structure of the data. This miscalibration affects all class probabilities and undermines the reliability of uncertainty-based active learning strategies built solely on raw softmax scores.

canonical_topic.name: Overconfidence and Uncertainty Calibration in DAL
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns the tendency of deep neural networks to be over-confident in their predicted probabilities and the impact of this miscalibration on deep active learning. Simple probability-based uncertainty metrics derived from a single forward pass can assign extremely high confidence to incorrect or inherently ambiguous cases, distorting the underlying uncertainty structure of the data. Such miscalibrated softmax scores undermine uncertainty-based query selection, since samples may be chosen due to artifacts of overconfidence rather than genuine epistemic uncertainty. To enable reliable active learning, methods are needed that improve the calibration and quality of uncertainty estimates so that queried samples truly correspond to regions of high model uncertainty.

canonical_topic.name: Class-Balanced Sampling in Medical Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses how redundancy and class imbalance in medical images affect sampling strategies in deep active learning. At the same time, healthy cases vastly outnumber diseased ones, producing skewed label distributions that standard selection strategies typically do not correct. Deep active learning methods therefore need class-balance-aware acquisition functions or sampling schemes that explicitly counteract label skew while avoiding redundant queries. This is crucial to maintain performance on rare but clinically important classes under limited annotation budgets.

local_topics.description: Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) outputs evidence parameters of a Dirichlet distribution instead of point probability estimates, enabling the model to represent both predictions and associated uncertainty. This framework explicitly distinguishes confidence from uncertainty, making it naturally suited for active learning, where uncertain cases should be prioritized for labeling. In medical image analysis, an uncertainty-aware model with EDL can better identify ambiguous cases such as atypical lesions or poor-quality scans.

local_topics.title: Evidential Deep Learning for uncertainty
local_topics.description: Some methods adopt uncertainty-aware models based on Evidential Deep Learning (EDL), which output Dirichlet distribution parameters instead of point estimates. Uncertainty is measured using mutual information and entropy expectation over the Dirichlet distribution, providing a principled Bayesian-style confidence estimate. These evidential uncertainties are then used as acquisition scores in active learning loops.

canonical_topic.name: Evidential Deep Learning for Uncertainty-based Acquisition
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) to produce Dirichlet-distributed outputs that jointly encode class predictions and calibrated uncertainty for deep active learning. By modeling evidence parameters rather than point probabilities, EDL enables principled estimation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty via measures such as mutual information and expected entropy, which are then used directly as acquisition scores in active learning loops. In medical image analysis, this uncertainty-aware modeling helps prioritize ambiguous or low-quality cases, such as atypical lesions, for annotation. For object detection, specialized evidence heads are used to adaptively scale Dirichlet parameters and compute box-level epistemic uncertainty, which is then aggregated to image- or sample-level scores, enabling fine-grained selection of informative images under a labeling budget.

canonical_topic.name: Future Research Directions in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Future research in deep active learning focuses on improving query selection strategies, optimizing training procedures tightly coupled with querying, and developing task- and dataset-agnostic methods. Key open problems include establishing a stronger theoretical foundation for why and when specific acquisition functions work, and how they interact with deep model dynamics under limited label budgets. Scalability and robustness are central challenges, particularly for handling large unlabeled pools, distribution shifts, and noisy or adversarial labels in human-in-the-loop settings. Another important direction is better designing the human interaction loop—e.g., annotator guidance, feedback integration, and cost-aware querying—to maximize labeling efficiency. Finally, integrating DeepAL with self-supervised, semi-supervised, and continual learning paradigms is expected to yield more efficient, reliable, and broadly applicable active learning systems.

local_topics.title: Label-free gradient computation with pseudo labels
local_topics.description: Since true labels are unavailable for unlabeled samples in active learning, the described methods compute gradients without using ground truth. Instead, they rely on supervised losses with pseudo-labels (e.g., cross-entropy with pseudo-labels) or unsupervised losses (e.g., entropy loss), making gradient computation independent of true labels. This enables gradient-based uncertainty estimation directly on unlabeled data.

local_topics.title: Label-free gradient-norm sampling strategy
local_topics.description: This topic covers an active learning strategy where sample selection is based on gradient norms computed without ground-truth labels. Wang et al. (2022b) show mathematically that larger gradient norms correspond to a lower upper bound on test loss, motivating the use of such norms as an informativeness measure. They compute gradients using the expected empirical loss (a probability-weighted sum over class losses) and the entropy loss, both relying only on predicted class probabilities (Eqs. 5 and 6). This approach is applied to cryo-electron tomography subtomogram classification and shown to outperform competing methods.

canonical_topic.name: Label-Free Gradient-Based Acquisition in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on deep active learning strategies that compute gradient-based informativeness scores without access to true labels. Instead of using ground-truth annotations, gradients are obtained from supervised losses with pseudo-labels or from unsupervised objectives such as entropy, allowing uncertainty estimation directly on unlabeled data. A central idea is to use the norm of these label-free gradients as an acquisition score, with theoretical results indicating that larger gradient norms correspond to tighter upper bounds on test loss. In practice, this is implemented through expected empirical loss and entropy-based objectives that only depend on predicted class probabilities, enabling efficient sample selection in domains like cryo-electron tomography subtomogram classification. These methods extend gradient-based active learning (e.g., BADGE-style approaches) to settings where labels are entirely absent at query time, improving performance over competing selection strategies.

canonical_topic.name: Gradient-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers gradient-based uncertainty measures where a sample’s gradient with respect to model parameters quantifies its influence on learning and thus its informativeness for active querying. In deep active learning, especially for medical image analysis, larger gradient norms indicate samples that would induce larger parameter updates and are therefore treated as more uncertain and valuable for annotation. These methods are explicitly decoupled from predictive probabilities, making them less vulnerable to over-confident posterior estimates that can mislead probability-based acquisition functions. Several concrete metrics are used in this paradigm, including raw gradient norms, Fisher information approximations, and influence-function-based scores, which underpin multiple gradient-driven querying strategies.

local_topics.title: Fisher information-driven active learning objective
local_topics.description: This topic describes using Fisher information (FI) to quantify how data influence uncertainty in model parameters for active learning. FI is defined as the expectation of the squared gradients (or Hessian) of the loss with respect to model parameters (Eq. 7), capturing sensitivity of the model to data. The AL objective minimizes the trace of the inverse FI for a queried subset relative to the unlabeled pool (Eq. 8), so that selected samples accelerate convergence to optimal parameters. However, computing FI exactly scales quadratically with the number of parameters, making naive FI-based methods impractical for deep networks.
