canonical_topic.name: Fisher Information and Gradient-Based Acquisition
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that use gradients and Fisher Information (FI) to define acquisition functions. FI, computed from gradients or Hessians of the loss with respect to model parameters, quantifies how strongly candidate samples can influence parameter uncertainty and convergence, and selection objectives may minimize the trace of the inverse FI for the labeled subset relative to the pool. In practice, samples that induce large parameter gradients or high FI are treated as more informative and prioritized for annotation, directly tying query selection to the model’s local loss landscape rather than just output probabilities. Related methods extend this idea with influence scores measuring the impact of individual samples on the training loss, or with submodular coverage objectives that use gradient-based metrics to build diverse yet informative query sets. These approaches are particularly relevant in deep neural networks, but their exact FI computation can be expensive, motivating approximations to make FI- and gradient-based DAL scalable.

local_topics.title: Drift change rate and drift types
local_topics.description: The section introduces change rate as a key characteristic of distribution shifts, distinguishing how quickly new concepts enter the data stream. Four drift types are defined: abrupt drift, where the distribution changes sharply between consecutive time steps and requires immediate model updating; gradual drift, where overlapping distributions make detection and adaptation more difficult; incremental drift, where extremely slow and small-step changes in the data-generating process hinder detection; and recurring concepts, where previously seen concepts reappear cyclically, such as seasonal product popularity. These patterns inform the design of drift detection and adaptive learning strategies in streaming environments.

local_topics.title: Handling data drift in streams
local_topics.description: In streaming environments, underlying data distributions can shift over time, causing models to degrade if they cannot adapt. Such drift also affects which instances are considered informative, potentially invalidating previously effective query criteria. The text points to methods discussed in earlier sections that explicitly deal with dynamic, ever-changing behaviors as necessary tools in these scenarios.

canonical_topic.name: Concept Drift in Stream-Based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses how different types and rates of concept drift affect active learning in data streams and how models must adapt. Drift is characterized by how quickly the data-generating distribution changes, influencing when and how often active learners should update their models. Abrupt, gradual, and incremental drifts, as well as recurring concepts, each pose distinct challenges for detecting changes and maintaining reliable query criteria. Because drift alters which instances are most informative, active learning strategies for streams must integrate drift detection and adaptation to preserve the effectiveness of their selection mechanisms over time.

local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Active learning in prostate histopathology analysis
local_topics.description: This topic involves applying deep active learning to prostate histopathology images, typically for tasks such as cancer detection, grading, or region-level classification. Histopathology image annotation is particularly labor-intensive, so active learning aims to minimize expert labeling effort by selectively querying the most informative tissue patches. The focus is on improving diagnostic performance in prostate pathology while controlling annotation costs in whole-slide image analysis. The section briefly references this application area under 'Histopathology Prostate'.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Histopathology Gland Analysis
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods applied to histopathology, with a focus on patch-based classification and gland segmentation in colon and prostate tissue. Studies on the GlaS dataset formulate tasks at the patch level to capture fine-grained gland structures and reduce the need for exhaustive whole-slide annotations. Within an active learning framework, only subsets of patches are queried (e.g., small batch sizes, varying labeled proportions such as 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 50%), reflecting the high cost and effort of expert pathology labeling. These approaches extend active learning from diagnostic image-level classification to detailed structural segmentation, aiming to improve performance while tightly controlling the annotation budget. Similar strategies are discussed for prostate histopathology, where informative tissue patches are selectively labeled to support cancer detection and grading.

local_topics.title: DeepAL for Entity Resolution and NER
local_topics.description: Several works [34, 197, 199] explore combining deep learning and active learning to improve Named Entity Recognition and related entity resolution (ER) tasks under small training sets. The focus is on recognizing identical real-world entities across databases when labeled data is scarce. [109] extends this by integrating transfer learning with AL to build ER models transferable from high-resource to low-resource environments, improving performance under label constraints.

local_topics.title: Named entity recognition with DeepAL
local_topics.description: Deep active learning is used to train named entity recognition (NER) models over both general and domain-specific corpora. Benchmarks such as CoNLL, NCBI, MedMentions, OntoNotes, DBLP, FZ, AG, and Cora include entities from news, biomedical text, and scientific literature. Query strategies select the most informative sentences or spans for entity labeling, potentially incorporating sequence uncertainty and diversity. This reduces the cost of annotating entities across multiple ontologies and domains.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Entity-Centric NLP
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to build efficient models for entity-centric NLP tasks, particularly named entity recognition (NER) and entity resolution (ER), under limited labeling budgets. Deep models are trained on both general and domain-specific corpora, including news, biomedical text, and scientific literature, where annotated entities are expensive to obtain. Query strategies focus on selecting the most informative sentences or spans for annotation, often leveraging sequence-level uncertainty and diversity to maximize information gain per labeled example. In ER, deep active learning is further combined with transfer learning to adapt models from high-resource to low-resource domains, improving cross-database entity matching when labeled pairs are scarce. Overall, these methods aim to reduce annotation cost while preserving or improving performance across multiple ontologies and domains.

local_topics.title: Iterative annotation rounds in AL
local_topics.description: Active learning is structured into T annotation rounds, where each round incrementally improves the model using newly labeled data. In the t-th round (1 ≤ t ≤ T), the system operates on the current unlabeled pool and model state from the previous round. This iterative process allows gradual refinement of the model while controlling labeling cost over multiple cycles.

local_topics.title: Multi-round active learning procedure
local_topics.description: The study conducts active learning in T = 5 iterative annotation rounds. In each round, a batch of samples is queried according to a predefined annotation budget, then used to update the model. This setup allows observing performance evolution as labeled data accumulates over multiple AL cycles.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Multi-round Annotation in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Deep active learning experiments are often organized into multiple annotation rounds, where each round queries a batch of unlabeled samples and updates the model with the newly obtained labels. The process typically assumes a fixed total number of rounds T, with each t-th round operating on the current model state and remaining unlabeled pool. This iterative setup enables gradual refinement of model performance while explicitly controlling and monitoring the labeling cost across cycles. By evaluating performance after each round, researchers can analyze how the accumulation of labeled data influences learning dynamics and the efficiency of different query strategies under a fixed annotation budget.

local_topics.title: Disagreement-based query-by-committee methods
local_topics.description: Disagreement-based strategies use multiple models (a committee) and query instances where these models disagree most, exemplified by query-by-committee (QBC). Disagreement can be quantified via vote entropy, KL-divergence between predictive distributions, or variation ratio. Committees can be built from distinct models or via Bayesian treatments of a single model’s parameters, and dropout in neural networks provides a practical deep Bayesian approximation for estimating uncertainty.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Committee-based uncertainty via learner disagreement
local_topics.description: Committee-based active learning quantifies the uncertainty of a pixel by assembling a committee of learners, each based on different hypotheses about the classification problem. Each committee member independently labels candidate pixels in the pool, and the algorithm selects those samples that exhibit maximal disagreement among the committee’s predictions. This disagreement serves as the acquisition criterion for querying new labels. The approach is highlighted as the first major family of methods in the survey.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Committee-based batch active learning
local_topics.description: Several methods, such as EQB and AMD, are characterized as batch-mode active learning algorithms that rely on a committee of learners. They operate on multiclass problems (M), consider all candidates for selection, and require training k models, indicating that multiple classifiers jointly decide which samples to label. The absence of classifier diversity (marked ×) suggests that the committee members may be similar or identically parameterized models.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Disagreement-based active learning
local_topics.description: Disagreement-based strategies rely on multiple models or experts and focus on instances where their predictions diverge. By querying labels for points with high disagreement, the learner targets regions of hypothesis space that are poorly constrained by current data. Query by committee is a canonical method, using an ensemble of models to identify and score conflicting predictions.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Disagreement-Based and Committee Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers disagreement-based query strategies, particularly query-by-committee (QBC), where a committee of models is used to identify instances on which predictions most disagree. Disagreement is quantified via measures such as vote entropy, variation ratio, or KL-divergence between predictive distributions, and these scores define the acquisition criterion. Committees may be composed of heterogeneous models, or arise from Bayesian treatments of a single model’s parameters, with dropout in neural networks serving as a practical deep Bayesian approximation for uncertainty estimation. The methods extend naturally to batch-mode selection, where multiple samples are chosen jointly based on committee disagreement, although training k committee members can be computationally expensive for deep models and classifier diversity is not always guaranteed. Overall, these strategies target regions of the hypothesis space that remain poorly constrained by current labeled data, making them a core family of query methods for (deep) active learning in both pool-based and streaming settings.

local_topics.title: Entropy-based disagreement and informativeness
local_topics.description: Entropy of committee predictions is used as a measure of disagreement and thus informativeness of unlabeled samples. If all classifiers in the committee agree on a label for a candidate pixel, the entropy is zero, indicating that querying this sample would add little information to the training set. Conversely, when there is maximum disagreement among the classifiers, the entropy is high, and adding that pixel’s label is expected to be highly beneficial for the model. This links the nEQB criterion directly to the active learning objective of prioritizing uncertain and informative instances.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Model disagreement and vote entropy
local_topics.description: This topic focuses on committee-based active learning where multiple inferences from a model (or models) are used to measure disagreement. Vote Entropy quantifies how diverse the predictions are across the committee, with higher entropy indicating more informative, uncertain samples. Selection is often done at the patch level, choosing Top-k patches whose predictions show the greatest disagreement for annotation in dense prediction tasks.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Model disagreement with entropy-weighted Dice
local_topics.description: Multiple inference or ensemble-based active learning measures the disagreement between several segmentation predictions on the same medical image. Entropy-weighted Dice distance combines predictive uncertainty (via entropy) with segmentation overlap (Dice coefficient) to quantify how inconsistent and uncertain the predictions are. Samples with high entropy-weighted Dice distance are prioritized for annotation, as they are likely to be challenging and informative for improving the model.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Committee Disagreement and Entropy-Based Querying
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers committee- and ensemble-based query strategies in deep active learning that select samples by measuring prediction disagreement. Methods such as vote entropy and entropy over committee outputs quantify how diverse the predicted labels are, with higher entropy indicating greater uncertainty and expected informativeness. For dense prediction and segmentation tasks, selection can be done at the pixel or patch level, prioritizing regions where models disagree most. More advanced measures like entropy-weighted Dice distance combine predictive entropy with segmentation overlap to capture both uncertainty and structural inconsistency, focusing annotation on the most challenging medical images. These approaches directly operationalize the active learning objective of querying the most uncertain and informative instances under limited annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Active learning for multiple domains and languages
local_topics.description: In multi-target scenarios, active learning may need to select examples across multiple domains or multiple languages rather than a single setting. Strategies that consider all targets jointly, often via a single shared model, tend to outperform naively splitting budgets or focusing only on high-resource settings followed by transfer. This raises questions of how to optimally allocate annotation effort across heterogeneous but related targets.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Interaction of active learning and multi-task learning
local_topics.description: When there are multiple target tasks, multi-task learning (MTL) can be combined with active learning so that queried instances benefit several tasks simultaneously. Query strategies that consider all target tasks jointly can yield better overall performance than task-specific selection. This setting involves designing acquisition functions that exploit shared representations while balancing the needs of different tasks.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

canonical_topic.name: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Active Learning in NLP
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on active learning settings where annotation must be allocated across multiple domains, languages, or tasks, often in natural language processing. Instead of running separate active learning processes per target, a single shared model and joint selection strategy are used so that queried examples benefit several domains or tasks simultaneously. Central questions include how to design acquisition functions that consider all targets jointly, how to exploit shared representations, and how to balance improvements across heterogeneous but related targets. A key concern is how to optimally allocate a limited labeling budget across multiple domains or languages to avoid over-focusing on high-resource settings while still enabling effective transfer.

local_topics.title: Membership query synthesis and generative AL
local_topics.description: Membership query synthesis allows a learner to query any point in the input space for annotation, including synthetic samples generated by models, and is referred to in this survey as generative active learning. It is generally suitable for low-dimensional spaces, but in high-dimensional domains like images, generated instances may be unrecognizable to human annotators. This raises practical challenges when integrating generative models with human-in-the-loop labeling.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis
local_topics.section_heading: Problem Settings and Formulations of Active Learning

local_topics.title: Membership query synthesis scenario
local_topics.description: Membership query synthesis is an active learning scenario where the learner can request labels for any point in the input space, including synthetically generated instances not present in an existing unlabeled pool. This gives maximal flexibility to probe specific regions of the space, for example by generating adversarial or boundary-centered points. It is particularly relevant when the cost or feasibility of evaluating arbitrary queries is acceptable for the oracle.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Membership query synthesis active learning
local_topics.description: Membership query synthesis is an active learning strategy where the learner generates new synthetic instances and asks an oracle (e.g., a human annotator) for their labels. Instances can be created by modifying, combining, or transforming existing data to explore regions of the input space that have not yet been observed. A key drawback is that some generated samples may be unnatural or uninterpretable, making it impossible for annotators to assign meaningful labels. The process is typically iterated until a labeling budget is exhausted or a performance-based stopping criterion is met.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Synthetic query generation across domains
local_topics.description: Membership query synthesis is illustrated across several domains, each using domain-specific transformations to create informative synthetic data. In image classification and object detection, the learner generates modified or composite images from existing ones, while in NLP tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis, it creates synthetic sentences or paragraphs to cover a wider range of linguistic variations. In speech recognition, the system generates speech samples with different accents, pronunciations, and speaking styles to better model acoustic variability and improve recognition accuracy. These examples show how synthetic query design is tightly coupled to the structure and variability of the target domain.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Membership Query Synthesis and Generative Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers membership query synthesis, an active learning setting in which the learner is free to query labels for any point in the input space, including synthetically generated instances not present in a fixed unlabeled pool. In deep active learning, this often manifests as generative active learning, where models create or transform data (e.g., adversarial or boundary-centered examples) to probe informative regions of the feature space under a label budget and possible performance-based stopping criteria. While the approach offers maximal flexibility and can be tailored with domain-specific transformations in vision, NLP, and speech, it faces practical constraints: in high-dimensional domains like images or complex text, generated instances may be unnatural or uninterpretable for human annotators. Consequently, the design of synthetic query generation must balance informativeness with human interpretability and annotation feasibility in human-in-the-loop systems.

local_topics.title: Hybrid and combined DAL strategies
local_topics.description: Hybrid/combined DAL strategies integrate multiple querying criteria, typically by either weighted-sum optimization or two-stage optimization. Weighted-sum approaches jointly optimize a composite objective that balances, for example, uncertainty and diversity, while two-stage methods apply different criteria sequentially. The section associates these paradigms with methods such as CCAL, Exploitation-Exploration, WAAL, BADGE (DPPS version), and DBAL.
local_topics.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Combined querying and uncertainty–diversity trade-off
local_topics.description: Combined DAL strategies explicitly balance uncertainty-based informativeness with representative/diversity criteria, aiming to select large, diverse, yet decision-boundary-refining batches. The section frames this as a multi-objective optimization problem over uncertainty, diversity, and related metrics, and identifies combined methods as dominant in DAL practice. It distinguishes optimization approaches such as weighted-sum and multi-stage refinement.
local_topics.article_title: A comparative survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Hybrid Deep Active Learning Query Strategies
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers hybrid and combined deep active learning strategies that integrate multiple querying criteria, most prominently uncertainty and diversity. Such methods formulate sample selection as a multi-objective optimization problem, often realized via weighted-sum objectives that trade off informativeness against representativeness, or via two-stage/multi-stage pipelines that apply different criteria sequentially. These strategies aim to construct large, diverse batches that both refine the decision boundary and cover the data distribution well. The cluster emphasizes that these combined approaches, including methods like CCAL, exploitation–exploration frameworks, WAAL, and BADGE variants, have become dominant in practical DAL due to their improved effectiveness over single-criterion querying.

local_topics.title: Families of active learning heuristics
local_topics.description: The section explains that successful active learning for remote sensing requires strategies to rank pixels in the unlabeled pool U according to their utility for labeling. It groups these strategies into three main families—committee-based, large margin-based, and posterior probability-based heuristics—each relying on different underlying models of uncertainty. A fourth, more recent family, cluster-based heuristics, is mentioned as conceptually distinct and therefore excluded from detailed treatment. This taxonomy structures the subsequent survey of algorithms.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Cluster-based active learning via clustering trees
local_topics.description: Cluster-based heuristics are described as an alternative family of active learning methods that operate by pruning a hierarchical clustering tree. The goal is to refine clusters until they become consistent with the labels provided by the user, effectively guiding exploration of the data space. These methods rely on an unsupervised model of the data distribution rather than on a predictive classifier, making their aim different from the other families. Because of this differing objective, they are mentioned but not detailed further in the survey.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Four families of active learning heuristics
local_topics.description: The survey organizes diverse active learning algorithms into four main heuristic families based on their characteristics. For each family, specific selection strategies have been detailed and systematically compared. This taxonomy structures the variety of methods and enables a clearer analysis of their relative behaviors and design principles.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

canonical_topic.name: Taxonomy of Active Learning Heuristic Families
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the main families of heuristics used to rank unlabeled instances for querying in active learning, which directly underpin acquisition strategies in Deep Active Learning. The survey distinguishes committee-based, large-margin-based, and posterior probability-based heuristics, each modeling classifier uncertainty in different ways to select informative samples from a pool. A fourth family, cluster-based heuristics, operates by refining a hierarchical clustering of the data until clusters become label-consistent, relying on an unsupervised data distribution model rather than a predictive classifier. This taxonomy provides a structured view of how different query strategies trade off exploration of the data space versus exploitation of current model uncertainty, and it informs the design and comparison of DAL acquisition functions. Although illustrated in remote sensing image classification, the families are generic and directly transferable to deep model settings.

local_topics.title: Probabilistic view of distribution shift
local_topics.description: The section formalizes distribution shifts in data streams through time-dependent probability distributions p_t(x), p_t(y|x), and p_t(y). It explains that shifts can affect the input distribution, the conditional label distribution, or the marginal label distribution, each with different consequences for the underlying predictive model. This probabilistic framing underpins later distinctions between virtual drift, real concept drift, and label distribution shift, and motivates the need for model updates when these distributions change.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Virtual drift affecting input distribution
local_topics.description: Virtual drift (also referred to as covariate shift) is defined as a situation where the input distribution p_t(x) changes over time while the conditional distribution p_t(y|x) remains stable. This implies that the relationship between features and labels does not change, but the regions of the input space that are frequently observed do, as in seasonal or environmental changes that alter observed features. The model’s mapping from x to y is still valid, but its performance may be affected due to mismatches between training and current input frequencies.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Real concept drift and model degradation
local_topics.description: Real concept drift occurs when the conditional distribution p_t(y|x) changes over time, meaning that the underlying relationship between inputs and labels evolves. This leads to a severe deterioration in predictive performance because the learned model no longer reflects the true mapping from features to labels, necessitating model updates or replacement. Examples include shifts in consumer behavior after major events like the COVID-19 pandemic.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Combined virtual and real concept drift
local_topics.description: The text highlights that in many practical scenarios, virtual drift and real concept drift co-occur, leading to simultaneous changes in both the input distribution p_t(x) and the conditional distribution p_t(y|x). This compound shift creates a more challenging adaptation problem, as models must cope with changing feature frequencies and evolving label relationships at the same time. Such situations are typical in complex, non-stationary environments.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Label distribution shift over time
local_topics.description: Label distribution shift is described as a change that affects only the marginal distribution of labels p_t(y), while p_t(x) and p_t(y|x) may remain stable. This phenomenon is common in real-world settings where the prevalence of certain classes varies over time, such as seasonal patterns in disease incidence (e.g., influenza) or sudden outbreaks. It alters class priors and can significantly impact model calibration and performance if not properly handled.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Distribution Shift and Concept Drift in Active Learning Streams
canonical_topic.description: This topic formalizes different types of distribution shifts in data streams using time-dependent probability distributions p_t(x), p_t(y|x), and p_t(y), providing the foundation for active learning in non-stationary environments. It distinguishes virtual drift (covariate shift), where only the input distribution p_t(x) changes while p_t(y|x) remains stable, from real concept drift, where the conditional distribution p_t(y|x) itself evolves and can severely degrade model performance. The text also emphasizes that in many real-world streaming scenarios, virtual and real concept drift co-occur, jointly altering both feature frequencies and label relationships and thus complicating model adaptation and labeling decisions. Additionally, it highlights label distribution shift, where only the marginal label distribution p_t(y) changes, affecting class priors and calibration over time. These probabilistic distinctions are crucial for designing stream-based active learning strategies that decide when to query labels and update deep models under evolving data distributions.

local_topics.title: Neural network-based learnable sampling
local_topics.description: Recent deep AL work employs neural networks directly to perform sample selection, moving beyond explicit informativeness evaluation. In this learnable sampling paradigm, a model is trained to predict which unlabeled samples are most beneficial for annotation, effectively learning a selection policy from data or from proxy signals. This contrasts with handcrafted metrics by allowing the selection mechanism itself to be parameterized and optimized as part of the learning pipeline.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Learnable sampling with neural selectors
local_topics.description: Learnable sampling replaces the traditional two-step active learning paradigm—informativeness evaluation followed by heuristic selection—with a single, end-to-end trainable process. A neural network, termed a neural selector, directly outputs which samples to query without explicitly computing informativeness scores. This shifts sample selection from hand-crafted criteria to learned, data-driven policies.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Learnable Sampling with Neural Selectors in DAL
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning approaches where the sampling strategy itself is parameterized and learned by a neural network. Instead of computing explicit informativeness scores followed by heuristic selection, a neural selector directly outputs which unlabeled samples should be queried, forming an end-to-end trainable selection policy. These methods move beyond hand-crafted uncertainty or diversity metrics by optimizing the selection mechanism from data or proxy supervision signals. Within the DAL pipeline, learnable sampling tightly couples representation learning and query selection, aiming to better exploit structure in the unlabeled pool under constrained annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: DeepAL for Wearable-Based Activity Recognition
local_topics.description: [83, 96] use sensor data from wearable devices or mobile terminals to perform human activity recognition with DeepAL. [96] proposes a context-aware annotator selection framework, choosing which annotator to query based on context and uncertainty. ActiveHARNet [83] introduces a resource-efficient deep ensemble that supports on-device incremental learning and uses approximate Bayesian neural networks to quantify uncertainty, demonstrating feasibility on public datasets.

local_topics.title: Activity recognition in smart environments with DeepAL
local_topics.description: Deep active learning is applied to sensor-based activity recognition in smart homes and ubiquitous computing environments. Datasets such as OPPORTUNITY, WISDM, SenseBox, Skoda, Daphnet, and CASAS contain multimodal sensor streams describing human activities and context. Active learning selects the most informative sensor segments or activity windows for annotation, reducing the burden of labeling continuous time-series data. Performance is assessed via activity recognition accuracy and label-efficiency in complex real-world environments.

local_topics.title: Smart device-based activity recognition
local_topics.description: Deep active learning is applied to human activity recognition using data from smart devices such as smartphones and wearables. Datasets like HHAR and NWFD contain accelerometer or usage traces annotated with user activities or application usage. Active learning strategies query the most uncertain signal segments for labeling, reducing the number of user-labeled activity episodes. This is important for building personalized models without extensive manual annotation.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods for human activity recognition using sensor data from wearables, smartphones, and smart environments. DeepAL is used to select the most informative sensor segments or activity windows, typically based on uncertainty measures, to reduce the labeling burden on users and annotators. Approaches include context-aware annotator selection frameworks that adaptively choose which annotator to query, as well as resource-efficient deep ensembles and approximate Bayesian neural networks to quantify predictive uncertainty on-device. These methods target both generalized activity recognition on public datasets and personalized models that can incrementally adapt to individual users with minimal manual annotation, improving label efficiency in continuous, multimodal time-series settings.

local_topics.title: Set-cover-based Core-Set and variants
local_topics.description: Set-cover-based methods like Core-Set formulate active learning as a k-center location problem, solved via farthest-first traversal to select representative samples that minimize the maximum distance to all points. Similarity between samples is originally measured by L2 distance in deep feature space, and later extended by contextual diversity metrics that fuse uncertainty and spatial/semantic diversity. Graph convolutional networks are also introduced to model relations between labeled and unlabeled data, improving feature representations before Core-Set sampling. These methods embody a set-cover constraint aiming for complete coverage, but can be prone to selecting outliers when the labeled set is small.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Core-set diversity and cover-based selection
local_topics.description: This topic concerns diversity-driven active learning where the unlabeled pool is approximated by a representative core-set using cover-based criteria. Methods such as those inspired by Sener and Savarese (2018, ICLR) frame sample selection as a covering or core-set optimization problem in feature space, often using L2 distances. The goal is to select a subset of samples that well-cover the data manifold, reducing redundancy in the labeled set.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Cover-based sampling for active learning
local_topics.description: Cover-based methods aim to select unlabeled samples so that they well 'cover' the representation space of the data, reducing redundancy while maintaining representativeness. In deep active learning for medical images, this typically involves selecting images or slices that span the feature manifold learned by a network. Such strategies help ensure that annotated data provide broad coverage of anatomical and pathological variations.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Cover-based submodular sample selection
local_topics.description: This topic refers to cover-based strategies that use submodular optimization to select informative samples in deep active learning. The method aims to choose a subset of unlabeled medical images that best "cover" the feature space, ensuring diversity and representativeness while keeping labeling costs low. Submodular functions provide theoretical guarantees for near-optimal selection via greedy algorithms.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Cover-based sampling with feature embeddings
local_topics.description: Core-set based active learning is implemented as cover-based sampling in the feature-embedding space of each sample. The goal is to select a subset of points whose feature embeddings well cover the unlabeled pool, improving representativeness of queried samples. This design assumes that proximity in embedding space correlates with redundancy in information content.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: Core-set k-center formulation and scalability
local_topics.description: The Core-set approach formulates active learning as a k-center problem, seeking a subset such that a model trained on it performs competitively with one trained on the full dataset. It constructs a core subset by maximizing coverage in feature space, effectively trying to minimize the maximum distance from any unlabeled point to the selected set. However, building the required distance matrix over all unlabeled samples is computationally expensive, making this strategy challenging for large-scale unlabeled datasets.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Cover-Based Core-Set Selection in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers cover-based and core-set methods that formulate deep active learning as a k-center or set-cover problem in feature space. These approaches select a representative subset of unlabeled samples whose deep feature embeddings well cover the data manifold, minimizing redundancy and the maximum distance from any pool point to the selected set. Implementations often rely on L2 distances in learned embeddings, sometimes enhanced with contextual or semantic diversity metrics and graph convolutional models to better capture relationships between labeled and unlabeled data. Submodular formulations provide greedy algorithms with approximation guarantees for near-optimal coverage under labeling budget constraints, particularly in medical image analysis. Despite their effectiveness, core-set methods can be computationally expensive due to distance matrix construction and can over-select outliers when the labeled set is small.

local_topics.title: Cold-start problem in active learning
local_topics.description: The cold-start problem arises when active learning (AL) methods have little or no initial labeled data, causing informativeness estimates to be unreliable and performance to degrade, sometimes below random sampling. Simply combining self-supervised learning with standard AL baselines can also underperform random sampling, showing that naive pretraining is insufficient. This issue is pervasive across domains, including medical image analysis where labeling is expensive. canonical_topic.name: Cold-Start Problem in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: The cold-start problem in (deep) active learning arises when there is little or no labeled data available at the beginning of the process, so the model is too poorly trained to provide reliable uncertainty or informativeness estimates. In this phase, standard query strategies can make misleading sampling decisions and may even perform worse than random sampling because the underlying model is inaccurate. This issue is prominent in data-hungry deep models and in domains with expensive annotation, such as medical image analysis and data streams. Mitigation strategies include careful design of initial seed selection that differs from the later-stage query policy, as well as pretraining or self-supervised learning to bootstrap the model before active querying begins. Addressing cold-start is thus a critical design aspect for practical deep active learning systems, especially in low-label and streaming scenarios.

local_topics.title: Prequential evaluation for online active learning
local_topics.description: Prequential evaluation assesses performance on streaming data by predicting each incoming instance before deciding whether to query its label and update the model. Algorithm 6 formalizes this for online active learning under a labeling budget: for each time step, the model predicts, the active strategy decides whether to request the true label, and the model is updated only when a label is acquired, consuming budget. This scheme is particularly suitable for drifting data streams, where using a static holdout set would not reflect evolving data distributions.

local_topics.title: Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation
local_topics.description: Prequential evaluation, also called the test-then-train approach, assesses performance in online learning by first predicting on each incoming instance, then optionally querying its label, and finally updating the model with that instance. This method produces a time series of prediction errors, enabling monitoring of performance evolution in data streams. Algorithmically, at each time step t, the model predicts, a query decision is made, and then the model is updated with the instance and its label. It is a natural fit for streaming settings where data arrive sequentially and immediate evaluation is desired.

canonical_topic.name: Prequential Evaluation in Streaming Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation is a standard protocol for assessing active learning methods in data streams, where instances arrive sequentially and must be processed online. At each time step, the model first predicts on the incoming instance, the active learning strategy then decides whether to query its label under a labeling budget, and the model is updated only when a label is acquired. This produces a time series of prediction errors that reflects how performance evolves over time in non-stationary environments. The approach is particularly suitable for streaming and drifting data, where static holdout sets are inadequate because they do not capture changing data distributions. In the context of online and stream-based active learning, prequential evaluation tightly couples prediction, query decisions, and budget consumption within a unified, temporally ordered framework.

canonical_topic.name: Loss-Prediction-Based Acquisition in Deep Active Learning

An auxiliary network is trained to regress the target model’s loss (or error reduction) on inputs, using labeled data to match predicted and actual losses. canonical_topic.name: Learning Loss Prediction for Deep Active Learning

local_topics.title: Margin-based uncertainty heuristic
local_topics.description: This topic explains the core heuristic that underlies large-margin active learning: samples close to the decision boundary are considered uncertain and informative, while samples far from it are deemed uninteresting for labeling. The process uses the magnitude of the decision function f(xi) as a metric, with low absolute values indicating candidates for querying. This establishes the general uncertainty-sampling principle specialized to margin-based classifiers.

local_topics.title: Diversity-constrained margin-based heuristics
local_topics.description: Margin-based active learning heuristics rank unlabeled samples by their decision margin (e.g., distance between class posteriors), but can still select highly similar points. To counter this, the base margin sampling heuristic is augmented by a diversity constraint that penalizes or filters candidates that are too similar to already selected ones. This combination exploits both uncertainty (small margin) and spatial or spectral diversity in feature space, leading to more representative labeled sets in remote sensing. The process involves computing margins (Equations (7), (8) or (9)) and then applying a diversity measure on the candidate subset.

canonical_topic.name: Margin-Based Uncertainty with Diversity Constraints
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers margin-based uncertainty sampling, where unlabeled instances close to the classifier's decision boundary (i.e., with small absolute decision function values or small posterior margins) are treated as the most informative for labeling. It explains how this large-margin heuristic operationalizes uncertainty by ranking samples according to the magnitude of a decision function or class-posterior gap. The topic further addresses a key limitation of pure margin sampling—its tendency to select highly redundant, similar points—and describes augmenting it with diversity constraints. These diversity-aware variants penalize or filter candidates that are too similar to already selected samples, combining uncertainty and representativeness in feature space. Although exemplified in supervised remote sensing image classification, the same margin-based and diversity-constrained principles directly inform acquisition strategies in deep active learning, where decision margins are computed from deep models' outputs.

local_topics.title: Measuring annotation cost realistically
local_topics.description: Annotation cost in AL is often oversimplified as a uniform per-instance value, despite real efforts varying with factors such as sequence length and instance difficulty. Because AL tends to select hard and ambiguous instances, unit-cost assumptions can distort evaluation and change which strategies appear best. Time-based cost—measuring actual annotation time in user studies—is advocated as the most accurate metric, and regression-based cost models learned from input features are proposed to predict real costs for use in evaluation and querying.

canonical_topic.name: Annotation Cost Modeling in Active Learning for NLP
canonical_topic.description: This topic examines how to model and measure annotation cost in active learning for NLP, where labeling effort is highly heterogeneous. Costs can vary with sentence length, label complexity, span boundary decisions, and the need for agreement checks, and active learners typically query harder, more ambiguous instances that are especially expensive. Treating annotation as a uniform per-instance cost can therefore distort both evaluation and the apparent ranking of query strategies. The topic highlights time-based cost, measured in user studies, as the most realistic metric, and discusses regression-based cost models that predict annotation time or effort from input features. Such cost models can be integrated into the querying process to balance expected information gain against true labeling effort, leading to more cost-effective deep active learning workflows for NLP tasks.

canonical_topic.name: Reinforcement Learning for Learnable Query Policies

In medical image analysis, reinforcement learning is used both for instance-level querying and for patch selection, guiding annotation effort toward the most informative regions. In supervised remote sensing image classification, incorporating diversity helps reject near-duplicate pixels and yields a more informative training set. local_topics.title: Label scarcity and annotation costs
local_topics.description: Many real-world machine learning applications lack sufficient labeled data because annotation requires costly and time-consuming manual inspection or quality checks. local_topics.title: Evaluation under label scarcity
local_topics.description: This topic concerns how active learning methods for data streams are evaluated in research versus real-world settings. In research, query strategies are commonly assessed assuming ground-truth labels are available for a held-out test set or the entire data stream. In practice, label scarcity is the very reason for using active learning, which makes comprehensive evaluation of deployed sampling strategies difficult or unrealistic. This gap raises questions about how to reliably measure performance when labels are limited or costly.

canonical_topic.name: Label Scarcity and Annotation Cost in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on label scarcity and high annotation costs as the primary motivation for deep active learning, particularly in domains like medical imaging and data streams. In such settings, raw data are abundant but manual labeling by experts is slow, expensive, and often the main bottleneck for deploying accurate deep models. Deep active learning methods are designed to improve label efficiency by strategically selecting the most informative instances to query under a limited annotation budget. The topic also covers the challenge of evaluating active learning strategies when comprehensive ground-truth labels are unavailable, creating a discrepancy between controlled research protocols and realistic deployment scenarios. This raises methodological questions about how to design evaluation schemes that remain faithful to the core constraint of scarce labels while still enabling reliable performance comparison.

local_topics.title: Threshold-based querying in online AL
local_topics.description: Online active learning for data streams often relies on requesting labels only for data points deemed sufficiently informative according to a pre-determined threshold. This threshold is derived from an instance selection criterion that evaluates the informativeness of unlabeled observations. local_topics.title: Margin Thresholding for Online Active Learning
local_topics.description: This topic covers a threshold-based strategy where unlabeled instances are selected if their margin |p_t| is below a dynamically adjusted threshold ε. The threshold starts high and is iteratively halved until sufficient misclassifications are observed among queried examples, adapting the aggressiveness of sampling to observed errors. The underlying linear classifier is updated using a reflection-based update rule to emphasize more recent data points, making the method suitable for evolving data streams.

canonical_topic.name: Threshold-Based Querying in Stream-Based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns threshold-based querying policies for online active learning on data streams, where labels are requested only for instances whose informativeness exceeds a predefined or dynamically adjusted threshold. Informativeness is typically measured via an instance selection criterion, such as the classifier’s margin, and the threshold controls how aggressively the learner queries over time. In margin-based approaches, unlabeled instances are queried if their absolute margin falls below a current threshold that is gradually tightened, for example by iteratively halving it until a sufficient number of misclassifications is observed among queried examples. Such error-driven adaptation allows the query budget to concentrate on regions of uncertainty that are actually associated with classification mistakes. In evolving data streams, these strategies can be combined with update rules (e.g., reflection-based updates of a linear classifier) that emphasize recent data, making the overall active learner responsive to concept drift while still limiting annotation costs.

canonical_topic.name: Standardized Pipelines and Frameworks for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on resolving pipeline inconsistency in Deep Active Learning (DeepAL) by developing standardized, modular frameworks. Different DAL studies often combine deep models, acquisition functions, and training schedules in ad hoc ways, making results hard to reproduce and compare. Redesigned DeepAL pipelines aim to decouple components (model, query strategy, labeling loop, retraining schedule) through clear interfaces so they can be reused and recomposed across tasks and domains. Common framework initiatives explicitly target this standardization, providing unified implementations that bring consistency to experimental protocols and ease transfer to new applications. Such frameworks help establish more reliable benchmarks and facilitate systematic evaluation of DAL methods under comparable conditions.

local_topics.title: Single-pass vs window-based sampling
local_topics.description: This topic contrasts single-pass online active learning algorithms, which must decide on querying immediately for each arriving instance, with window- or batch-based methods that process fixed-size chunks of data. Window-based approaches perform best-out-of-window sampling by evaluating an entire buffer and selecting the top k most informative observations for labeling, with k and buffer size constrained by storage and computation. Window-based strategies suit high-volume streams without strict time constraints, whereas single-pass methods are required when decisions must be made instantly on each data point.

local_topics.title: Single-pass online sampling for streams
local_topics.description: This topic concerns sampling strategies that process each instance from a dynamic data stream only once, without revisiting or storing large portions of the stream. Such single-pass methods avoid maintaining or updating multiple models, making them more practical in settings with strict time or memory constraints. They are proposed as an alternative to dominant ensemble and batch-based methods in online classification when continuous, high-velocity data cannot be easily batched.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Single-pass and window-based sampling in stream active learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on sampling strategies for stream-based deep active learning, contrasting single-pass online querying with window- or batch-based selection. Single-pass methods must decide immediately for each incoming instance whether to request a label, typically under strict time and memory constraints and without storing or revisiting past data. In contrast, window-based approaches buffer a fixed-size chunk of the stream and then perform best-out-of-window selection, choosing the top-k most informative instances for labeling given storage and computational limits. Window-based strategies are particularly suitable for high-volume streams without hard real-time constraints, enabling more informed acquisition decisions by comparing candidates within the buffer. Single-pass approaches are favored when latency or resource restrictions preclude maintaining multiple models or large buffers, offering a lightweight alternative to ensemble- and batch-based methods in online classification.

local_topics.title: Representativeness and sampling bias in AL
local_topics.description: Representativeness-based strategies address the risk that purely informativeness-driven selection can lead to sampling bias and over-focus on outliers. Representativeness evaluates how well selected instances reflect the structure and distribution of the broader unlabeled pool. It thus complements informativeness by incorporating correlations and redundancy among instances when designing query strategies.

canonical_topic.name: Hybrid Informativeness–Representativeness Query Strategies
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers active learning strategies that jointly exploit informativeness and representativeness when selecting data points for annotation, a design that directly transfers to Deep Active Learning. Rather than relying solely on uncertainty (which can over-sample outliers or noisy instances), these hybrid methods also assess how well candidate points reflect the overall structure and distribution of the unlabeled pool. Representativeness is used to mitigate sampling bias by encouraging coverage of dense regions and reducing redundancy among queried instances. In practice, these criteria are integrated to favor samples that are both challenging for the current model and broadly representative, leading to more efficient use of annotation budgets in deep models as well.

canonical_topic.name: Slice- and Region-Based Sampling in Medical Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns how the choice of sampling unit in deep active learning for medical image analysis affects annotation efficiency and learning performance. Instead of querying labels at the whole-image or whole-volume level, many methods operate at finer granularity, such as 2D slices or local regions within 3D scans. In volumetric imaging (e.g., CT, MRI), neighboring slices exhibit strong semantic redundancy, which can be exploited by selectively querying only the most informative slices, thereby reducing annotation costs while preserving performance. Slice-based active learning strategies typically integrate uncertainty, representativeness, and diversity criteria over slices to identify which subparts of a volume deserve expert annotation, enabling more targeted use of limited labeling budgets. These design choices reflect DAL-specific concerns about how to structure queries in complex, high-dimensional medical data.

local_topics.title: DeepAL applications across domains
local_topics.description: Deep Active Learning has been applied beyond vision to a wide range of fields, including NLP, speech and audio processing, social network analysis, medical imaging, wildlife protection, industrial robotics, and disaster analysis. In each domain, DeepAL aims to reduce labeling effort while maintaining high performance, tailoring query strategies and deep architectures to the data type and task. The survey introduces this broad application landscape before detailing domain-specific work.

local_topics.title: Dominance of Vision Tasks in DeepAL
local_topics.description: Deep active learning applications are reported to concentrate mainly on visual image processing tasks. Although there are also applications in natural language processing and other domains, the survey notes that vision-related problems currently constitute the primary focus of DeepAL research.

local_topics.title: Application-Oriented Review of DeepAL
local_topics.description: This topic refers to analyzing DeepAL methods in the context of specific application domains such as computer vision, NLP, medical imaging, or recommendation systems. It involves comparing how different task characteristics (e.g., output space, label noise, data modality) influence the choice and effectiveness of active learning strategies. The focus is on practical deployment considerations and domain-specific adaptations.

canonical_topic.name: Application Domains of Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers how Deep Active Learning (DeepAL) is applied across a broad spectrum of domains and tasks. While DeepAL has been used for image recognition, object detection, visual question answering, and other computer vision problems, current research is still dominated by vision-centric applications. The survey also highlights successful uses of DeepAL in NLP, speech and audio processing, social network analysis, medical imaging, wildlife protection, industrial robotics, and disaster analysis, where query strategies and deep architectures are adapted to domain-specific data characteristics. It emphasizes that different task properties—such as data modality, output space, and label noise—shape the choice and performance of active learning strategies. Overall, the survey argues for a more systematic, application-oriented view of DeepAL, noting the lack of a unified classification framework and pointing to future directions in domain-specific method design and evaluation.

local_topics.title: DeepAL in visual data processing
local_topics.description: Given deep learning’s success in computer vision, visual data processing is presented as a primary area for realizing DeepAL’s potential. The survey partitions this area into specific tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and, initially, image classification and recognition. DeepAL methods in this domain focus on handling high-dimensional imagery with minimal labeled data.

local_topics.title: Image classification challenges in DeepAL
local_topics.description: In image classification and recognition, DeepAL must efficiently query informative samples from high-dimensional input spaces, a setting where traditional AL often struggles. The central issue is achieving strong classification performance while incurring the smallest possible labeling cost. This subsection frames image classification as a foundational task upon which more complex vision tasks in DeepAL build.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Visual Recognition
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning to visual data processing, where high-dimensional imagery makes label acquisition particularly costly. Image classification and recognition are treated as foundational tasks, providing the basis for extending DeepAL methods to more complex computer vision problems such as object detection and semantic segmentation. The focus is on designing query strategies that can identify the most informative unlabeled images in large visual pools, thereby achieving strong classification performance with minimal annotation effort. DeepAL in this domain explicitly addresses the challenges of scaling active learning to high-dimensional input spaces while tightly controlling labeling budgets.

local_topics.title: H-divergence and VAAL framework
local_topics.description: H-divergence measures the distance between labeled and unlabeled distributions using a discriminator, typically derived from GAN-style architectures, whose ability to distinguish the two sets correlates with the divergence. Variational Adversarial Active Learning (VAAL) combines a VAE that maps samples to a latent space with a discriminator that predicts whether latent codes come from labeled or unlabeled data. Through adversarial training, the VAE tries to fool the discriminator, and the system selects samples the discriminator deems most likely to be unlabeled for annotation.

local_topics.title: Adversarial representativeness: DiscAL, VAAL, WAAL
local_topics.description: Adversarial representative methods learn to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data in a latent space and use this signal to guide selection. DiscAL employs a discriminator reminiscent of GANs to separate samples from labeled and unlabeled distributions. VAAL uses a VAE plus adversarial discriminator trained with reconstruction and adversarial losses, and selects points by the discriminator’s probability of being unlabeled (αVAAL). WAAL leverages adversarial training framed via H-divergence to find unlabeled batches that are both diverse and distributionally distinct from labeled data.

local_topics.title: TA-VAAL: task-aware variational adversarial AL
local_topics.description: TA-VAAL (Task-Aware Variational Adversarial Active Learning) enhances VAAL by explicitly accounting for both data distribution and task structure. It addresses the limitation that uncertainty-based methods underuse global data distribution and distribution-based methods overlook task structure, by integrating a loss prediction module and RankCGAN into VAAL. This yields a framework that jointly exploits data distribution and model uncertainty, achieving strong performance on balanced and imbalanced benchmarks.

local_topics.title: VAAL adversarial representation learning for AL
local_topics.description: VAAL tackles limitations of batch uncertainty sampling (low diversity, outlier sensitivity) and density-based methods (p-norm distance concentration in high dimensions) by learning an adversarial latent representation that distinguishes labeled from unlabeled data. It jointly trains a VAE in a semi-supervised fashion on both labeled and unlabeled datasets while an adversarial discriminator is trained to classify whether latent codes originate from the labeled pool, pushing the encoder to align their distributions. This yields a low-dimensional latent space that supports an effective sampling strategy combining representation learning with uncertainty to reduce outlier influence and distance concentration issues.

local_topics.title: ARAL and TA-VAAL extensions of VAAL
local_topics.description: ARAL builds on VAAL and adversarial representation learning to minimize manual annotations while exploiting both real and generated data. The framework uses VAAL to learn the latent feature space of labeled and unlabeled data, selects unlabeled samples with maximal information, and then enhances learning with adversarial representation training on both actual and synthetic samples produced by a deep generative network; its architecture includes an encoder, generator, discriminator, classifier, and sampler trained jointly. TA-VAAL further extends VAAL by combining the global data structure learned by VAAL with local task-related information derived from learning loss for more informed sample querying.

canonical_topic.name: Adversarial Representation Learning for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that use adversarial representation learning to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data and guide query selection. Frameworks such as VAAL train a VAE to map both labeled and unlabeled samples into a latent space while an adversarial discriminator predicts whether latent codes originate from the labeled or unlabeled pool, effectively estimating an H-divergence–like discrepancy between the two distributions. Query strategies then select those points that the discriminator deems most likely to be unlabeled or distributionally distinct, improving diversity and mitigating issues like outlier sensitivity and distance concentration that affect uncertainty and density-based methods. Extensions like DiscAL and WAAL generalize this idea by using discriminators to capture representativeness and batch-level distributional differences, while TA-VAAL and ARAL integrate task-aware uncertainty (e.g., loss prediction) and synthetic samples from generative models to better exploit both global data structure and task-specific information under limited annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Batch Mode Deep Active Learning concept
local_topics.description: Batch Mode Deep Active Learning (BMDAL) replaces classical one-by-one querying with batch-based sample selection to better suit deep model training. One-by-one querying causes frequent retraining with little change in data, leading to inefficiency and potential overfitting. BMDAL instead scores candidate unlabeled batches B ⊆ U using an acquisition function a and a trained deep model f_θ(L), and selects an optimal batch B* that maximizes a_batch(B, f_θ(L)). This reframes acquisition as a batch-level optimization problem aligned with deep learning training dynamics.

local_topics.title: Information vs diversity in batch queries
local_topics.description: This topic contrasts batch query strategies that select samples solely based on information content with those that also account for sample diversity and inter-sample similarity. The visualization with dot size (information amount) and distance (similarity) illustrates how ignoring correlations among samples can lead to locally optimal but globally suboptimal batch selections. It frames the core challenge in Batch Mode Deep Active Learning (BMDAL) as jointly considering information volume and correlations/diversity when forming query batches.

local_topics.title: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning and Diversity
local_topics.description: Batch-mode Deep Active Learning (BMDAL) underlies many query strategies by framing selection as choosing informative batches for updating deep models. The survey notes that query methods often aim to balance uncertainty and diversity within each batch, contrasting with earlier uncertainty-only approaches. It distinguishes strategies that explicitly enforce diversity in input or representation space from those that directly optimize or measure mutual information over entire batches.

canonical_topic.name: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning and Diversity
canonical_topic.description: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning (BMDAL) replaces sequential, one-by-one querying with batch-based selection to better match the training dynamics and computational costs of deep models. Instead of frequently retraining on nearly identical datasets, BMDAL scores candidate batches from the unlabeled pool via a batch acquisition function that depends on the current model trained on the labeled set, turning acquisition into a batch-level optimization problem. A central challenge is that selecting the most informative individual points can lead to highly redundant batches if correlations between samples are ignored. Consequently, modern BMDAL strategies aim to jointly maximize information content and within-batch diversity, either by explicitly enforcing diversity in input or representation space or by directly optimizing mutual information over whole batches. These designs seek globally effective query sets that provide large information gains while avoiding overlap and redundancy.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning with Self-Supervised Pretraining
canonical_topic.description: This topic examines how self-supervised pre-trained models are integrated into deep active learning pipelines, particularly in medical image analysis. Powerful feature extractors trained on large-scale unlabeled data are used as backbones for active learning, providing richer representations that improve uncertainty and diversity estimation in query strategies. By starting from self-supervised encoders instead of training from scratch, active learning can achieve stronger performance with fewer labeled samples, enhancing label efficiency under strict annotation budgets. The studies highlight that even with randomly selected small labeled sets, fine-tuning self-supervised models yields strong baselines, and further active selection on top of these representations can amplify gains in downstream performance.

local_topics.title: Wasserstein-based adversarial active learning
local_topics.description: Wasserstein distance is used as a more diversity-preserving distribution metric compared to H-divergence in discrepancy-based active learning. WAAL (Wasserstein Adversarial Active Learning) extends VAAL by adding a sample-selection module trained to minimize the Wasserstein distance between labeled and unlabeled sets. This design encourages querying samples that are both highly uncertain and most likely unlabeled while maintaining representativeness and diversity of the selected subset.

local_topics.title: WAAL: Wasserstein adversarial active learning
local_topics.description: WAAL (Wasserstein Adversarial Active Learning) explicitly balances uncertainty and diversity within a hybrid query strategy while modeling the AL interaction as a distribution matching problem via Wasserstein distance. Losses are derived from this formulation, and the method is decomposed into deep neural network parameter optimization and query batch selection stages. This adversarial, distribution-based approach targets alignment between labeled and unlabeled data distributions while maintaining informative selections.

canonical_topic.name: Wasserstein Adversarial Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers Wasserstein Adversarial Active Learning (WAAL), a discrepancy-based deep active learning method that models annotation as a distribution matching problem between labeled and unlabeled data. WAAL replaces traditional H-divergence with the Wasserstein distance to better preserve diversity while aligning the two distributions. It extends VAAL by adding a sample-selection module trained adversarially to minimize the Wasserstein distance, encouraging queries that are both highly uncertain and likely unlabeled. The method explicitly balances uncertainty and diversity in a hybrid query strategy and decomposes the procedure into neural network parameter optimization and query batch selection. Overall, WAAL exemplifies adversarial, distribution-based DAL where acquisition is driven by aligning data distributions under a principled optimal transport metric.

local_topics.title: Data processing in online AL
local_topics.description: Online active learning methods are categorized by how they process incoming data streams, distinguishing between single-pass and batch processing. Single-pass methods see each instance once and must decide immediately whether to query, while batch methods can accumulate instances before making joint querying decisions. This categorization constrains memory usage, latency, and the design of query strategies for streaming environments.

canonical_topic.name: Data Processing Paradigms in Online Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses how online active learning methods process data streams under strict single-pass or streaming constraints. It contrasts single-pass schemes, where each instance is seen once and must be immediately evaluated for querying, with approaches that temporarily accumulate instances to enable joint or batch querying decisions. These processing paradigms directly shape how acquisition strategies are implemented in streaming settings, including when and how informativeness is assessed. They also determine memory usage, computational efficiency, and latency, thereby constraining the design of practical query strategies for real-time or resource-limited environments.

local_topics.title: Principle of discrepancy-based active learning
local_topics.description: Discrepancy-based active learning selects unlabeled samples that are farthest from the labeled set in distribution space, treating them as most representative. By repeatedly querying such samples, the method aims to reduce the discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled distributions so that a small labeled subset approximates the full dataset. The core technical challenge is defining and computing a distance between two high-dimensional probability distributions.

local_topics.title: Discrepancy-based sampling using H-divergence
local_topics.description: Discrepancy-based active learning strategies compare distributions between labeled and unlabeled sets to identify regions where the model is poorly supported by annotations. H-divergence is used as a formal measure of distributional discrepancy, guiding the selection of samples that reduce this gap. By repeatedly querying top-scoring examples under this divergence, the learner aims to better align the labeled set with the overall data distribution.

canonical_topic.name: Discrepancy-Based Sampling in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Discrepancy-based active learning selects unlabeled samples that maximize a distributional distance between the labeled and unlabeled sets, aiming to make the labeled pool more representative of the overall data distribution. The core idea is to iteratively query points from regions where the labeled distribution poorly covers the unlabeled data, thus reducing the discrepancy between the two. This requires defining and efficiently computing distances between high-dimensional probability distributions, a non-trivial problem in deep learning settings. Formal measures such as H-divergence are used to quantify this distributional gap and to rank unlabeled instances for annotation. By repeatedly querying the top-scoring samples under such discrepancy measures, the method aligns the labeled set with the full data distribution and can improve DAL performance under limited annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Discrepancy-Based Selection with Statistical Distances
local_topics.description: Discrepancy-based methods select unlabeled samples by measuring distributional or prediction discrepancies between models or between labeled and unlabeled sets. Metrics such as Wasserstein distance, H-divergence, and KL divergence quantify how much a candidate sample differs from what the model has already seen or what an ensemble predicts. These criteria are often combined with uncertainty or diversity in hybrid strategies.
