local_topics.title: Discrepancy-based distribution alignment measures
local_topics.description: Some surveyed works measure how well labeled and unlabeled sets align by computing discrepancies between their feature distributions. These include cosine similarity-based discrepancies, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and Wasserstein distance, which quantify gaps between empirical distributions or feature embeddings of candidate samples and the existing labeled pool. Selection then targets samples that maximally reduce such discrepancies, promoting distribution alignment. This perspective treats active learning as minimizing a statistical distance between training and target data distributions.

canonical_topic.name: Discrepancy-Based Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that select samples by minimizing statistical discrepancies between labeled and unlabeled data or between model predictions. Methods instantiate this idea using distances such as Wasserstein distance, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), cosine-based measures, H-divergence, and KL divergence to quantify how candidate samples differ from the current training distribution or ensemble predictions. Active learning is framed as a distribution alignment problem, where selected samples are those expected to most reduce these empirical gaps in feature or latent spaces. Several approaches embed data into a latent representation and apply Wasserstein distance, combined with latent space optimization and nearest-neighbor search, to guide sample acquisition. These discrepancy criteria are often integrated with uncertainty or diversity measures in hybrid selection schemes, particularly in medical image analysis settings.

local_topics.title: Superpixel-based pre-segmentation and informativeness
local_topics.description: In region-based active learning, images are first pre-segmented into superpixels using color- and texture-based algorithms, and then informativeness is computed at the superpixel level. The informativeness score of a superpixel is defined as the average informativeness of its constituent pixels, turning pixel-wise uncertainty into region-wise measures. This enables querying compact, coherent regions rather than individual pixels, improving annotation efficiency.

local_topics.title: Superpixel-Based Querying in Interactive Segmentation
local_topics.description: Superpixel-based strategies are used to identify informative regions for interactive annotation in medical image segmentation. In early work on interactive cell segmentation, the most informative superpixels are selected using expected prediction error as the acquisition metric, guiding user interaction to areas that would most improve the model. Later, an approach is described where the most informative foreground and background superpixels are chosen for annotation, refining the segmentation boundary by focusing expert effort on critical regions.

canonical_topic.name: Superpixel-Based Region Selection for Deep Active Segmentation
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that operate at the superpixel level for medical image segmentation. Images are first pre-segmented into superpixels using color- and texture-based methods, and pixel-wise uncertainty is aggregated (e.g., by averaging) to define informativeness scores for each superpixel. Querying then targets compact, coherent regions instead of individual pixels, improving annotation efficiency while preserving spatial consistency. In interactive segmentation settings, acquisition functions such as expected prediction error are used to select the most informative foreground and background superpixels, directing expert effort to regions that most refine segmentation boundaries. These approaches instantiate region-based active learning tailored to dense prediction tasks, integrating uncertainty-based acquisition with structured image representation.

local_topics.title: Batch-mode active learning and diversity
local_topics.description: Batch-mode active learning selects multiple instances at once, which is more practical than querying a single instance per iteration. This requires controlling redundancy within the selected batch, not just dissimilarity to labeled data, so that each new labeled example contributes distinct information. Batch diversity thus becomes an additional design objective on top of informativeness and representativeness.

local_topics.title: Batch-mode vs one-by-one querying
local_topics.description: For large neural networks and high-dimensional data, such as image classification or detection tasks, batch-mode active learning is generally more efficient and effective than querying one instance at a time. Retraining a complex model after adding a single high-dimensional data point often yields minimal performance gains relative to the computational cost. Batch-mode querying amortizes the retraining cost over multiple informative instances, improving resource utilization. This motivates preferring larger batches in deep learning scenarios.

canonical_topic.name: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning and Diversity
canonical_topic.description: Batch-mode active learning selects multiple unlabeled instances in each iteration instead of querying a single point, which is especially important for deep models where retraining is computationally expensive. In deep learning scenarios with high-dimensional data, such as images or complex NLP tasks, retraining after a single newly labeled instance often yields negligible performance gains relative to its cost, making larger batches more efficient. This shifts the design objective toward constructing batches that are not only highly informative but also diverse, reducing redundancy so that each queried example contributes distinct information. Batch selection therefore balances informativeness, representativeness, and intra-batch diversity to better exploit limited annotation budgets in deep active learning setups.

local_topics.title: BatchBALD for uncertainty-diversity trade-off
local_topics.description: BatchBALD extends the single-example BALD uncertainty criterion to batch mode, explicitly modeling mutual information between labels and model parameters over a batch of samples. By considering joint information gain, it avoids selecting redundant high-uncertainty points, thereby improving sampling diversity within each batch compared to earlier BALD implementations. This method exemplifies integrating diversity directly into uncertainty-based active learning.

local_topics.title: BatchBALD and joint mutual information
local_topics.description: BatchBALD extends the BALD acquisition function to batch mode by modeling the joint mutual information between the labels of multiple queried samples and the model parameters. It represents a batch of inputs and outputs as joint random variables and defines the batch acquisition score as the difference between the predictive entropy over the batch and the expected conditional entropy given parameters. This explicit joint mutual information mechanism captures correlations between query samples to construct a more informative batch.

local_topics.title: BatchBALD joint mutual information

canonical_topic.name: BatchBALD for Batch-wise Mutual Information Acquisition
canonical_topic.description: BatchBALD generalizes the BALD acquisition function from single-instance to batch active learning by computing the joint mutual information between a batch of unlabeled samples and the model parameters. Instead of scoring each candidate independently, it treats the batch as a joint random variable over inputs and labels, allowing it to explicitly model correlations between queried points. This joint mutual information formulation reduces redundancy among highly uncertain samples and naturally balances uncertainty with diversity within each selected batch. As a result, BatchBALD provides more informative and complementary batches for labeling, improving label efficiency in deep active learning compared to independent BALD or purely uncertainty-based batch selection.

local_topics.title: Adversarial-based uncertainty estimation framework
local_topics.description: This topic treats uncertainty in active learning as a function of a sample’s robustness to adversarial perturbations. Adversarial samples are generated by adding carefully designed, visually imperceptible perturbations that move inputs across the model’s decision boundary with minimal cost. The required perturbation magnitude (attack strength) is used as a proxy for the sample’s distance to the decision boundary: smaller perturbations imply closer proximity and therefore higher uncertainty. This links adversarial robustness analysis with sample selection strategies in deep active learning.

canonical_topic.name: Adversarial-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that estimate uncertainty via adversarial robustness, treating the required perturbation strength to cross a decision boundary as a proxy for a sample’s uncertainty. By generating visually imperceptible adversarial examples and measuring how easily an input can be pushed across the model’s decision boundary, these methods rank unlabeled data such that points closer to the boundary (requiring smaller perturbations) are selected as most informative. Selection is typically implemented by ordering unlabeled samples by their adversarial distance and querying labels for the Top-k, directly coupling adversarial example generation with pool-based query strategies. In medical image analysis, such adversarial-based uncertainty is used both to target inherently uncertain, boundary-near cases and to improve model robustness, though its adoption remains limited. The literature also points to future extensions, including federated learning scenarios where adversarially informed uncertainty sampling must be balanced with communication and robustness constraints.

local_topics.title: Patch-Based Region Active Learning

canonical_topic.name: Region-Based Query Units in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that query labels at sub-image granularity, using regions, patches, slices, superpixels, or points instead of whole images. By redefining the labeling unit to localized regions, these approaches focus the annotation budget on the most informative parts of medical images, which is especially beneficial for dense prediction tasks such as segmentation, lesion detection, and volumetric analysis. Region-based strategies often sample only a fraction of patches or superpixels within selected images, sometimes in multi-scale setups (e.g., slice- and pixel-level, pixel- and point-level), aligning annotation effort with clinical workflows. Some methods further leverage latent space optimization and nearest-neighbour search to select representative or uncertain slices or regions, integrating region granularity directly into the acquisition function. Overall, region-based deep active learning improves label efficiency by targeting uncertain or complex local structures rather than exhaustively annotating full images or volumes.

local_topics.description: Active Domain Adaptation (ADA) augments domain adaptation by selectively querying and annotating informative target-domain samples to reduce the performance gap with fully supervised target training. canonical_topic.name: Active Domain Adaptation in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Active Domain Adaptation (ADA) integrates deep active learning with domain adaptation by selectively querying labels for target-domain samples to mitigate distribution shift under a limited annotation budget. Methods prioritize target examples that are both uncertain for the current model and representative of the target distribution, aiming to close the gap to fully supervised target training with minimal labels. In medical image analysis, ADA is commonly instantiated at the image-wise level, where entire target images are selected for annotation based on their expected contribution to domain alignment and task performance. Region-wise ADA refines this further by querying labels for sub-image units such as patches or superpixels, which is especially beneficial for dense prediction tasks like segmentation. By operating at different granularities of selection, ADA offers a principled way to allocate labeling effort where it most improves cross-domain generalization.

canonical_topic.name: Performance-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers active learning strategies that estimate uncertainty through predicted task performance rather than directly from output probabilities. Methods use surrogate metrics (e.g., loss, Dice score, IoU, temporal output discrepancy, or loss rank) and learnable performance estimators to approximate how well a model would perform on unlabeled samples if they were labeled. These estimated performance scores are then converted into query criteria, typically prioritizing samples predicted to yield low performance as more informative for annotation. This paradigm contrasts with classical probabilistic uncertainty (e.g., entropy or margin) by tightly coupling the acquisition function to task-specific outcome metrics, which is particularly useful in domains like medical image segmentation. The approach enables DAL systems to align sample selection with downstream evaluation objectives even when true labels are unavailable.

local_topics.title: Data hunger of DL vs AL’s limited labels
local_topics.description: Active Learning typically assumes that models are trained and updated with small labeled sets, whereas Deep Learning is highly data-intensive and requires large numbers of labeled examples. Classic AL settings provide too few labeled training samples to adequately train traditional DL models, and the common one-by-one query strategy is ill-suited to DL’s mini-batch training regime. This mismatch creates practical difficulties in directly coupling conventional AL loops with DL training.

local_topics.title: Processing pipeline mismatch between AL and DL
local_topics.description: Most traditional Active Learning algorithms assume fixed feature representations and focus on training a classifier on top of them, with query strategies defined in this static feature space. Deep Learning, in contrast, jointly optimizes feature representations and classifier parameters, tightly coupling representation learning and prediction. Simply fine-tuning DL models within a classic AL loop, or treating feature learning and querying as separate problems, can lead to divergence and suboptimal behavior.

local_topics.title: Pipeline inconsistency between AL and DL
local_topics.description: This topic describes a common 'split-and-splitting' approach where deep learning models are first trained via conventional supervised learning and only afterward combined with active learning for sample querying. Examples include systems that pretrain on session datasets, DBN-based AL-DL, ADN for sentiment classification, and CNN-based captcha recognition, all treating AL and DL as largely independent problems. The text argues that this processing pipeline inconsistency can cause divergence between AL and DL objectives and motivates the need for a unified, general DeepAL framework that tightly couples model training and querying.

canonical_topic.name: Mismatch Between Classical Active Learning and Deep Learning Pipelines
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses the fundamental mismatch between traditional active learning assumptions and the requirements of deep learning models. Classic active learning typically operates with very small labeled sets and one-by-one query strategies, which conflicts with deep networks’ need for large labeled datasets and mini-batch training. Traditional AL methods also assume a fixed feature representation and focus on querying in a static feature space, whereas deep learning jointly learns feature representations and classifiers, tightly coupling representation learning and prediction. As a result, naïvely wrapping deep models in conventional AL loops or splitting supervision and querying into separate stages can cause divergence between learning and querying objectives and lead to suboptimal performance. These challenges motivate unified deep active learning frameworks that integrate model training and query selection in a coherent process.

canonical_topic.name: Generative Models for Synthetic Querying and Augmentation in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on integrating generative models into deep active learning pipelines to synthesize informative samples and augment limited labeled datasets. GANs and related generative networks are used to create additional training images, especially in medical imaging, to increase diversity, balance class distributions, and enrich the pool between query iterations without proportional labeling cost. Beyond passive augmentation, generative models support membership query synthesis, explicitly generating instances in regions of high model uncertainty or disagreement. Approaches with VAEs and Bayesian data augmentation model the uncertainty of generated data itself, allowing the learner to target contentious areas of the hypothesis space while accounting for the reliability of synthetic samples. Collectively, these methods aim to improve label efficiency and robustness of deep active learners by coupling acquisition strategies with learned generative priors over the input space.

The idea is that instances near adversarial decision boundaries reveal model weaknesses and thus are informative when labeled. canonical_topic.name: Adversarial and Generative Query Synthesis in DAL
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that use adversarial representations and generative models to synthesize or identify highly informative queries. Adversarial perturbation–based approaches such as AdvDeepFool locate samples near decision boundaries, exposing model weaknesses and targeting boundary regions for labeling and data augmentation. Generative Adversarial Active Learning (GAAL) employs GANs to synthesize candidate queries, aiming for samples near the classifier’s decision boundary, though naïve boundary-focused generation can produce semantically meaningless or hard‑to‑label instances. Bayesian Generative Active Deep Learning (BGADL) refines this idea by combining Bayesian acquisition (e.g., BALD), VAE/ACGAN generators, and disagreement-based targeting of regions with high epistemic uncertainty, so that synthetic data are as informative as pool‑selected points. Overall, these methods integrate robustness and generative modeling into the active learning loop to improve label efficiency while carefully managing the trade‑off between informativeness and human labelability.

local_topics.title: DeepFool-based query strategy in DAL
local_topics.description: This topic focuses on using the DeepFool algorithm to generate adversarial perturbations and drive active learning queries. DeepFool iteratively finds minimal perturbations that change a model’s prediction, thereby approximating the distance from each sample to the decision boundary. In this setting, samples requiring only small adversarial perturbations are considered most uncertain and are prioritized for labeling. The approach operationalizes uncertainty sampling through explicit computation of minimal adversarial noise.

AdvDeepFool uses DeepFool to compute the minimal perturbation rx required to change a sample’s predicted label and queries points with the smallest such perturbations, interpreting them as closest to the decision boundary. These approaches estimate each unlabeled sample’s distance to the decision boundary via the minimal adversarial perturbation required to change the model’s prediction, and interpret small perturbations as high uncertainty. Query strategies such as DFAL and AdvDeepFool select points with the smallest perturbations, effectively operationalizing boundary-based uncertainty sampling in a deep setting. Variants may use other attacks like the Basic Iterative Method, but share the core idea of ranking samples by adversarial distance. While these methods can speed up convergence of deep models like CNNs, they may reduce batch diversity because they concentrate queries near the current decision boundary rather than covering the broader data distribution.

Acquisition functions can then target epistemic uncertainty, focusing on regions where the model lacks knowledge. This framework underpins methods like BALD for information-theoretic querying.

canonical_topic.name: Bayesian Deep Active Learning (DBAL)
canonical_topic.description: Bayesian Deep Active Learning uses Bayesian treatments of deep neural networks to obtain principled uncertainty estimates for query selection. Instead of relying on overconfident softmax scores, it employs approximate Bayesian inference methods such as Monte Carlo dropout, deep ensembles, or Bayesian convolutional neural networks to approximate posterior distributions over model parameters. These posterior-based estimates emphasize epistemic uncertainty, allowing acquisition functions like BALD and related mutual-information criteria to target regions where the model lacks knowledge. By providing more reliable uncertainty for high-dimensional data and mini-batch querying, DBAL addresses key challenges in combining deep learning with uncertainty-driven active learning strategies.

local_topics.description: The survey introduces a structured taxonomy of sampling strategies in AL, categorizing approaches into diversity sampling, class-balanced sampling, hybrid sampling, and learnable sampling. Diversity sampling focuses on reducing redundancy by selecting varied samples, while class-balanced sampling targets label distribution issues by enforcing or approximating balance across classes. canonical_topic.description: This topic covers a structured taxonomy of sampling strategies in deep active learning, with particular emphasis on medical imaging applications. It extends beyond traditional informativeness-based querying to explicitly categorize approaches such as diversity sampling, class-balanced sampling, hybrid sampling, and learnable sampling. Diversity sampling aims to reduce redundancy by selecting varied samples that better cover the data manifold, while class-balanced sampling counters skewed label distributions by enforcing or approximating class balance during query selection. Hybrid strategies combine multiple criteria (e.g., uncertainty and diversity) to improve selection robustness, and learnable strategies employ neural networks to adaptively learn selection policies from data. Together, this taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for designing, analyzing, and comparing deep active learning methods under realistic labeling constraints.

local_topics.title: Stationary versus drifting data streams
local_topics.description: This topic describes the distinction between stationary data streams, where the underlying data-generating distribution and its statistical properties remain stable, and drifting streams, where these properties change over time. It highlights that active learning strategies designed for stationary streams can perform suboptimally on drifting streams because concept drift may modify the scale of informativeness measures or necessitate model replacement and additional labeled observations. Accurately assessing whether a stream is stationary or drifting is thus critical for designing effective online active learning strategies and fully exploiting active learning benefits.

local_topics.title: Assumptions on data stream dynamics
local_topics.description: The survey distinguishes active learning strategies by assumptions about the temporal behavior of data streams: stationary, drifting, and evolving. Stationary streams assume fixed data distribution, drifting streams model gradual or abrupt changes (concept drift), and evolving streams allow for structural evolution such as new concepts or classes. These assumptions drive different algorithmic requirements for model updating and query selection.

canonical_topic.name: Data Stream Dynamics in Online Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on how assumptions about data stream dynamics affect the design and performance of online active learning methods. It distinguishes stationary streams, where the data-generating distribution remains stable, from drifting streams, where gradual or abrupt concept drift changes informativeness scales, may invalidate existing models, and requires additional labeled data. It also considers evolving streams, where new concepts or classes can appear, imposing stronger requirements on model updating and query selection strategies. Correctly identifying whether a stream is stationary, drifting, or evolving is crucial for choosing appropriate acquisition strategies, scheduling model replacement or adaptation, and maintaining the effectiveness of active learning over time.

Such continual, online updating is presented as an optimization of the active learning routine for data streams.

canonical_topic.name: Online Model Updating in Stream-based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns active learning in data streams where the model is updated online as queried instances are labeled. A subset of incoming stream instances is selected for annotation, and their labels are immediately incorporated into the classifier, enabling real-time adaptation of the decision boundary. The setting typically assumes stationary data streams so that incremental updates remain valid over long periods without expensive retraining from scratch. Immediate feedback from queried labels allows the active learner to continuously refine its selection strategy and explore new regions of the input space using the most up-to-date model state. This online updating mechanism is a core component of stream-based active learning systems that must operate under latency and budget constraints while tracking evolving data distributions.

The focus is on online classification tasks where a model continuously receives data but assumes long-term stability in the generative process. Such approaches can exploit stationarity to simplify model adaptation and reduce the need for complex drift detection mechanisms.

local_topics.title: Adaptive learning in non-stationary streams
local_topics.description: This topic concerns data-stream scenarios where the underlying data distribution changes over time, requiring models that can continuously adapt to maintain high classification accuracy. It highlights the need for techniques that track distributional shifts and update decision boundaries or parameters accordingly in streaming environments.

local_topics.title: Online classification with stationary and drifting streams
local_topics.description: Existing research is reported to focus predominantly on online classification models for data streams. These models are designed to cope with both stationary environments and drifting data streams where the underlying concept may change over time. The emphasis has been on maintaining good predictive performance while updating models incrementally as new labeled examples are acquired.

canonical_topic.name: Active Learning in Stationary and Drifting Data Streams
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses how active learning operates in data stream settings under both stationary and non-stationary (drifting) distributions. In stationary streams, the relative stability of the generative process allows stream-based active learners to focus on selective labeling and incremental model refinement without extensive drift detection mechanisms. In contrast, non-stationary streams require adaptive models that can track distributional shifts and update decision boundaries or parameters while querying labels efficiently over time. Work in this area predominantly studies online classification models that incrementally update with newly acquired labeled examples, aiming to maintain predictive performance under both stable and drifting concepts while respecting a limited annotation budget.

local_topics.title: Cost-sensitive querying and proactive learning
local_topics.description: Cost-sensitive querying incorporates annotation cost directly into selection criteria so that instances with high utility per unit cost are preferred, often operationalized as a return-on-investment (ROI) ratio. Variants include imposing per-instance cost caps and combining utility and cost ranks, with empirical evidence that ROI-based strategies can lower total annotation cost. In more realistic settings with multiple annotators of varying expertise and reliability, proactive learning jointly selects both the instance and the oracle, accounting for refusal and error rates and extending to specific tasks such as named entity recognition.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Cost-sensitive annotator and instance selection
local_topics.description: Cost-sensitive querying strategies in active learning can jointly select both which instances to label and which annotators to query, based on estimated annotator reliability. Additional mechanisms include collecting multiple labels per instance and consolidating them, as well as automatic crowd consolidation frameworks tailored to sequence labeling tasks. These methods explicitly model noise and cost trade-offs in crowd-based active learning.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

canonical_topic.name: Cost-Sensitive and Proactive Annotation in Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers cost-sensitive active learning strategies that explicitly incorporate annotation cost into the query selection process. Methods prioritize instances based on a utility-per-cost or return-on-investment (ROI) criterion, sometimes with per-instance cost caps or combined utility–cost ranking, to reduce total labeling expenditure under a fixed budget. In more realistic multi-annotator settings, proactive learning jointly selects both the instance and the oracle, modeling annotator expertise, reliability, refusal, and error rates. For crowd-based and sequence labeling tasks, these approaches may collect multiple labels per instance and apply consolidation frameworks that account for noise–cost trade-offs. In Deep Active Learning, the same principles guide which high-impact examples to query and from which annotators, making better use of limited annotation budgets when training deep models.

local_topics.title: Scope and contributions of the survey
local_topics.description: The survey aims to comprehensively review recent query strategies for online active learning over data streams, analyzing their strengths and limitations. It also covers evaluation strategies for such algorithms, highlights real-world application domains, and identifies open challenges and future research opportunities. The focus is explicitly on the core problem of selecting the most informative data points to label in an online streaming context.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Gap in online active regression research
local_topics.description: The authors highlight a comparative lack of work on online active linear regression and online regression models in general. While classification in streaming settings has been extensively studied, regression-oriented active learning for streams remains underdeveloped. This gap motivates calls for methods that can handle continuous targets in dynamic environments.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Streaming AL for classification tasks
local_topics.description: Classification is a primary task for online active learning in data streams, appearing under stationary, drifting, and evolving scenarios. Methods are grouped by whether they maintain a single classifier or an ensemble while actively querying labels, reflecting different strategies for robustness and adaptability to changing distributions. The extensive reference lists under these rows indicate that classification is the most heavily studied task in streaming active learning.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Regression in streaming active learning
local_topics.description: Regression tasks in online active learning are treated primarily with single-model approaches for both stationary and evolving data streams. These methods focus on selectively querying continuous-valued labels while the underlying functional relationship may remain stable or gradually evolve. The relatively small set of cited works highlights that regression is less explored than classification in the streaming AL context.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Online learning tasks and paradigms
local_topics.description: The surveyed active learning strategies are applied across several online learning formulations. These include online classification, where class labels are predicted for streaming instances; online regression, where continuous targets are modeled; and online semi-supervised learning, which leverages both labeled and unlabeled streaming data. The topic covers how active querying is adapted to different predictive tasks in a streaming context.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Online Active Learning for Data Streams
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers active learning in streaming or online settings, where instances arrive sequentially and the learner must decide on-the-fly whether to query their labels. The survey emphasizes query strategies tailored to data streams, focusing on selecting the most informative points under constraints such as non-stationarity, label budget, and real-time processing. Online classification is identified as the dominant task, with methods using either single classifiers or ensembles to handle stationary, drifting, and evolving distributions while actively querying labels. In contrast, online active regression—selectively querying continuous-valued targets in streams—is far less explored, creating a notable research gap. The topic also includes online semi-supervised formulations that combine labeled and unlabeled streaming data, highlighting how active querying is adapted across different predictive paradigms in the streaming context.

local_topics.title: Data Expansion Strategies for Labeled Sets in DeepAL
local_topics.description: DeepAL must reconcile AL’s small labeled set assumption with DL’s need for large labeled datasets, motivating strategies that expand effective training data without proportional manual labeling cost. The text criticizes methods that only train on explicitly labeled samples, overlooking the utility of unlabeled data. It emphasizes the importance of data expansion and training strategies that exploit unlabeled sets to mitigate label scarcity in DeepAL.

local_topics.title: Data expansion for scarce labels
local_topics.description: When labeled data are insufficient, DeepAL can be supported by techniques that expand the effective labeled set, such as augmentation, pseudo-labeling, or other label-efficient strategies. Table 1 groups such work under 'Data expansion of labeled samples' as a response to the challenge of insufficient labeled samples. These methods aim to increase model performance without proportionally increasing annotation cost.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Labeled Sample Data Expansion Techniques
local_topics.description: This topic addresses methods that effectively expand the labeled dataset in deep active learning beyond direct human annotation. It involves data augmentation, semi-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling, or generative approaches that synthesize or infer labels to increase training data diversity and volume. The goal is to amplify the benefit of each queried label while maintaining label quality and improving model performance.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Data Expansion Techniques in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers strategies to expand the effective labeled dataset in deep active learning, reconciling the small labeled set assumption of active learning with deep models’ need for large training corpora. Instead of training solely on explicitly annotated samples, these approaches exploit the abundant unlabeled pool through data augmentation, semi-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling, and generative methods. The objective is to amplify the utility of each queried label, improving model performance without proportionally increasing annotation cost. Within the DeepAL setting, such techniques are tightly coupled with the querying process, aiming to mitigate label scarcity while maintaining label quality and label-efficiency.

local_topics.title: Cost-Effective Active Learning (CEAL)
local_topics.description: CEAL integrates pseudo-labeling with uncertainty-based active learning to balance label quality and annotation cost. The method forwards the most uncertain unlabeled samples to human experts for annotation while assigning pseudo-labels only to samples for which the model is highly confident. This selective strategy aims to reduce labeling cost while limiting noise from incorrect pseudo-labels, and has inspired many subsequent works in medical imaging.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

local_topics.title: CEAL Pseudo-Labeling for Cost-Effective DeepAL
local_topics.description: CEAL (Cost-Effective Active Learning) augments the training set by combining oracle-labeled uncertain samples with pseudo-labeled high-confidence samples. An initialized CNN is fed unlabeled data and outputs a small set of uncertain instances for manual labeling and a large set of high-confidence predictions to which pseudo-labels are automatically assigned. Both types of samples are then used to fine-tune the CNN iteratively, expanding the effective labeled data without increasing annotation cost proportionally.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: CEAL framework with pseudo-labeling
local_topics.description: The CEAL framework integrates deep convolutional neural networks with active learning for image classification by jointly leveraging uncertain and high-confidence unlabeled samples. At each iteration, unlabeled data are passed through a CNN, producing a small set of uncertain samples sent to a human oracle and a large set of high-confidence samples that receive pseudo-labels from the model. Both human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data are then used to fine-tune the CNN iteratively, forming a closed-loop DeepAL process that efficiently expands the labeled set.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: CEAL: pseudo-labeling with uncertainty queries
local_topics.description: CEAL addresses high labeling costs by assigning pseudo-labels to high-confidence unlabeled samples and adding them to the training set, alongside highly uncertain samples selected via an uncertainty-based AL strategy. This dual use of confident and uncertain examples expands the training data without fully relying on manual annotations. The approach targets efficient DeepAL-based image classification.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Cost-Effective Deep Active Learning with Pseudo-Labels (CEAL)
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the CEAL framework, which integrates uncertainty-based active learning with pseudo-labeling to reduce annotation costs in deep active learning. At each iteration, a CNN evaluates unlabeled samples, forwarding the most uncertain instances to a human oracle while automatically assigning pseudo-labels to high-confidence predictions. Both oracle-labeled and pseudo-labeled data are then used jointly to fine-tune the network in a closed-loop process, effectively enlarging the labeled training set without proportional increases in manual labeling. The approach explicitly trades off label quality and annotation cost, aiming to limit noise from incorrect pseudo-labels while exploiting confident predictions. CEAL has been particularly influential in deep active learning for image classification, including medical image analysis, where labeling is expensive.

local_topics.title: Online active learning for streams
local_topics.description: Online active learning addresses scenarios where data arrives as a continuous stream and instances cannot be stored in a pool for greedy selection. The learner must decide immediately, for each incoming instance, whether to request its label, similar to the sequential decision structure of the secretary problem. This setting is crucial when real-time sampling decisions are required and latency or storage constraints prohibit batch-based active learning.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Online active learning for drifting streams
local_topics.description: This topic describes a generic online active learning loop that operates over a data stream under a labeling budget. At each timestamp, a sampling strategy decides whether to query the label of the incoming instance, incurring labeling cost and updating both a classifier and a drift detector. The process is constrained by a global budget and stream length, and includes mechanisms to manage classifier updates continuously as labeled data arrive.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Online active learning for data streams
local_topics.description: Online active learning is applied in settings where data arrives at high velocity, labels are expensive, and it is infeasible to store all unlabeled instances prior to selection. The process involves making labeling decisions on-the-fly, querying only the most informative observations to update the model. It is particularly suited to dynamic, evolving environments where models must adapt in real time to new data distributions.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Online active learning under distribution shift
local_topics.description: This topic calls for online active learning strategies capable of handling a wide variety of distribution shifts in data streams. The goal is to design query and labeling policies that remain effective when underlying data distributions change in different ways, as categorized earlier in the survey (Sect. 3.2). Such methods must detect and adapt to shifting conditions while still judiciously selecting data points for labeling.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Online Active Learning for Non-Stationary Data Streams
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers online active learning in streaming settings where unlabeled instances arrive sequentially and cannot be stored in a pool for batch selection. At each time step, the learner must immediately decide whether to query the label of the current instance, operating under labeling cost and global budget constraints. The setting is particularly important for high-velocity, real-time applications and evolving environments, where models must be updated continuously as new labeled examples become available. Methods must also cope with various forms of distribution shift and concept drift, often coupling query policies with drift detectors to maintain performance over time. For deep active learning, these ideas translate into designing streaming query strategies and budget-aware policies that can efficiently update deep models under non-stationary conditions.

local_topics.title: Practical challenges in active learning
local_topics.description: The text highlights that the survey also addresses practical challenges of active learning, such as implementation issues, computational constraints, and interaction with human annotators. These challenges involve applying theoretical methods to real-world data, coping with noise, and managing labeling costs under operational constraints. Addressing such issues is crucial for deploying active learning in practice, especially in dynamic environments like data streams.

local_topics.title: Real-world applications and challenges
local_topics.description: This topic covers how stream-based active learning is applied in practice and the practical obstacles encountered. Applications may include monitoring systems, user interaction logs, sensor networks, or financial streams, where labels are expensive or delayed. Challenges include noisy or delayed labels, strict latency requirements, changing data distributions, and limited human annotation capacity.

local_topics.title: Challenges in streaming active learning
local_topics.description: Online active learning with data streams must operate in real time on continuously arriving, exponentially growing data. A central bottleneck is the difficulty and cost of obtaining annotated data to train complex predictive and decision-making models. This scarcity of labels limits the effective deployment of such models in domains like healthcare, autonomous driving, and industrial production. The topic involves data streams, real-time learning constraints, label acquisition costs, and application-specific requirements.

canonical_topic.name: Practical Challenges in Stream-based Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on the practical obstacles encountered when deploying stream-based active learning systems in real-world settings. Methods must operate in real time on continuously arriving, potentially unbounded data streams while querying labels under strict annotation budgets and latency constraints. Key challenges include the high cost and limited availability of labels, noisy or delayed annotations, and the need to coordinate effectively with human annotators. Furthermore, systems must cope with changing data distributions and application-specific requirements in domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and industrial monitoring. These constraints directly affect the design of active querying strategies, the management of labeling costs, and the overall robustness of deployed active learning pipelines.

local_topics.title: Adapting active learning to imbalanced data
local_topics.description: Data imbalance is common in NLP and requires adapting active learning to avoid over-focusing on majority classes. Approaches include modifying the underlying model, altering the learning algorithm, and designing imbalance-aware query strategies that better target minority or rare phenomena. These adaptations aim to maintain model performance across classes despite skewed label distributions.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Using active learning to mitigate imbalance
local_topics.description: Active learning can also be used proactively to alleviate data imbalance by preferentially sampling underrepresented instances, thereby constructing more balanced training sets. By directing annotation effort toward rare classes or difficult regions of the data space, active learning helps build better datasets for imbalanced NLP problems. This reframes active learning as a tool for dataset curation as well as model training.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Active Learning for Class-Balanced Annotation
local_topics.description: Active learning can be used to mitigate class imbalance at the data acquisition and annotation stage rather than only during model training. By selectively querying labels that avoid over-annotating majority classes and prioritize minority-class samples, AL helps construct more balanced labeled datasets. This class-balance sampling strategy aims to improve model performance on underrepresented classes.

local_topics.title: Class-balance aware query strategies
local_topics.description: This topic involves active learning methods that explicitly consider class balance when selecting new samples. The acquisition function is adjusted so that underrepresented classes in medical image datasets are preferentially queried, helping to mitigate skewed label distributions. This can improve performance on rare but clinically important conditions.
local_topics.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

canonical_topic.name: Imbalance-Aware Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep and traditional active learning methods that explicitly address class imbalance during data selection and annotation. Instead of passively inheriting skewed label distributions, the acquisition function is modified to prioritize underrepresented or rare classes, both in NLP and in medical image analysis. Such class-balance aware querying helps construct more balanced training sets and improves performance on minority classes, including rare but clinically critical conditions. The perspective also reframes active learning as a tool for dataset curation, not just model training, by steering annotation budgets toward difficult or infrequent phenomena. Across applications, these strategies integrate imbalance considerations directly into the selection criterion for new labels, rather than relying solely on post-hoc reweighting or resampling.

local_topics.title: Pool-Based Active Learning Scenario
local_topics.description: The survey focuses on the pool-based AL setting, where there exists a fixed pool of unlabeled instances and the learner selectively draws instances from this pool for annotation. This scenario contrasts with stream-based or membership-query AL and is widely used in NLP due to the availability of large unlabeled corpora. The pool serves as the central resource for iterative querying and labeling.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: General pool-based active learning loop
local_topics.description: This topic describes the standard iterative procedure of pool-based active learning. Starting from an initial labeled training set X^ε and an unlabeled pool U^ε, a model is trained, candidate samples are evaluated, and a subset is selected, labeled, and used to update both the training set and the pool. The loop repeats until a stopping criterion is met, defining the core active learning cycle.

local_topics.title: Pool-based active learning with oracle annotators
local_topics.description: Pool-based active learning operates on a large pool of unlabeled data, from which the learner selects informative samples to be labeled by an oracle, such as medical doctors. This setting allows exploitation of sample correlations and global selection strategies across the pool. It is the dominant framework in active learning research, especially in data-rich domains like medical imaging.

local_topics.title: Pool-based active learning cycle
local_topics.description: Pool-based active learning operates on an unlabeled pool U, from which samples are iteratively selected via a query strategy and sent to an oracle for labeling, forming a labeled set L. The model is trained on L using supervised learning, then uses the newly acquired knowledge to guide subsequent queries. This cycle repeats—updating L each time—until the annotation budget is used up or a stopping condition is met.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Pool-based active learning framework
local_topics.description: Pool-based active learning operates on a closed, static pool of unlabeled data, aiming to select the most informative subset of instances for labeling. It is predominantly used for classification tasks, notably image classification, where manual labeling is costly. Sampling schemes are typically iterative and governed by a parameter k, the number of unlabeled instances queried per round, with k often set to one for traditional models that are relatively cheap to retrain. This framework structures the query process around batch selection from the pool to optimize label efficiency under computational and annotation constraints.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Pool-Based Deep Active Learning Framework
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the standard pool-based active learning (AL) setting, where a fixed, unlabeled pool serves as the source from which informative instances are iteratively queried for annotation. The core loop starts from an initial labeled set and an unlabeled pool, trains a model, applies a query strategy over the pool to select one or more samples, obtains labels from an oracle (e.g., domain experts such as medical doctors), and updates the labeled set and model until a stopping criterion or annotation budget is reached. Pool-based AL contrasts with stream-based and membership-query settings and is the dominant framework in deep active learning, especially in data-rich domains like NLP, medical imaging, and image classification. The framework often assumes a static pool and uses batch or single-instance querying governed by a parameter k, balancing label efficiency against the computational cost of retraining deep models. Within DAL, this scenario defines the experimental setup in which acquisition functions, uncertainty measures, and diversity strategies are evaluated under realistic labeling-budget constraints.

local_topics.title: Pool-based deep active learning process
local_topics.description: The paper formalizes DAL in a pool-based active learning setting, where an initial labeled set and a large unlabeled pool of i.i.d. samples are maintained. At each iteration, a batch of unlabeled instances is selected via an acquisition function α(x, M) applied to a current model M, labels for these instances are queried from an oracle, and the labeled/unlabeled sets are updated before retraining M. The process continues until a labeling budget is exhausted or a target performance level is reached, and is described for classification tasks but extends to other domains like image segmentation.

local_topics.title: Deep active learning iterative workflow
local_topics.description: Deep active learning (DeepAL) initializes or pre-trains the deep model parameters θ on an initial labeled dataset L₀, then uses the model to extract features from an unlabeled pool U. A query strategy selects informative samples from U, which are labeled and added to an expanded labeled set L, while U is updated to remove queried instances. The deep model is retrained on the evolving L, and this process iterates until the label budget or predefined termination criteria are reached.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

local_topics.title: Iterative Deep Active Learning framework
local_topics.description: Deep active learning (DeepAL) initializes or pre-trains a deep model on an initial labeled set L₀, then uses the model to extract features from an unlabeled pool U. A query strategy selects informative samples from U, an oracle provides their labels to form an updated labeled set L, and the model is retrained while U is updated. This cycle repeats until a label budget is exhausted or stopping criteria are met. The framework is conceptually split into query strategy design and deep model training, with further attention to generalization and stopping strategies.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of deep active learning

canonical_topic.name: Iterative Pool-based Deep Active Learning Workflow
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the standard pool-based deep active learning workflow, in which a deep model is initialized or pre-trained on an initial labeled set and then iteratively improved by querying labels for selected unlabeled samples. At each iteration, the current model is used to score an unlabeled pool via an acquisition function or query strategy, and the most informative instances are selected and sent to an oracle for labeling. The labeled and unlabeled sets are updated accordingly, and the deep model is retrained on the expanded labeled set, often using the model’s feature extraction capabilities to guide selection. The process continues until a labeling budget is exhausted or predefined stopping criteria or performance targets are met. The framework is typically decomposed into query strategy design and deep model training, with additional attention to generalization and stopping strategies, and while commonly applied to classification, it naturally extends to other domains such as image segmentation.

local_topics.title: Uncertainty Estimation with Multiple Inferences
local_topics.description: This topic refers to computing uncertainty by aggregating multiple model inferences per image. Techniques such as Monte Carlo dropout, test-time augmentation, or model ensembles can be used to generate multiple predictions, whose disagreement quantifies uncertainty. This can yield more reliable query criteria for active learning in medical image tasks where prediction confidence is critical.

local_topics.title: Multiple inferences for uncertainty estimation
local_topics.description: Uncertainty-based active learning can mitigate model over-confidence by performing multiple stochastic inferences under perturbations. Two main strategies are described: averaging prediction probabilities across runs to compute classic metrics like entropy and margin, and measuring disagreement between predictions as a direct proxy for uncertainty. The text also distinguishes whether perturbations are applied to model parameters or to the input data. This framework underpins subsequent methods such as MC dropout, ensembles, model disagreement, and data disagreement.

local_topics.description: The table organizes surveyed works by how they estimate uncertainty, distinguishing approaches like single-model prediction scores, distance to the decision boundary, and multiple inferences such as MC Dropout and data disagreement. It further lists specific uncertainty metrics including entropy, BALD, least confidence, variance, KL divergence, and distance-based scores. These metrics quantify how unsure a model is about its predictions and guide which samples to query in active learning pipelines.

canonical_topic.name: Multiple-Inference Uncertainty Estimation in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that estimate uncertainty by performing multiple stochastic inferences per sample and aggregating the resulting predictions. Techniques such as Monte Carlo dropout, model ensembles, and test-time/data augmentation introduce variability either in model parameters or in the input to generate diverse outputs. Disagreement or dispersion among these outputs is then quantified using metrics like entropy, margin-based scores, BALD, variance, variance ratio, KL divergence, and gradient-based measures. These richer uncertainty signals are used as acquisition functions to select informative samples for annotation, particularly in safety-critical medical imaging applications where over-confident but wrong predictions must be mitigated. The topic highlights how multi-inference schemes systematically organize and enhance uncertainty-based querying strategies in deep active learning pipelines.

local_topics.title: Monte Carlo dropout in deep active learning
local_topics.description: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout applies random neuron dropping at inference time to generate multiple predictive samples, enabling Bayesian-style uncertainty quantification. These samples are aggregated to compute metrics such as entropy, standard deviation, and BALD for sample selection. The section highlights that MC dropout significantly improves uncertainty-based deep active learning performance and notes early applications in medical image analysis, including skin lesion analysis (ISIC 2016), brain cell type classification, and endoscopy imaging.

local_topics.title: Multiple inferences with MC Dropout
local_topics.description: This topic refers to active learning strategies that obtain multiple stochastic predictions from a neural network using Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout. By sampling different dropout realizations at test time, these methods estimate predictive uncertainty (e.g., via variance or BALD) and query the most informative samples. Such approaches are well suited to deep models in medical image analysis where labeling is costly, and uncertainty must be quantified robustly.

local_topics.title: MC Dropout for Multiple Inferences
local_topics.description: MC Dropout is used to perform multiple stochastic forward passes through a single network to estimate predictive uncertainty in deep active learning. These multiple inferences provide sample-wise variance or entropy estimates that guide which medical images or regions to query. It appears as a core component of several methods in the table and is often combined with other criteria like BALD or KL divergence.

local_topics.title: MC Dropout multiple inferences for uncertainty
local_topics.description: MC Dropout performs multiple stochastic forward passes at inference time by keeping dropout active, generating a distribution of predictions per image. The variability across these predictions is used to estimate model uncertainty, which guides active learning sample selection. In this context, multiple inferences with MC Dropout are applied to medical images to identify cases where the model is least confident and most in need of annotation.

local_topics.title: DBAL with MC dropout entropy
local_topics.description: DBAL combines entropy-based uncertainty with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout to improve uncertainty estimation. During acquisition, the model performs multiple stochastic forward passes with all dropout layers activated, and the average predicted probabilities across these passes are used to compute entropy. This approach seeks to better capture model epistemic uncertainty when selecting samples.

canonical_topic.name: MC Dropout Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the use of Monte Carlo (MC) dropout to obtain multiple stochastic inferences from deep models for uncertainty-based active learning. By keeping dropout active at test time and running many forward passes, practitioners estimate epistemic uncertainty via measures such as variance, entropy, and BALD, and use these scores to select informative samples. In medical image analysis, this mechanism is exploited to prioritize expensive annotations for tasks like skin lesion analysis, brain cell type classification, and endoscopy imaging. Methods such as DBAL further refine this idea by combining MC dropout with entropy-based acquisition, averaging predictive probabilities across passes before computing entropy to better capture uncertainty. Overall, MC dropout serves as a practical Bayesian-style tool that integrates naturally with deep active learning pipelines where robust uncertainty estimates are critical.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification

This setting requires acquisition strategies that model label dependencies and multi-output uncertainty instead of assuming a single, mutually exclusive class. Query criteria and uncertainty estimates need to be adapted to complex output spaces so that informative images are selected with respect to all possible disease labels. Such modality-specific active learning methods better reflect clinical reality and can improve annotation efficiency in large-scale chest X-ray datasets.

local_topics.title: Single-model entropy-based uncertainty sampling
local_topics.description: Entropy-based methods use the predictive class probability distribution of a single model to quantify uncertainty. Samples with the highest output entropy are considered most ambiguous and therefore most informative for labeling. This simple yet effective strategy is widely used as a baseline in deep active learning for medical image analysis.

local_topics.title: Entropy-based top-k query strategy
local_topics.description: Entropy over the predictive probability distribution quantifies uncertainty by measuring how spread out the model’s predictions are across classes. In an active learning loop, samples with the highest entropy are considered most informative. A top-k strategy then selects the k images with the largest entropy scores from the unlabeled pool for annotation, optimizing the use of labeling resources.

local_topics.title: Single-model entropy uncertainty sampling

local_topics.title: Maximum Entropy acquisition strategy
local_topics.description: This topic covers the Maximum Entropy (Entropy) acquisition function in deep active learning, which selects data points x that maximize the model’s predictive entropy over labels. The function α_entropy(x, M) is used as a query strategy to prioritize the most uncertain samples according to the classifier M. It operationalizes uncertainty sampling by preferring instances where the model’s label predictions are most dispersed.

local_topics.title: Entropy as an active learning acquisition function
local_topics.description: Entropy quantifies the randomness or disorder in a probability distribution and is used to measure predictive uncertainty in active learning. Given a model’s predicted class probabilities for a data point, higher entropy indicates greater uncertainty about the correct class label. Acquisition strategies that select examples with maximal entropy prioritize points where the model is most unsure, aiming to improve decision boundaries efficiently. Entropy thus serves as a principled scalar metric derived from the model’s output distribution.

canonical_topic.name: Entropy-Based Uncertainty Acquisition in DAL
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers entropy-based acquisition functions for deep active learning, where predictive entropy over class probabilities is used to quantify model uncertainty. A single deep model produces a probability distribution over labels, and samples with the highest entropy—i.e., the most dispersed predictions—are selected as the most informative for annotation. Such strategies often use a top-k selection from the unlabeled pool, prioritizing data points where the model is least confident to efficiently refine decision boundaries under a limited labeling budget. These methods serve as simple yet strong baselines in deep active learning, particularly in medical image analysis and data stream settings, avoiding the computational overhead of ensembles while still leveraging principled uncertainty estimates.

The FCN is first trained on a small labeled set, then used to extract feature representations for unlabeled images, from which uncertainty and similarity metrics are computed. Active learning strategies select the most uncertain or diverse image slices or regions for segmentation labeling, significantly reducing the manual delineation effort. Evaluation tracks segmentation quality metrics (e.g., Dice, IoU) against annotation budget.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns deep active learning frameworks for medical and biomedical image segmentation, where dense pixel- or voxel-level expert annotations are expensive. Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) and related segmentation architectures are first trained on small labeled sets and then used to derive uncertainty and feature similarity measures for unlabeled images or regions. Query selection strategies combine uncertainty-based criteria with diversity or similarity-aware formulations, including casting sample selection as an extended maximum set cover problem to avoid redundant annotations. Some approaches integrate transfer learning with active learning to improve segmentation performance in low-annotation regimes. Evaluation typically measures segmentation quality (e.g., Dice coefficient, IoU) as a function of annotation budget, demonstrating substantial reductions in manual delineation effort compared to passive learning.

canonical_topic.name: Hybrid Fusion and Pseudo-Labeling in Deep Active Learning

By adding pseudo-labeled data to the training set without extra annotation cost, these methods strengthen the model-driven signal that guides active querying. Extensions incorporate additional weak supervision such as box-level or localization cues, enabling active selection strategies that leverage both predicted labels and coarse annotations. Such hybrid approaches are tailored to medical imaging scenarios with limited, weak, or partial labels, aiming to maximize performance under tight annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Information-theoretic uncertainty measures
local_topics.description: Entropy, margin, and BALD are standard uncertainty measures used to rank unlabeled samples in DAL. Entropy quantifies overall predictive dispersion across classes, while margin uses the difference between the top two class probabilities as a simpler uncertainty proxy. BALD (Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement) measures mutual information between predictions and model parameters, targeting epistemic uncertainty in Bayesian setups. These metrics directly define the querying criterion for uncertainty-based strategies.

local_topics.title: BALD acquisition strategy in DAL
local_topics.description: Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreements (BALD) defines an acquisition function that selects data points expected to maximize information gained about the model parameters ω. In deep active learning, this means querying samples that are most informative with respect to the posterior over parameters, rather than merely uncertain predictions. The criterion explicitly links the selection of new data to improving knowledge of the model itself. This approach is formalized as α_BALD(x, M), which is computed for each candidate input x and model M.

local_topics.title: BALD-based naive batch construction
local_topics.description: A naive BMDAL approach repeatedly applies a one-by-one acquisition rule, such as BALD (Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement), to select the top-K highest-scoring samples. The BALD acquisition function sums mutual information terms I(yᵢ; ω | xᵢ, D_train) over batch elements, where mutual information is defined as predictive entropy minus expected conditional entropy over model parameters. Here, ω ∼ P(ω | D_train) represents Bayesian model parameters, H(·) is predictive entropy, and E[H(·)] averages entropy under the posterior. This approach treats each sample independently when forming the batch.

canonical_topic.name: BALD Information-Theoretic Acquisition in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement (BALD) defines an information-theoretic acquisition function that selects unlabeled samples by maximizing the mutual information between model predictions and model parameters. In deep active learning, BALD targets epistemic uncertainty, distinguishing it from simpler predictive entropy or margin-based measures, and is often approximated via Bayesian deep models such as MC Dropout. This acquisition function explicitly links query selection to expected reduction in posterior parameter uncertainty, formalized as α_BALD(x, M) for each candidate input. BALD is a core uncertainty-based strategy and is frequently contrasted with other information-theoretic measures like entropy and margin in DAL surveys. In batch-mode DAL, BALD is often naively extended by repeatedly applying the one-by-one acquisition rule to select the top-K highest-scoring samples, effectively summing per-sample mutual information terms while ignoring interactions within the batch.

Convolutional neural networks are trained in a pool-based AL setting, where the most informative unlabeled images (e.g., specific tissue types such as stroma, tumors, mucosa, and other structures) are selectively queried for expert annotation to reduce labeling costs while maintaining diagnostic performance. In biomedical and related domains such as plankton classification and automatic cell counting, uncertainty- or informativeness-based sampling is used to prioritize expensive expert labels, highlighting the value of DAL in high-stakes, annotation-intensive settings.

local_topics.title: Ensemble variance and diversity-based sampling
local_topics.description: This topic involves active learning with model ensembles where both uncertainty and diversity are considered in query selection. Variance across ensemble predictions serves as an uncertainty measure, while cover-based criteria and cosine similarity promote diversity among selected samples. A hybrid, multi-round strategy iteratively applies these measures to refine the labeled set over several active learning cycles.

local_topics.title: Ensemble variance for query selection
local_topics.description: Within the ensemble-based active learning framework, unlabeled instances are selected for querying based on having the largest ensemble variance across classifier predictions. This variance acts as a global uncertainty measure over time, yielding more robust sampling decisions than treating each chunk as an independent static dataset. By focusing labeling effort on instances with high disagreement among ensemble members, the method targets informative points for model improvement under streaming constraints.

canonical_topic.name: Ensemble-Based Uncertainty and Diversity Sampling
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that use ensembles to drive query selection via both uncertainty and diversity criteria. Ensemble variance, measured as disagreement across model predictions, is used as a robust uncertainty estimator to identify highly informative unlabeled instances. Diversity is promoted through cover-based criteria and similarity measures (e.g., cosine similarity) to avoid redundant queries and better explore the input space. These ideas are applied in both pool-based and streaming/online scenarios, where ensemble variance is treated as a global criterion over time rather than on isolated data chunks. Multi-round or cyclical selection strategies iteratively refine the labeled set by combining these uncertainty and diversity signals across successive active learning iterations.

local_topics.title: Motivation and scope of deep AL
local_topics.description: Deep Active Learning (DAL) arises from combining deep neural networks’ representation learning capabilities with active learning’s selective labeling to reduce annotation costs. DAL targets scenarios where collecting and annotating large training datasets for over-parameterized DNNs is expensive and time-consuming. It has been applied across diverse tasks such as named entity recognition, semantic parsing, object detection, image segmentation, and counting, and is supported by several unified DAL frameworks.

local_topics.title: Limitations of classic AL and DeepAL motivation
local_topics.description: Classic active learning algorithms are noted as struggling with high-dimensional data, limiting their applicability in modern deep learning contexts. At the same time, AL can theoretically yield exponential gains in labeling efficiency, creating a strong incentive to integrate it with DL. This motivates Deep Active Learning (DeepAL), which aims to combine DL’s representation power with AL’s label-efficiency to overcome high-dimensionality challenges and reduce annotation cost.

local_topics.title: Complementary strengths motivating DeepAL
local_topics.description: Deep Learning excels at high-dimensional data processing and automatic feature extraction, while Active Learning reduces labeling costs by querying informative samples. Combining them into Deep Active Learning (DeepAL) aims to leverage these complementary advantages to expand application potential. This topic covers the conceptual motivation and expectations behind integrating DL and AL into a unified framework.

local_topics.title: Combined strengths of DL and AL

It is particularly valuable in domains where labels are expensive and require high levels of expertise. This positions DeepAL as a promising approach for efficiently building high-performance models with limited labeled data.

canonical_topic.name: Motivation and Scope of Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: Deep Active Learning (DAL) combines deep neural networks’ representation learning capabilities with active learning’s selective querying to reduce annotation costs in data-hungry settings. It is motivated by the limitations of classic active learning on high-dimensional data and the high labeling demands of modern over-parameterized deep models. By leveraging deep learning to handle complex, high-dimensional inputs and active learning to prioritize the most informative samples, DAL aims to achieve strong performance with substantially fewer labeled examples. This paradigm is particularly attractive in domains where labels are expensive and require domain expertise, and it has been applied to tasks such as named entity recognition, semantic parsing, object detection, image segmentation, and counting. The field has also led to unified DAL frameworks that systematize these ideas and support practical deployment.

local_topics.title: Consistency regularization in semi-supervised training
local_topics.description: Consistency regularization is presented as another key perspective for combining active learning with semi-supervised learning. It typically enforces that the model’s predictions on unlabeled images remain stable under input perturbations or augmentations, serving as a regularization signal. Within an AL–SSL framework, consistently predicted unlabeled samples can further inform the model while labeled queries handle more ambiguous cases. This synergy helps improve robustness and generalization without proportionally increasing labeled data.

local_topics.title: Consistency regularization for unlabeled data
local_topics.description: Consistency regularization enforces that model outputs remain similar under perturbations of the input data or model parameters. This consistency objective is used as an unsupervised loss on unlabeled samples, which improves robustness, reduces overfitting, and enhances overall model performance. In deep active learning settings, it provides a way to exploit large pools of unlabeled data during training.
