local_topics.title: Pseudo-labeling with consistency and dual augmentations
local_topics.description: Another approach combines active learning with pseudo-labeling and consistency regularization using strong and weak data augmentations. Unlabeled images are first processed with both weak and strong augmentation pipelines; when the model’s prediction on the weakly augmented version exceeds a confidence threshold, that prediction is used as a pseudo-label. Consistency regularization then encourages agreement between predictions under the different augmentations, while AL governs which samples to label, jointly improving label efficiency.

local_topics.title: Consistency regularization with pseudo-labels
local_topics.description: Consistency regularization encourages the model to produce stable predictions for the same image under different perturbations or augmentations. When combined with pseudo-labels, the method pushes the network to match its pseudo-labeled predictions across these transformations, acting as a semi-supervised signal. In deep active learning, this helps leverage large pools of unlabeled medical images to improve robustness while still focusing expert labeling on the most uncertain samples.

canonical_topic.name: Consistency Regularization in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers how consistency regularization is integrated into deep active learning to better exploit large pools of unlabeled data. By enforcing that model predictions remain stable under input perturbations or weak/strong augmentations, consistency regularization provides an unsupervised or semi-supervised loss that improves robustness and reduces overfitting. Within an AL–SSL framework, confidently and consistently predicted unlabeled samples are used as additional training signals, while active learning focuses expert labeling on more ambiguous or uncertain instances. Pseudo-labeling is often combined with consistency losses, where confident predictions on weakly augmented images are treated as labels and the model is trained to match them across stronger augmentations. This synergy increases label efficiency, which is especially valuable in domains like medical imaging where annotations are costly.

local_topics.title: Active label cleaning for noisy annotations
local_topics.description: To address annotation noise in chest X-ray datasets, Bernhardt et al. (2022) proposed an active learning framework termed 'active label cleaning'. The method ranks samples according to estimated label-related properties, prioritizing potentially noisy or unreliable labels for corrective action. This integrates noise handling directly into the active learning process, aiming to improve label quality alongside model performance.

local_topics.title: Active learning to reduce label noise
local_topics.description: An active learning method is described that leverages correctness and labeling difficulty to guide query selection on chest X-ray data. By prioritizing samples that help correct noisy labels while being informative, the approach improves performance with fewer expert annotations than random selection. The focus is on mitigating label noise, which is common in large-scale medical image datasets.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Noisy Label Correction
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that explicitly target correction of noisy annotations in medical imaging datasets, particularly chest X-rays. Methods such as active label cleaning rank samples based on estimated label reliability, correctness, and labeling difficulty to prioritize instances with potentially incorrect or uncertain labels. By integrating noise detection and relabeling into the query strategy, these approaches jointly improve label quality and model performance under a limited expert annotation budget. Compared to random selection, they achieve better performance with fewer additional labels by focusing annotation efforts on the most suspect or impactful samples.

local_topics.title: Labeling bottleneck and active learning
local_topics.description: Collecting large-scale annotations for NLP tasks is expensive, labor-intensive, and often challenging, creating a labeling bottleneck. Active learning is introduced as an approach that allows a model to select which data points should be annotated, aiming to reach high accuracy using fewer labeled instances. This process explicitly targets the reduction of annotation cost while maintaining or improving model performance.

local_topics.description: Active learning is introduced as query learning that studies how to achieve maximal model performance gains while labeling as few samples as possible. It assumes samples differ in their value for updating the model and focuses on selecting the most informative instances from an unlabeled pool for annotation by an oracle (e.g., human annotator). local_topics.title: Active learning as cost-efficient labeling

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning for Annotation Cost Reduction
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on using active learning to alleviate the labeling bottleneck created by expensive and time‑consuming annotation, especially for large deep learning models in domains such as NLP, medical imaging, and remote sensing. Deep active learning frameworks iteratively select the most informative unlabeled samples from a pool or stream, query an oracle (typically a human expert), and retrain the model, aiming to match or approach the performance of fully supervised training with far fewer labels. Query strategies are designed to balance labeling cost and model quality by exploiting differences in the value of individual samples for updating the model. In medical image analysis and segmentation, where expert annotations by radiologists or pathologists are particularly scarce and costly, DAL is emphasized as a core component of practical deep learning workflows. Across domains, the central objective is to maximize performance gains per labeled instance, thereby reducing annotation budgets while maintaining or improving model accuracy.

canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the integration of deep active learning with interactive segmentation in medical image analysis, where clinicians iteratively refine model-generated segmentations. Instead of allowing completely free placement of user annotations (clicks, scribbles, bounding boxes), active learning is used to propose the most informative pixels or regions for interaction, tailoring the acquisition strategy to dense, pixel-level labeling tasks. By focusing expert input on high-uncertainty or high-impact areas, the active learning loop reduces annotation difficulty and cost while improving adaptation to domain shifts and unseen regions of interest. The model thus becomes a proactive assistant during annotation, suggesting and updating segmentations based on expert corrections within a DAL-driven feedback cycle.

canonical_topic.name: Integrating Deep Active Learning with Label-Efficient Paradigms
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers frameworks that combine deep active learning with other label-efficient learning paradigms to further reduce annotation requirements. Methods integrate active querying with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to exploit large pools of unlabeled data while selectively labeling only the most informative samples. Other approaches leverage transfer learning and domain adaptation to reuse knowledge from related domains, and region-based annotation schemes that query subregions (e.g., image patches) instead of full instances to save labeling effort. Generative models are also used for data augmentation or synthetic sample generation, complementing active selection. Overall, these synergistic designs target data-scarce, high-cost annotation settings such as medical imaging and NLP, where combining acquisition strategies with alternative supervision forms is particularly beneficial.

local_topics.title: Uncertainty-based Query Strategies
local_topics.description: This topic covers methods that select informative samples based on model uncertainty estimates in deep active learning. It includes gradient-based uncertainty, performance estimation techniques, uncertainty-aware model architectures, and adversarial-based uncertainty measures. These approaches typically rely on model outputs, gradients, or adversarial perturbations to quantify how unsure the model is about each unlabeled instance and prioritize them for annotation.

local_topics.title: Uncertainty-based query strategies
local_topics.description: Multiple works characterize informativeness by model uncertainty, using single-model scores such as entropy, margin, and least confidence, or gradient-based uncertainty derived from network gradients. Some methods extend this with adversarial samples to probe decision boundaries or with multiple inferences to measure data disagreement via inequality-based metrics. Other works frame uncertainty as performance estimation, learning surrogate or directly learnable estimators (e.g., using Dice) to predict per-sample segmentation quality. These uncertainty scores drive which instances are selected for annotation in each active learning round.

local_topics.description: Uncertainty-based querying strategies select samples for annotation where the current deep model is least confident in its predictions. These methods estimate predictive uncertainty using model outputs or internal representations, assuming that labeling such ambiguous instances will most improve the model. They are central in deep active learning because they directly target the model’s decision boundaries. Typical implementations rely on probability distributions over classes or Bayesian uncertainty estimates.

Typical uncertainty measures include prediction entropy, margin, or confidence scores. local_topics.title: Uncertainty-based sampling with margin and entropy
local_topics.description: Uncertainty-based query strategies select samples that the current model finds most uncertain, and are especially common in shallow models such as SVMs and KNN. Margin sampling defines uncertainty via the difference between the highest and second-highest predicted class probabilities, with smaller margins indicating more uncertain samples, and selects the top-K smallest margins. Entropy-based sampling measures uncertainty using the Shannon entropy of the predictive class distribution and selects samples with the highest entropy, with both approaches forming standard baselines for batch construction.

local_topics.title: Uncertainty and diversity query strategies
local_topics.description: Deep active learning is currently centered on query strategies that explicitly or implicitly combine uncertainty-based and diversity-based sample selection. Uncertainty measures how unsure the model is about a sample's label, while diversity aims to cover varied regions of the input space to avoid redundancy. Hybrid selection strategies that jointly consider both criteria are increasingly favored by researchers as they better balance informativeness and coverage.

local_topics.title: Uncertainty-based query strategies

In classification settings, these approaches often rely on measures such as decision margins or related confidence scores to identify ambiguous points. By querying labels for these uncertain examples, the model is expected to learn decision boundaries more efficiently.

canonical_topic.name: Uncertainty-Based Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on deep active learning strategies that rank unlabeled instances by how uncertain a model is about their predicted labels. Core approaches use single-model uncertainty scores such as least confidence, margin, and entropy, often computed from the softmax output of deep networks. More advanced DAL methods derive uncertainty from gradients, adversarial perturbations probing decision boundaries, or performance-estimation surrogates (e.g., Dice-based quality predictors for segmentation) to approximate per-sample expected improvement. In both pool-based and stream-based settings, these uncertainty scores drive which samples are queried under a limited annotation budget, but can introduce sampling bias if the most uncertain points are not representative of the overall data distribution. Consequently, recent work increasingly combines uncertainty with diversity criteria to form hybrid selection strategies that better balance informativeness and coverage.

They typically construct a joint acquisition function or a two-stage procedure: first filtering by uncertainty and then refining by diversity (or vice versa). This helps avoid pathological selections where many similar uncertain samples are chosen. The goal is to maximize expected information gain under a labeling budget.

local_topics.title: Uncertainty-based and hybrid query strategies
local_topics.description: Uncertainty-based strategies rank unlabeled samples by model uncertainty and preferentially query the most uncertain ones, assuming these will most improve the model. However, focusing solely on uncertainty can ignore relationships among samples, such as diversity or representativeness. Hybrid strategies incorporate multiple attributes—e.g., uncertainty plus diversity or density—to better balance informativeness and coverage of the data space. This reflects a move from single-criterion to multi-criterion query design in DeepAL.

canonical_topic.name: Hybrid Uncertainty–Diversity Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers hybrid query strategies that jointly exploit uncertainty and diversity criteria in deep active learning. Instead of relying solely on uncertainty, which can lead to many redundant queries around the same decision boundary region, these methods explicitly encourage selection of informative yet non-redundant samples. They often implement a joint acquisition function or a staged pipeline, for example first filtering candidates by high uncertainty and then subselecting a diverse subset, or the reverse. By balancing informativeness with representativeness of the unlabeled data distribution, these hybrid strategies mitigate sampling bias from pure uncertainty sampling and avoid wasting labeling budget on low-information but diverse points. Overall, they reflect a broader move from single-criterion to multi-criterion query design in DeepAL.

local_topics.title: Pseudo-labeling for AL–SSL integration
local_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling is identified as one perspective for integrating active learning and semi-supervised learning. In such approaches, the model assigns tentative labels to unlabeled medical images, which are then used as additional training targets alongside truly labeled data. Active learning can govern which samples receive true labels versus pseudo-labels, balancing reliability and coverage. This mechanism enables the exploitation of large unlabeled pools without fully relying on expert annotation.

local_topics.title: Pseudo-labeling in semi-supervised learning
local_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling uses a model’s own predictions on unlabeled data as surrogate labels and combines them with labeled data for supervised training. This approach can leverage large unlabeled datasets but risks introducing noisy labels when predictions are unreliable. The method is a foundational strategy in semi-supervised learning pipelines and underpins several deep active learning extensions discussed in this section.

local_topics.title: Pseudo-labeling to augment labeled data
local_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling assigns provisional labels to unlabeled samples using the current model, treating confident predictions as additional training data. In an active learning context, pseudo-labels can be combined with human-annotated data to improve representation learning while focusing expensive queries on truly uncertain cases. This reduces the effective labeling cost while still leveraging the large pool of unlabeled images.

local_topics.title: Pseudo-Labeling within Active Learning Loops
local_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling assigns model-predicted labels to unlabeled samples to augment the training set without explicit annotation. In the context of active learning, pseudo-labeled data can be combined with truly labeled examples, while the querying mechanism focuses on the most uncertain or diverse cases. This synergy can reduce labeling costs while still improving model performance.

local_topics.title: Pseudo-labeling of unlabeled medical images
local_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling assigns labels to unlabeled images using the current model’s predictions, treating high-confidence predictions as if they were ground truth. These pseudo-labeled samples are then included in training to effectively expand the labeled dataset without manual annotation. In deep active learning for medical imaging, this strategy complements queried labels to improve data efficiency.

local_topics.title: Pseudo-Labeling High-Confidence Samples

canonical_topic.name: Pseudo-Labeling in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the integration of pseudo-labeling into deep active learning pipelines, especially for medical image analysis. In these approaches, the model assigns labels to unlabeled samples when its predictions are sufficiently confident, expanding the effective labeled set without additional expert effort. Active learning then prioritizes truly ambiguous or diverse cases for manual annotation, while pseudo-labeled data provide broader coverage of the unlabeled pool. This AL–SSL synergy aims to reduce annotation cost, mitigate label scarcity, and improve representation learning by jointly exploiting queried labels and reliably pseudo-labeled examples. Across implementations, pseudo-labeling is embedded directly within the active learning loop, iteratively refining the model as both human and pseudo labels accumulate.

local_topics.title: Semi-supervised learning with unlabeled data
local_topics.description: Semi-supervised learning aims to improve model performance by leveraging large quantities of unlabeled data alongside a smaller labeled set. In this context, it is positioned as an extension of supervised deep learning, where unlabeled medical images help regularize and guide the model beyond what purely labeled data could achieve. The approach is particularly relevant when annotation is costly and limited, as in medical imaging. It serves as a foundational concept for later integration with active learning.

local_topics.title: Semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labels
local_topics.description: Unlabeled images undergo weak augmentation to generate predictions that are treated as pseudo-labels. Strongly augmented versions of the same images are then trained to match these pseudo-labels, enforcing consistency between weak and strong augmentations. This semi-supervised scheme exploits abundant unlabeled data while maintaining label efficiency.

local_topics.description: Active learning for medical image segmentation typically leaves many samples unlabeled after each selection cycle. By integrating active learning with semi-supervised learning, these remaining unlabeled samples can be exploited to further improve model performance. local_topics.title: Complementarity of active and semi-supervised learning
local_topics.description: Active learning and semi-supervised learning are described as complementary strategies for reducing human annotation effort in medical image analysis. Active learning focuses on querying the most informative samples for labeling, while semi-supervised learning exploits the remaining unlabeled samples to further improve performance. Their combination is motivated by the desire to reduce tedious expert annotations from doctors. This complementarity underpins the proposed integrated training frameworks.

canonical_topic.name: Integrating Deep Active Learning with Semi/Self-Supervision
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on combining deep active learning with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to better exploit the large pool of unlabeled medical images between query rounds. In these frameworks, active learning selects the most informative samples for expert annotation, while semi-supervised methods (e.g., pseudo-labeling and consistency regularization) leverage the remaining unlabeled data to further improve model performance. Self-supervised learning is used to learn rich representations from unlabeled images that can enhance the effectiveness of subsequent active querying. The overall goal is to increase label efficiency and reduce costly expert annotations by jointly optimizing query strategies and unlabeled-data utilization within the active learning loop.

local_topics.title: Semi-supervised learning with active learning
local_topics.description: Semi-supervised learning is combined with active learning by exploiting the unlabeled pool via self-training, pseudo-labeling, and EM-based estimation. Unlabeled instances are assigned estimated labels or confidence scores and then used in training alongside actively labeled data. Additional strategies include using unsupervised algorithms to identify unambiguous instances for the active learner and applying AL on top of inherently unsupervised tasks like word alignment, where a small amount of supervision can yield further data-efficient gains.

local_topics.title: Relationship between active and semi-supervised learning
local_topics.description: Active learning is framed as a special case of semi-supervised learning, where a learner not only exploits unlabeled data but also actively selects which instances to query for labels. Semi-supervised techniques on data streams, such as those surveyed by Kulkarni et al. (2016), focus on leveraging unlabeled instances for classification but do not answer the core active learning question of when to query. Combining semi-supervised methods with active learning can improve data selection strategies, model updating, and retraining under limited labeled data, yielding more efficient learning than either approach alone.

canonical_topic.name: Integrating Semi-Supervised Learning with Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers methods that combine active learning with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to better exploit large unlabeled pools. Deep models are trained jointly on actively queried labels and pseudo-labeled or otherwise unlabeled data, using mechanisms such as self-training, EM-based estimation, and consistency regularization. These hybrid approaches are applied both in pool-based DAL (e.g., for medical images) and in streaming scenarios, where unlabeled stream instances are used for semi-supervised updates while only a subset is queried. Framing active learning as a special case of semi-supervised learning clarifies how leveraging unlabeled data can reshape sample informativeness and improve query strategies across AL cycles. Overall, such integrations aim to increase data efficiency and generalization under tight annotation budgets beyond what either paradigm can achieve alone.

local_topics.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for adaptation
local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems are a class of fuzzy systems that can adapt and change over time in response to new data or environmental changes. They dynamically modify their internal structure, particularly rules and membership functions, to maintain performance in non-stationary settings. This adaptability makes them suitable for streaming and continually changing data scenarios.

local_topics.title: Contrast with traditional fixed fuzzy systems
local_topics.description: Traditional fuzzy systems rely on fixed rules and membership functions that do not change once defined, limiting their ability to cope with evolving data distributions. In contrast, evolving fuzzy systems explicitly adjust these components based on incoming data, enabling continual learning. This comparison highlights the key structural and behavioral differences between static and adaptive fuzzy paradigms.

Example applications include control systems for autonomous vehicles that must adapt to varying traffic patterns, road conditions, and weather. local_topics.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for streaming data
local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems (EFS) are presented as soft-computing models tailored to time-varying data streams, capable of dealing with novelty and ongoing knowledge expansion. They are self-developing, self-learning fuzzy rule-based or neuro-fuzzy systems that adapt both their parameters and structure on the fly as new data arrive. By dynamically growing and updating fuzzy rule bases, EFS aim to mimic human-like reasoning over data streams through a formal learning process. This provides an alternative paradigm for handling evolving concepts compared to traditional parametric models.

local_topics.title: Evolving Fuzzy Systems architecture
local_topics.description: Evolving Fuzzy Systems (EFS) use fuzzy rules of the form mapping input variables to outputs via parametric consequents, with each rule associated to prototypes (focal points) and parameters. Their architecture includes a structure-evolving scheme and a parameter-updating scheme that together maintain and adapt the rule base. With every new labeled example, these learning modules update both structure and parameters to track the evolution of the data stream in an online manner.

local_topics.title: Rule generation, merging, and pruning in EFS
local_topics.description: The structure-evolving scheme in an EFS decides when to add new fuzzy rules, based on criteria indicating that the current rule base is insufficient to model new data. It also merges rules whose similarity exceeds a threshold and prunes redundant rules, thereby simplifying the model while preserving performance. This process controls model complexity in streaming settings where concepts and data distributions change over time.

local_topics.title: Overlap and novelty in fuzzy rule antecedents
local_topics.description: In evolving fuzzy rule-based models, the overlap degree in the antecedent space is used to reduce the number of data points that fall into regions where two rules overlap, thereby improving rule distinctiveness and reducing ambiguity. Novelty content in the antecedent space quantifies how much new information incoming data bring, guiding when rule evolution or knowledge expansion is needed. Together, these measures steer the adaptive refinement of the fuzzy rule base in data streams.

canonical_topic.name: Batch Active Learning with Costly Field Surveys
canonical_topic.description: This topic addresses active learning scenarios in remote sensing where labels are obtained through expensive field or ground surveys, severely limiting the number of pixels that can be annotated. Because only a few labeling iterations are feasible, each must involve relatively large batches of samples, pushing active learning towards compact yet highly informative training sets. In this regime, common heuristics (e.g., MCLU, BT, EQB) tend to converge to similar performance, making the spatial design of sampling—rather than the exact uncertainty heuristic—the dominant factor. Spatially adaptive cost functions and constraints are used to maximize spatial separation among queried points, balancing acquisition cost and information gain. Ground-truth collected via terrain campaigns remains essential both for training the model (which may be deep or shallow) and for rigorously evaluating active learning strategies under strict annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Fixed-confidence and fixed-budget linear bandits
local_topics.description: Subsequent work on pure exploration linear bandits distinguishes fixed-confidence and fixed-budget settings. Jedra and Proutiere propose algorithms that, given a target confidence level, adaptively sample arms until the best arm can be identified with that confidence. Azizi et al. study the complementary fixed-budget case, determining how to optimally use a given number of pulls, and extend the framework to generalized linear models, broadening the class of reward-generating processes beyond simple linearity.

local_topics.title: Fixed-confidence evaluation in bandit algorithms
local_topics.description: In the fixed-confidence setting for bandit algorithms, the goal is typically to identify the best arm with a guaranteed confidence level under a limited budget. Performance is assessed by relating label complexity—the number of labeled observations required—to factors such as problem dimensionality or the number of arms pulled. This framing emphasizes sample efficiency and theoretical bounds on how many interactions are needed to reach a target confidence.

canonical_topic.name: Fixed-Confidence and Fixed-Budget Bandits for Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers pure-exploration bandit formulations, especially linear and generalized linear bandits, used to model query selection under labeling constraints. The key distinction is between fixed-confidence settings, where the learner adaptively samples arms until the best arm is identified with a prescribed confidence level, and fixed-budget settings, where the learner must optimally allocate a pre-specified number of pulls. These frameworks allow analysis of label complexity by relating the number of required labeled observations to properties such as the dimensionality of the feature space or the number of arms. In the context of active learning for data streams, they provide a principled way to reason about budgeted querying and performance guarantees, aligning bandit-style sampling strategies with accuracy or confidence targets.

local_topics.title: Linear margin-based online prediction
local_topics.description: The learner uses a linear predictor parameterized by a weight vector w ∈ R^d to classify each incoming instance in a data stream. At time t, after observing xt, the predicted label is the sign of the inner product wᵀ_{t−1} xt, and this inner product defines the margin p_t. The margin quantifies the confidence of the current model on xt and later serves as a key quantity in the querying rule.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Second-order online active learning
local_topics.description: Second-order online active learning augments traditional margin-based (first-order) strategies by explicitly modeling the classifier’s parameter uncertainty. The weight vector w ∈ R^d is assumed to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution w ~ N(μ, Σ), where μ encodes the current estimate and the variances and covariances in Σ encode confidence about each feature weight and their dependencies. This allows the method to consider both the margin value and the associated uncertainty when deciding whether to query a label and update the model.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

canonical_topic.name: Margin-Based and Second-Order Online Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers stream-based active learning where a learner processes instances sequentially and decides online whether to query their labels. Linear margin-based prediction is used to define a confidence score for each incoming instance via the inner product between the current weight vector and the input, and this margin is central to the querying rule. Beyond first-order methods, second-order online active learning models the classifier’s weight vector as a multivariate Gaussian, explicitly capturing uncertainty through the covariance matrix. This probabilistic view allows query decisions to consider both the predicted margin and the parameter uncertainty, leading to more informed label requests under a streaming, budget-constrained setting. Such methods provide a principled foundation for stream-based acquisition strategies that can be extended or adapted to more complex (e.g., deep) models.

local_topics.title: Adaptive Maximum Disagreement query rule
local_topics.description: The Adaptive Maximum Disagreement (AMD) heuristic selects unlabeled samples whose predictions across views are most uncertain according to a multiview entropy criterion. Formally, given a partition of the d-dimensional input space into V views, AMD selects the candidate ˆxAMD in the unlabeled pool U that maximizes HMV(xi). This aligns active learning with areas where committee members (views) disagree the most, focusing labeling effort on the most informative pixels. AMD thus operationalizes disagreement in a principled, entropy-based way.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: Candidate subset selection to reduce computation
local_topics.description: To alleviate computational cost, the AMD approach restricts selection to a subset of the unlabeled pool containing only the most uncertain pixels. Specifically, candidate pixels are those for which the committee (the set of view-based classifiers) has predicted the largest number of distinct classes, indicating high disagreement. AMD is then applied within this reduced subset, maintaining informativeness while lowering processing effort. This strategy balances query quality and scalability for large remote sensing datasets.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

canonical_topic.name: Adaptive Maximum Disagreement for Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers the Adaptive Maximum Disagreement (AMD) query rule, a disagreement-based active learning strategy defined over multiple views or committee members. AMD selects unlabeled samples that maximize a multiview entropy criterion, thereby targeting regions of the input space where the committee’s predictions most strongly disagree. This operationalizes disagreement in a principled way, using entropy over view-specific predictions to guide label queries. To maintain scalability on large unlabeled pools (e.g., dense pixel-level remote sensing data), AMD can be restricted to a candidate subset consisting of points for which the committee predicts the largest number of distinct classes, indicating high disagreement. By first filtering to this highly contentious subset and then applying AMD, the method preserves query informativeness while reducing computational cost, a consideration directly relevant to deep active learning systems operating on large-scale data.

local_topics.title: Batch selection of informative pixels
local_topics.description: The algorithm selects a batch of q pixels S^ε from the ranked pool at each iteration. These pixels are chosen to jointly maximize expected performance gain and reduce model uncertainty when incorporated into the training set. Once labeled, the batch is added to X^ε and removed from U^ε, ensuring progressive refinement of the labeled set.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

local_topics.title: General diversity-based batch selection algorithm
local_topics.description: Algorithm 2 formalizes a generic procedure for diversity-based selection in a single active learning iteration. Starting from a reduced candidate set U* (already filtered by a base heuristic like margin sampling), the algorithm first picks the best candidate under the base criterion, then repeatedly adds samples that maximize a user-defined diversity measure with respect to the current batch S. After q pixels are selected, the batch is labeled, added to the training set, and removed from the candidate pool. This process operationalizes batch-mode active learning where exploitation (uncertainty) and exploration (diversity) are explicitly balanced.
local_topics.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

canonical_topic.name: Batch-Mode Uncertainty and Diversity Selection
canonical_topic.description: This topic focuses on batch-mode active learning strategies that jointly consider informativeness and diversity when querying new samples, here illustrated at the pixel level for remote sensing imagery. At each iteration, a batch of q samples is selected from a ranked pool to maximize expected performance gain and reduce model uncertainty once their labels are acquired. A generic diversity-based algorithm first narrows the candidate set using a base uncertainty heuristic (e.g., margin sampling), then greedily constructs a batch by adding samples that maximize a user-defined diversity measure with respect to the already selected items. This explicitly balances exploitation (selecting the most uncertain instances) and exploration (covering varied regions of the input space) within each batch, which is crucial when labels are expensive and queries must be made in groups. The labeled batch is then incorporated into the training set and removed from the pool, enabling progressive refinement of the model—a procedure directly applicable to deep active learning settings where mini-batch querying is standard.

local_topics.title: Intra- and extra-cluster sampling for batch streams
local_topics.description: Ienco et al. (2013) adapt a pre-clustering-based active learning method from pool-based to stream-based batch scenarios where only part of each block can be labeled. Their sampling strategy uses an extra-cluster metric to rank clusters and an intra-cluster metric to rank instances, relying on cluster homogeneity (number of predicted classes) to detect uncertain clusters and on representativeness (distance to centroid) and posterior-class probabilities to measure instance certainty. The learner alternates label queries across ranked clusters and their top-ranked instances.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Micro-cluster based adaptive stream classification
local_topics.description: Yin et al. (2023) propose a data stream classification method that maintains and updates micro-clusters built from initial training data. local_topics.title: Margin sampling heuristic for SVMs
local_topics.description: Margin sampling (MS) exploits the geometric properties of SVMs, particularly that unbounded support vectors lie exactly on the margin with decision function value equal to one. The heuristic selects unlabeled samples whose minimum absolute distance to any class hyperplane is smallest, i.e., they are closest to some decision boundary. Formally, it chooses the unlabeled point minimizing the inner minimum over classes of |f(x_i, ω)|, where f(x_i, ω) is the SVM decision function (distance) for class ω. This operationalizes the idea of querying the most uncertain instances near the margin.

local_topics.title: Relationship between active and semi-supervised learning
local_topics.description: Active learning is framed as a special case of semi-supervised learning, where a learner not only exploits unlabeled data but also actively selects which instances to query for labels. Semi-supervised techniques on data streams, such as those surveyed by Kulkarni et al. (2016), focus on leveraging unlabeled instances for classification but do not answer the core active learning question of when to query. Combining semi-supervised methods with active learning can improve data selection strategies, model updating, and retraining under limited labeled data, yielding more efficient learning than either approach alone.

canonical_topic.name: Integrating Active and Semi-Supervised Learning in Deep AL
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers hybrid methods that combine active learning with semi-supervised and self-supervised training to better exploit large unlabeled pools. Unlabeled instances are leveraged via pseudo-labeling, self-training, EM-based label estimation, and consistency regularization, and then incorporated into training alongside actively queried labels. In deep active learning cycles, these semi-supervised components operate both within and across iterations, improving sample efficiency and representation quality as the labeled set grows. The connection is also explored in streaming scenarios, where incoming unlabeled stream data is used for semi-supervised updates while only a subset of informative instances is actively queried. Framing active learning as a special case of semi-supervised learning clarifies how exploiting unlabeled data and deciding when to query labels can be jointly optimized for better data-efficient performance.

local_topics.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for adaptation
local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems are a class of fuzzy systems that can adapt and change over time in response to new data or environmental changes. They dynamically modify their internal structure, particularly rules and membership functions, to maintain performance in non-stationary settings. This adaptability makes them suitable for streaming and continually changing data scenarios.

local_topics.title: Contrast with traditional fixed fuzzy systems
local_topics.description: Traditional fuzzy systems rely on fixed rules and membership functions that do not change once defined, limiting their ability to cope with evolving data distributions. In contrast, evolving fuzzy systems explicitly adjust these components based on incoming data, enabling continual learning. This comparison highlights the key structural and behavioral differences between static and adaptive fuzzy paradigms.

local_topics.title: Handling non-stationary environments and applications
local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems are positioned as particularly useful in non-stationary environments where data characteristics change over time. Example applications include control systems for autonomous vehicles that must adapt to varying traffic patterns, road conditions, and weather. The systems’ ability to update their rule base and membership functions allows robust performance under such dynamic operating conditions.

local_topics.title: Evolving fuzzy systems for streaming data
local_topics.description: Evolving fuzzy systems (EFS) are presented as soft-computing models tailored to time-varying data streams, capable of dealing with novelty and ongoing knowledge expansion. They are self-developing, self-learning fuzzy rule-based or neuro-fuzzy systems that adapt both their parameters and structure on the fly as new data arrive. By dynamically growing and updating fuzzy rule bases, EFS aim to mimic human-like reasoning over data streams through a formal learning process. This provides an alternative paradigm for handling evolving concepts compared to traditional parametric models.

local_topics.title: Evolving Fuzzy Systems architecture
local_topics.description: Evolving Fuzzy Systems (EFS) use fuzzy rules of the form mapping input variables to outputs via parametric consequents, with each rule associated to prototypes (focal points) and parameters. Their architecture includes a structure-evolving scheme and a parameter-updating scheme that together maintain and adapt the rule base. With every new labeled example, these learning modules update both structure and parameters to track the evolution of the data stream in an online manner.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Rule generation, merging, and pruning in EFS
local_topics.description: The structure-evolving scheme in an EFS decides when to add new fuzzy rules, based on criteria indicating that the current rule base is insufficient to model new data. It also merges rules whose similarity exceeds a threshold and prunes redundant rules, thereby simplifying the model while preserving performance. This process controls model complexity in streaming settings where concepts and data distributions change over time.
local_topics.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Overlap and novelty in fuzzy rule antecedents
local_topics.description: In evolving fuzzy rule-based models, the overlap degree in the antecedent space is used to reduce the number of data points that fall into regions where two rules overlap, thereby improving rule distinctiveness and reducing ambiguity. Novelty content in the antecedent space quantifies how much new information incoming data bring, guiding when rule evolution or knowledge expansion is needed. Together, these measures steer the adaptive refinement of the fuzzy rule base in data streams.

local_topics.title: Semi-supervised learning with unlabeled data
local_topics.description: Semi-supervised learning aims to improve model performance by leveraging large quantities of unlabeled data alongside a smaller labeled set. In this context, it is positioned as an extension of supervised deep learning, where unlabeled medical images help regularize and guide the model beyond what purely labeled data could achieve. The approach is particularly relevant when annotation is costly and limited, as in medical imaging. It serves as a foundational concept for later integration with active learning.

local_topics.title: Semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labels
local_topics.description: Unlabeled images undergo weak augmentation to generate predictions that are treated as pseudo-labels. Strongly augmented versions of the same images are then trained to match these pseudo-labels, enforcing consistency between weak and strong augmentations. This semi-supervised scheme exploits abundant unlabeled data while maintaining label efficiency.

canonical_topic.name: Semi-Supervised Learning with Unlabeled Data in DAL
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers how semi-supervised learning leverages large pools of unlabeled data alongside a limited labeled set to improve model performance and label efficiency in deep learning, particularly in medical imaging where annotations are costly. Within deep active learning pipelines, these methods provide a way to exploit the unlabeled pool beyond mere sample selection, serving as a foundational component that complements active query strategies. One prominent approach is pseudo-labeling, where predictions on weakly augmented unlabeled images are treated as labels, and the model is trained to match these pseudo-labels on strongly augmented versions of the same images, enforcing consistency. Such consistency-based semi-supervised schemes help regularize the model and make better use of scarce annotations, aligning well with the budget-conscious goals of deep active learning.

Their combination is motivated by the desire to reduce tedious expert annotations from doctors. This complementarity underpins the proposed integrated training frameworks.

canonical_topic.name: Deep Active Learning with Semi- and Self-Supervision
canonical_topic.description: This topic concerns the integration of deep active learning with semi-supervised and self-supervised methods to better exploit large pools of unlabeled medical images. In these frameworks, active learning selects the most informative samples for expert annotation, while semi-supervised learning leverages the remaining unlabeled data (e.g., via pseudo-labeling and consistency regularization) between query rounds to further improve performance. The combination aims to maximize label efficiency in medical image analysis and segmentation, reducing the overall annotation burden on clinicians. Such integrated training pipelines explicitly treat active and semi-/self-supervised learning as complementary components: acquisition functions drive selective labeling under a budget, and semi-/self-supervised objectives extract additional signal from the unlabeled pool throughout the active learning cycle.

Additional strategies include using unsupervised algorithms to identify unambiguous instances for the active learner and applying AL on top of inherently unsupervised tasks like word alignment, where a small amount of supervision can yield further data-efficient gains.

canonical_topic.name: Semi- and Self-Supervised Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers methods that integrate semi-supervised and self-supervised learning with deep active learning to better exploit large pools or streams of unlabeled data. Unlabeled instances are used with pseudo-labeling, self-training, EM-based estimation, and consistency regularization so that they contribute to model training alongside selectively queried ground-truth labels, improving sample efficiency and generalization across AL cycles. In pool-based DAL, these techniques modify how informativeness is estimated and how the acquisition function values unlabeled samples, while in stream-based settings, unlabeled stream instances can be continuously used for semi-supervised updates and only a subset is queried. Conceptually, active learning can be viewed as a special case of semi-supervised learning that additionally asks when to query labels, and hybrid approaches explicitly combine both paradigms to better allocate limited annotation budgets. Such combinations are used in NLP and medical imaging applications, and surveys highlight them as a key direction for reducing reliance on expensive manual labels in deep active learning pipelines.

canonical_topic.name: Integrating Semi-/Self-Supervised Learning with Deep Active Learning
canonical_topic.description: This topic covers hybrid methods that combine deep active learning with semi-supervised or self-supervised learning to better exploit large pools or streams of unlabeled data. Beyond querying labels for a small subset of instances, these approaches use pseudo-labels, self-training, EM-based estimation, and consistency regularization so that unlabeled examples can contribute to representation learning and model refinement between active learning queries. In pool-based DAL, jointly training on actively labeled data and model-generated labels alters the informativeness of remaining unlabeled samples and thus interacts with the acquisition strategy. In stream-based settings, incoming unlabeled instances may first be used for semi-supervised updates, while only a carefully chosen subset is queried, effectively viewing active learning as a special case of semi-supervised learning where the system controls which labels to acquire. Overall, these hybrids aim to increase data efficiency and generalization across AL cycles, especially under tight annotation budgets.
